title: How to buy safely on Marktplaats
meta_title: How to buy safely on Marktplaats: a practical checklist
description: How to buy safely on Marktplaats: check the seller, pick a safe way to pay, inspect at pickup and spot red flags before any money leaves your account.
intro: The safest way to buy on Marktplaats is to see the item, test it, and pay at the moment you take it home. Almost every bad story starts with paying in advance to someone you never met, or clicking a link a stranger sent you. Keep those two habits out of your routine and most of the risk disappears.

sections.heading: Default to pickup and pay on the spot
paragraphs: For anything you can reach within an hour, go and collect it. You see the condition with your own eyes, you can test it, and the money only moves when the item is in your hands. Dutch sellers expect this: the phrase is gelijk oversteken, which means both sides hand over at the same time.

Pay with cash, or with a bank transfer or payment request made in front of the seller and confirmed on their phone before you leave. For items over a few hundred euro, a bank transfer is easier to trace than cash if something turns out to be stolen.

sections.heading: Look at the listing before you message
paragraphs: A listing tells you a lot if you read it slowly. Photos taken in a home, from different angles, with the same background across the seller's other ads, are a good sign. Stock photos, a single blurry shot, or pictures that show up elsewhere on the web are not.
bullets: Price far below every similar listing
Text copied from a shop or in odd, machine translated Dutch
Seller says they are abroad, at sea or working away and can only ship
Account created this week with no other ads or reviews
Pressure: 'many people are interested, pay now to reserve'

sections.heading: Keep the conversation inside Marktplaats
paragraphs: Scammers like to move you to WhatsApp or email quickly, because their messages there are not visible to Marktplaats. Ask your questions in the Marktplaats chat first. Exchange phone numbers only when you are arranging the pickup time.
Never click a payment or shipping link someone sends you, even if it looks like a Marktplaats or bank page. If you want to pay through the platform, start that from inside the app yourself.

sections.heading: At the pickup: a short checklist
paragraphs: Take five minutes. A friendly seller will not mind, and a seller who does mind has told you something.
bullets: Switch it on, plug it in, open every drawer and door
Check serial or frame numbers match what the seller said
Look for damage hidden by the photo angle: back panels, undersides, corners
Ask for the receipt or box for electronics and branded bikes
Count the cash or confirm the transfer before you load it

sections.heading: When shipping is the only option
paragraphs: Sometimes the item is in Groningen and you live in Maastricht. Then use a payment method that holds the money until delivery, such as a pay-and-ship option offered inside the Marktplaats app when the seller enables it. Check the current terms in the app, since they change. A plain bank transfer to a stranger for a shipped item gives you very little protection.

sections.heading: Watch for stolen goods
paragraphs: A new phone sold without a box, a high-end bike for 150 euro, or a seller who wants to meet in a car park instead of at home are the classic signs. Buying stolen goods knowingly is a crime in the Netherlands, and even unknowingly you can lose the item without a refund. For bikes, phones and laptops you can check a serial number in the police Stop Heling register before you pay.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Yes, for the large majority of deals, especially when you pick up and pay on the spot. Most problems come from paying in advance for items that are shipped or from clicking links sent by the other party.

faq.q: Should I pay cash or by bank transfer?
faq.a: Both are fine at a pickup as long as the money moves when you take the item. Bank transfers leave a trace, which helps if the item later turns out to be stolen.

faq.q: Can I get my money back if I was scammed on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Report it to the police and to your bank straight away, and report the account to Marktplaats. Recovery is not guaranteed, so prevention matters more than the refund route.

faq.q: Is it safe to give my address to a Marktplaats seller?
faq.a: When you are buying you usually go to them, so you rarely need to share it. For shipped items, your address is needed, but never share bank login codes or card details.

example_wish: Used dishwasher, 60 cm wide, working, under 150 euro, pickup within 15 km of Utrecht

title: Marktplaats scams to avoid as a buyer
meta_title: Marktplaats scams to avoid: how buyers get caught
description: The Marktplaats scams that hit buyers most: fake payment links, advance payment, hijacked accounts and stolen goods, and the signs that give each away.
intro: As a buyer, nearly every Marktplaats scam comes down to one of two things: you pay for something that never arrives, or you click a link that steals your bank or card details. Each scam has a recognizable script. Learn the scripts and you will spot them in the first two messages.

sections.heading: The ship-only bargain
paragraphs: A popular item, often a phone, console, e-bike or designer bag, priced 30 to 50 percent under the going rate. The seller cannot meet: they moved, they work offshore, their mother is ill. They ask for a bank transfer and promise to post it with track and trace.

The money goes to a mule account and the parcel never comes, or a box arrives with a brick or a cheap copy inside. The tell is the combination of low price plus no pickup. One alone can be innocent. Both together almost never are.

sections.heading: The fake payment or delivery link
paragraphs: The 'seller' sends a link to a page that looks like Marktplaats, PostNL, DHL or your bank, asking you to pay through it, or to 'confirm your account' with a small amount like 1 cent. The page captures your login codes or card details, and the account is emptied shortly after.

Marktplaats payments never need a link from the other person. If you want to use a platform payment, start it from the app yourself. Check the address bar on anything you open; a lookalike domain with extra words or odd spelling is the giveaway.

sections.heading: The hijacked account
paragraphs: Scammers take over old, trusted accounts with years of good reviews and post fake listings from them. The profile looks perfect, but the listings are new, all priced low, often in categories the original owner never sold in, and the contact quickly moves to WhatsApp.
Scroll through the seller's earlier listings and reviews. A person who sold baby clothes for eight years and today lists four iPhones and a MacBook is a warning.

sections.heading: Deposit to reserve
paragraphs: 'Lots of interest, send 50 euro and I will hold it for you.' Sometimes the item exists, often it does not. Even when it does, you have no way to get the deposit back if the seller sells to someone else. Decline politely and offer to come today instead.

A variant is the 'courier will collect' story for large items: the seller asks you to pay the transport company up front, and the transport company is the scammer's own website. If you arrange transport, arrange it yourself with a company you found.

sections.heading: Stolen goods
paragraphs: This one costs you the item instead of the money. Signs: no box or receipt for recent electronics, a bike lock that has been cut, the seller meeting in a car park or station, or a price that only makes sense if it was free to the seller. Check serial numbers in the police Stop Heling register before buying bikes, phones and laptops.

Stolen goods are not always obvious. A phone that is still linked to someone's Apple ID or Google account is useless to you and often stolen, so ask the seller to show it has been reset and signed out before you pay.

sections.heading: Quick red flag list
paragraphs: Print this in your head before you message anyone.
bullets: Price far below other listings and no pickup possible
Any link sent to you for paying or receiving money
Request to pay a 'verification' amount
Pressure to decide within the hour
Story about being abroad or unable to meet
Request for a photo of your ID or bank card

faq.q: Is Marktplaats full of scammers?
faq.a: No. Most sellers are ordinary people clearing out a room. The scams cluster in a few categories: phones, consoles, e-bikes, concert tickets and anything priced well below the market.

faq.q: How do I know if a Marktplaats seller is a scammer?
faq.a: Look for the combination of a low price, ship-only, a new or recently revived account, and pressure to pay quickly. If two or more apply, walk away.

faq.q: What should I do if I clicked a fake link?
faq.a: Call your bank's fraud line at once and block your cards or app access, then change your passwords. Report the conversation to Marktplaats and file a report with the police.

faq.q: Can a seller scam me if I pay cash on pickup?
faq.a: The main risk then is fake or stolen goods, not lost money. Test the item before paying and be wary of meetings in public car parks for expensive items.

faq.q: Why does the seller want to switch to WhatsApp?
faq.a: Often for convenience, but scammers prefer it because Marktplaats cannot see those messages. Keep the chat in the app until you have agreed on a pickup.

example_wish: PlayStation 5 with disc drive and two controllers, seller with reviews, pickup only, under 350 euro near Rotterdam

title: How to use Marktplaats if you don't speak Dutch
meta_title: Marktplaats in English: how to use it without Dutch
description: Using Marktplaats in English: which Dutch words to search, how to read listings, how to message sellers politely and how to avoid missing the best deals.
intro: You can use Marktplaats without speaking Dutch, but you have to search in Dutch, because sellers write their titles in Dutch. Search 'bank' instead of 'sofa', translate listings with your phone, and message in short, polite English or simple Dutch. Most sellers will reply in English.

sections.heading: Search in Dutch, not English
paragraphs: Marktplaats search matches the words in the listing. A seller in Haarlem selling a sofa writes 'bank' or 'hoekbank', not 'sofa'. Search 'sofa' and you see a fraction of what is there. Learn the Dutch name of what you want and also try the plural and the obvious variants.

A few pairs to start with: bed is bed, but wardrobe is kledingkast, desk is bureau, chair is stoel, office chair is bureaustoel, washing machine is wasmachine, fridge is koelkast, and bike is fiets. Brand names and model numbers work in any language, so 'Gazelle' or 'iPhone 14' are safe.

sections.heading: Reading a listing
paragraphs: Your browser or the Google Translate camera handles the description well enough. The parts that matter most are short and worth recognizing on sight.
bullets: Vraagprijs: asking price
Bieden: make an offer
Zo goed als nieuw: as good as new
Gebruikt: used
Ophalen: pickup only
Verzenden: can be shipped
Defect or voor onderdelen: broken, for parts
Afmetingen: dimensions

sections.heading: Messaging a seller
paragraphs: Keep it short and specific. Dutch sellers get a lot of 'is this still available?' messages and answer the ones that sound like a serious buyer first. Name the item, ask the one or two questions that matter to you, and say when you can come.

A simple opening in Dutch earns goodwill even if you continue in English: 'Hoi, is dit nog beschikbaar? Ik kan morgen ophalen.' That means: Hi, is this still available? I can pick it up tomorrow. If the seller replies in Dutch, paste it into a translator and answer in English. Few people will mind.

sections.heading: Location and distance
paragraphs: Set your postcode and a radius. Most of what you buy has to be collected, and a cheap wardrobe is not cheap after a 90 minute train ride with no way to carry it. Start with 10 to 15 km in cities and widen only for rare items.

Dutch postcodes are four digits and two letters, like 1012 AB. The four digits are enough for a distance search. If you do not have a car, check whether the address is near a train station or ask the seller whether the item fits in a taxi or on a bike.

sections.heading: Arranging the pickup
paragraphs: Dutch sellers are usually direct and on time, and they expect the same. Agree a day and a time window, write down the address, and send a short message if you are running late. Bring cash or have your banking app ready, and bring a tape measure for furniture.
If the seller says 'bel even aan' it means ring the bell, and 'ik zet het buiten' means they will put it outside the door. For free items that is normal. For paid items, still ring and pay in person.

sections.heading: Let the language problem work for you
paragraphs: Many expats search in English and miss listings. The reverse is also true: Dutch sellers sometimes use words you would not guess, like 'kast' for almost any cabinet, or misspell brand names. Try two or three Dutch variants for anything important. If you would rather describe what you want in English and have the Dutch search and the filtering done for you, that is what vindje.com is built for.
Avoid sellers who only want to ship and pick up whenever you can. Pickup is where most of the value and safety comes from.

faq.q: Is there an English version of Marktplaats?
faq.a: The site and app are in Dutch, and listings are written by sellers in Dutch. Browser translation handles the interface well enough to use it.

faq.q: Will Dutch sellers reply in English?
faq.a: Most will, especially in cities and among younger sellers. Opening with one line of Dutch helps.

faq.q: Can expats sell and buy on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Yes. You need an account with an email address; some payment features need a Dutch bank account.

faq.q: What does 'ophalen' mean on Marktplaats?
faq.a: It means pickup: you collect the item at the seller's address. 'Alleen ophalen' means pickup only, no shipping.

example_wish: Desk at least 140 cm wide with drawers, good condition, under 80 euro, pickup in Amsterdam

title: Dutch words you need to search Marktplaats: a glossary
meta_title: Dutch words for Marktplaats: buyer's glossary
description: A glossary of Dutch words for Marktplaats: furniture, appliances, bikes, condition terms and listing phrases, so your searches find what sellers wrote.
intro: Sellers write in Dutch, so the right Dutch word is the difference between three results and three hundred. This glossary covers the words you will search for most, the condition terms, and the abbreviations you will see in titles. Use it as a reference while you search.

sections.heading: Furniture
paragraphs: Dutch is often more specific than English, so try the compound word too. 'Kast' on its own is a catch-all for almost any cabinet or cupboard, so add what kind: kledingkast, boekenkast, tv-meubel (TV stand), schoenenkast (shoe cabinet), vitrinekast (glass display cabinet).
bullets: Bank: sofa. Hoekbank: corner sofa. Slaapbank: sofa bed
Fauteuil: armchair
Eettafel: dining table. Eetkamerstoelen: dining chairs
Salontafel: coffee table
Kledingkast: wardrobe. Ladekast: chest of drawers
Boekenkast: bookcase. Dressoir: sideboard
Bureau: desk. Bureaustoel: office chair
Bed, matras (mattress), boxspring, bedbodem (slatted base)

sections.heading: Appliances and home
bullets: Wasmachine: washing machine. Droger or wasdroger: dryer
Koelkast: fridge. Vriezer: freezer. Koel-vriescombinatie: fridge-freezer
Vaatwasser: dishwasher
Magnetron: microwave. Oven, kookplaat (hob), afzuigkap (extractor)
Stofzuiger: vacuum cleaner
Lamp, hanglamp (pendant), vloerlamp (floor lamp)
Gordijnen: curtains. Vloerkleed: rug

sections.heading: Bikes and getting around
paragraphs: Bike listings are full of jargon. Frame size is in cm, measured along the seat tube, and sellers often only give that number in the title, like 'Gazelle 57 cm'.
bullets: Fiets: bike. Herenfiets and damesfiets: men's and women's frame
Stadsfiets or omafiets: city bike
Racefiets: road bike. Mountainbike or MTB
Elektrische fiets or e-bike
Bakfiets: cargo bike. Kinderzitje: child seat
Versnellingen: gears. Terugtraprem: coaster brake
Framemaat: frame size

sections.heading: Condition words
paragraphs: These are how sellers describe wear. They are self-reported, so treat them as an opening claim, not a guarantee. 'Zo goed als nieuw' on a five year old sofa usually means clean and undamaged, not unused. Ask for a close-up photo of the worn spots, such as armrests, seat cushions and corners, before you travel.
bullets: Nieuw: new. Nieuw in doos: new in box
Zo goed als nieuw (z.g.a.n.): as good as new
Gebruikt: used. Lichte gebruikssporen: light signs of use
Krasjes: small scratches. Deukje: small dent
Defect: broken. Voor onderdelen: for parts
Werkt prima: works fine

sections.heading: Price and deal words
bullets: Vraagprijs: asking price. Bieden: make an offer
N.o.t.k. (nader overeen te komen): price to be agreed
Gratis: free. Gratis af te halen: free, collect it yourself
Ophalen: pickup. Verzenden: shipping
Ruilen: swap. Z.g.a.n.: as good as new
Moet weg: must go, usually means room to haggle
Vaste prijs: fixed price, no haggling

sections.heading: Electronics and kids
paragraphs: Most electronics keep their English names (laptop, tablet, smartphone, monitor), which makes them easier to search. A few Dutch words still matter.
bullets: Oplader: charger. Snoer or kabel: cable
Accu: battery (bikes, tools, laptops)
Speakers or luidsprekers. Versterker: amplifier
Kinderwagen: pram. Buggy: stroller. Autostoeltje: car seat
Box: playpen (not a box). Kinderstoel: high chair
Speelgoed: toys. Kinderkleding: children's clothes

sections.heading: Measurements and details
paragraphs: Listings rarely include everything, so these words help you ask the right question.

Afmetingen means dimensions, written as lengte (length), breedte (width), hoogte (height) and diepte (depth), usually in cm. Zithoogte is seat height. Hout is wood, eiken oak, grenen pine, metaal metal, leer leather, stof fabric. Rookvrij means from a smoke-free home and huisdiervrij means no pets, both worth searching for if you have allergies.

Search tip: Dutch compound words can be split or joined by different sellers, so 'eet tafel' and 'eettafel' are both out there. Also try the diminutive, which ends in -je or -tje: kastje (small cabinet), tafeltje (small table), lampje (small lamp). Small items are often listed that way.

faq.q: What does z.g.a.n. mean on Marktplaats?
faq.a: It stands for 'zo goed als nieuw', which means as good as new. It is the seller's own judgment, so check the photos.

faq.q: What does n.o.t.k. mean?
faq.a: 'Nader overeen te komen': the price is to be agreed. The seller wants offers instead of naming a price.

faq.q: What is the Dutch word for sofa?
faq.a: Bank. A corner sofa is a hoekbank and a sofa bed is a slaapbank.

faq.q: What does 'moet weg' mean in a listing?
faq.a: 'Must go'. The seller is usually moving or clearing space, which often means a lower price and some room to negotiate.

faq.q: What does 'ophalen' or 'afhalen' mean?
faq.a: Both mean you collect the item at the seller's address. 'Alleen ophalen' means pickup only, so check the location before you message.

example_wish: Oak dining table for 6 with chairs, from a smoke-free home, under 300 euro near Eindhoven

title: How to negotiate a price on Marktplaats
meta_title: How to negotiate on Marktplaats without being rude
description: How to negotiate on Marktplaats: when an offer is fair, how much to bid below the asking price, what to write, and when to haggle at the pickup.
intro: On Marktplaats, offering 10 to 20 percent below the asking price is normal and rarely offends anyone, as long as the offer is polite and you are ready to collect quickly. Lowball offers of half the price usually get ignored. Your strongest card is being the easy buyer: clear, fast, and on time.

sections.heading: Know the going price first
paragraphs: Before you offer anything, look at five to ten similar listings and note what they ask. Then remember that asking prices are the top of the range; the sold price is often 10 to 25 percent lower, especially for furniture that has been listed for weeks.
Check the listing date. A wardrobe that has been online for six weeks has a seller who is getting tired of it. A listing posted this morning with twenty views per hour gives you much less room.

sections.heading: How much to offer
paragraphs: Rough rules that work in practice:
bullets: Fresh listing, fair price: offer the asking price or close to it, and be first
Listed a few weeks: 10 to 20 percent below
'Moet weg', moving soon: 20 to 30 percent below is reasonable
Overpriced compared to similar ads: offer what the others ask, and say so
Under 20 euro: haggling over 3 euro mostly costs you the item

sections.heading: What to write
paragraphs: Keep it friendly and concrete. Name your price, give a short reason if there is one, and offer a pickup time. 'Hoi, ik zou 120 euro willen bieden. Ik kan morgenavond ophalen.' (Hi, I would like to offer 120 euro. I can collect tomorrow evening.) That is a message a seller can say yes to in one tap.

Avoid messages that only ask 'last price?' or 'lowest?'. They sound like you are shopping around, and many sellers do not reply. Also avoid criticizing the item in writing to push the price down; it rarely works and sours the pickup.

sections.heading: Haggling at the pickup
paragraphs: If you agreed a price and the item matches the listing, pay that price. Renegotiating at the door when nothing is wrong is the fastest way to a bad reputation and an awkward ten minutes.

If something does not match, like an undisclosed stain, a missing shelf, a wobble, a dead battery, then say so calmly and propose a fair adjustment. Point at the problem, name a number, and accept that the seller may say no. Walking away is always an option, and the seller knows it.

sections.heading: Bundles and timing
paragraphs: Sellers clearing out a house often have more listings. Buying two or three items from one seller is the easiest discount you will get: 'I'd like the desk and the chair, would you do 90 for both?' It saves them a second buyer and a second appointment.

Timing also helps. Offers on Sunday evening or near the end of the month, when people are moving out, tend to land well. A seller who has to hand over their keys on Friday becomes flexible on Wednesday.

sections.heading: Using faults fairly
paragraphs: Faults visible in the photos are already in the price, so bringing them up again rarely moves the seller. Faults the seller did not mention are different. If the listing says 'werkt prima' and the washing machine leaks, you have a fair reason to offer less or leave.
Be specific: 'The left drawer runner is broken, a new one is about 15 euro, would you take 100 instead of 115?' is much easier to agree to than 'it's damaged, 70?'.

sections.heading: When not to negotiate
paragraphs: Items marked 'vaste prijs' (fixed price) mean exactly that; offer anyway only if the gap is large and the listing old. Rare items priced fairly will be gone while you haggle. And with free items, the only thing to negotiate is the pickup time.

faq.q: Is it rude to negotiate on Marktplaats?
faq.a: No, it is expected. A polite offer 10 to 20 percent below the asking price is normal. Offers around half the price usually get no reply.

faq.q: How do I make an offer on Marktplaats?
faq.a: On listings with bidding enabled you can place a bid, or you can send a message with your price. A message with a pickup time often gets a faster yes than a bare bid.

faq.q: Can I negotiate after agreeing a price?
faq.a: Only if the item turns out different from the listing. Otherwise pay what you agreed.

faq.q: What does 'vaste prijs' mean?
faq.a: Fixed price. The seller does not want offers, so expect a no unless the listing has been online a long time.

example_wish: Two-seat leather sofa in brown or cognac, listed for a while, under 250 euro, pickup near Leiden

title: Bieden, vraagprijs, n.o.t.k.: Marktplaats prices explained
meta_title: Bieden vs vraagprijs on Marktplaats explained
description: Bieden vs vraagprijs on Marktplaats: what each price type means, whether a bid is binding, how the bid list works and what to do with n.o.t.k. listings.
intro: A Marktplaats seller picks how the price is shown. 'Vraagprijs' means they name an asking price, 'bieden' means they want offers, and 'n.o.t.k.' means the price is to be agreed. In all three cases the seller decides who gets the item; the highest bid does not win automatically.

sections.heading: Vraagprijs: the asking price
paragraphs: The seller names a number. It is the price they hope for, not always the one they will take. Many vraagprijs listings also allow bids, which you will see as a bid option or a list of offers under the listing.
With a vraagprijs, an offer slightly below is normal. If the price is already fair and the listing is new, offering the full price and a quick pickup time is often how you beat other buyers.

sections.heading: Bieden: make an offer
paragraphs: The seller puts no price, or sets a starting price, and asks for bids. Bids show up in a list on the listing, often with the bidder's name and amount visible. That list is a useful signal: it tells you what others think the item is worth.

It is not an auction. There is no closing time and the highest bidder does not automatically win. The seller may pick a lower bid from someone who can come today, or ignore all bids and wait. So a bid alone is weak. Follow it with a message saying when you can collect.

sections.heading: Is a bid binding?
paragraphs: In everyday practice a Marktplaats bid is treated as an expression of interest, not a signed purchase. Sellers are free to accept another bid, and buyers who bid and then change their mind before agreeing anything are not chased. Once you and the seller have agreed in messages on a price and a pickup, though, it is a deal in both spirit and, under Dutch contract law, possibly in law. Treat it that way.
Do not place bids you would not honor. Sellers remember, and leaving bids on ten items at once to see who bites gets you blocked.

sections.heading: N.o.t.k. and other price types
paragraphs: You will see a few other labels in the price field.
bullets: N.o.t.k. (nader overeen te komen): price to be agreed. Send an offer by message
Zie omschrijving: see description, the price is in the text
Op aanvraag: on request, often a business listing
Gratis: free, usually pickup only
Ruilen: swap, the seller wants an item in return
Vaste prijs in the text: fixed, no offers

sections.heading: Reading the bid list
paragraphs: When bids are visible, look at the spread. A listing with bids at 40, 45 and 50 euro tells you the seller has had offers and not accepted them, so they probably want more than 50. A listing with one bid at 10 euro on a 100 euro item tells you that bid was a lowball.
Old bids are not a sign of high demand. If the top bid is three weeks old, the bidder has likely bought something else, and a fresh, fair message can get the item.

Bids from accounts with no history, or round numbers far above the rest, are sometimes placed by friends of the seller or by scammers fishing for contact. Do not raise your offer just because a strange bid appeared above yours.

sections.heading: A practical approach
paragraphs: For most items: check the price of similar listings, place a bid only if you want it on the record, and send a message with your number and a pickup time. For n.o.t.k. listings, ask what the seller has in mind before you name a figure; sometimes it is lower than you expected. When you search with a price filter, remember that bieden and n.o.t.k. listings may not have a price to filter on, so they can slip in or out of your results.

faq.q: What does bieden mean on Marktplaats?
faq.a: It means 'to bid'. The seller invites offers instead of, or as well as, an asking price.

faq.q: Does the highest bid win on Marktplaats?
faq.a: No. It is not an auction, and the seller chooses whichever buyer they prefer, often the one who can collect first.

faq.q: Can I withdraw a bid on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Yes, you can usually remove a bid from the listing. If you already agreed a deal in messages, tell the seller directly instead of disappearing.

faq.q: What does vraagprijs mean?
faq.a: Asking price. It is the price the seller hopes for, and polite offers somewhat below it are common.

faq.q: What does n.o.t.k. mean on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Nader overeen te komen, or price to be agreed. Send a message asking what the seller has in mind, or make an offer based on similar listings.

example_wish: Vintage teak sideboard around 180 cm long, asking price or open to offers, under 400 euro, within 30 km of Arnhem

title: Gelijk oversteken: paying on pickup without getting burned
meta_title: Gelijk oversteken: how to pay safely on pickup
description: What gelijk oversteken means on Marktplaats, how to pay on pickup with cash or a transfer, and how to avoid fake payment screenshots and swapped items.
intro: Gelijk oversteken literally means 'crossing over at the same time': the buyer hands over the money and the seller hands over the item in the same moment. It is the standard way to deal on Marktplaats when you meet in person. Done properly, neither side has to trust the other.

sections.heading: What the phrase means in practice
paragraphs: When a seller writes 'alleen gelijk oversteken' they are saying: no paying in advance, no reserving with a deposit, come and pay when you take it. That is good news for you as a buyer. It also means the seller will not hand over the item until they see the money, so come prepared.
Some sellers use the phrase loosely for any pickup deal. Either way, the rule is the same: nobody hands over their side until the other side is ready.

sections.heading: Paying with cash
paragraphs: Cash is the simplest form. Count it out in front of the seller after you have checked the item. For larger amounts, bring the exact sum; sellers often do not have change. Fewer people carry cash than ten years ago, so if you plan to pay cash, say so in advance and agree that the seller is fine with it.
For expensive items, think about carrying a large amount on the street. A bank transfer is then the better choice.

sections.heading: Paying by bank transfer at the door
paragraphs: Most pickups are now paid with a transfer or payment request on the spot. Do the transfer while you are standing there, then show your banking app's confirmation. Many Dutch banks process transfers between Dutch accounts within seconds, so the seller can see it arrive in their own app.
As the buyer, check the name on the account before you send. If the listing is from 'Sanne' and the account holder is a company or a different name, ask why before you pay.

sections.heading: The screenshot trick, and the swap
paragraphs: Two pickup tricks show up from time to time. The first is the fake payment screenshot, where a 'buyer' shows an edited image of a transfer that never happened. As a buyer you are not the target, but it is why sellers want to see the money land, so do not be offended if they wait.

The second targets you: the item you tested is swapped for a broken one while it goes back in its box. For phones, consoles and laptops, keep the item in your hands from test to bag, and check the serial number on the device against the box.

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
paragraphs: Run through this in the doorway.
bullets: Item matches the photos and description
It switches on, charges, opens, folds, rolls, whatever it should do
Serial number on device matches the box and receipt, if any
Account name matches the seller before you transfer
Transfer confirmed on both phones before you leave
Ask for the seller's name and number on a message, in case of a problem later

sections.heading: When gelijk oversteken is not possible
paragraphs: If you cannot meet, there is no way to cross over at the same time, and the trust has to come from somewhere else: a payment method that holds the money until delivery, or a seller with a long track record. Do not stretch the phrase to cover 'pay now and I ship tomorrow'. That is advance payment, whatever the seller calls it.

A middle ground for items a few hours away: ask a friend who lives nearby to look and pay for you, or agree a video call where the seller shows the item working and then hands it to a courier you booked yourself. Neither is as safe as being there, but both are far better than a transfer to a stranger.

faq.q: What does gelijk oversteken mean?
faq.a: Literally 'crossing at the same time'. On Marktplaats it means the buyer pays and the seller hands over the item in the same moment, at the pickup.

faq.q: Is a bank transfer safe at pickup?
faq.a: Yes, if you make it on the spot and the seller sees it arrive. Check that the account name fits the seller before you send.

faq.q: Should I pay cash on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Cash is fine for small amounts if the seller agrees. For larger amounts a transfer leaves a record, which helps if the item turns out to be stolen.

faq.q: Can I pay a deposit to reserve an item?
faq.a: It is risky. If the seller sells to someone else or disappears, the deposit is hard to recover, so offer to collect soon instead.

faq.q: What if the seller has no change?
faq.a: Bring the exact amount, or agree in advance to pay by transfer. A rounded-down price for a missing 5 euro is a common, friendly fix.

example_wish: iPhone 14 with 128 GB, battery health above 85 percent, with box and receipt, pickup and pay in person, under 400 euro near Den Haag

title: Tikkie and betaalverzoek scams on Marktplaats: how they work
meta_title: Tikkie scam on Marktplaats: how it works, how to spot it
description: How Tikkie and betaalverzoek scams on Marktplaats work, from the 1 cent verification trick to fake payment pages, and the checks that keep you safe.
intro: A Tikkie or bank payment request is a normal way to pay in the Netherlands, and most of the ones you will see are genuine. The scams copy the look of a payment request to get you onto a fake page that steals your bank login, or ask you to pay a tiny 'verification' amount that opens the door to a much larger theft. The rule that stops nearly all of them: never pay or 'verify' through a link a stranger sends you unless you know exactly what it is for.

sections.heading: What a normal Tikkie looks like
paragraphs: Tikkie is a payment request app from ABN AMRO that anyone with a Dutch bank account can pay. Most Dutch banks also have their own betaalverzoek (payment request) feature. You open the link, see who is asking and for how much, pick your bank, and approve the payment through iDEAL in your own banking app.

Two things are always true of a genuine request: you are sent to your own bank's app or site to approve, and you only ever pay. You never type in card numbers, PIN codes or login codes on a page outside your bank, and no request ever pays money to you.

sections.heading: The 1 cent verification scam
paragraphs: This one mostly targets sellers, so it matters if you also sell. A 'buyer' says they want to pay via Marktplaats or a delivery service, and to receive the money you first have to verify your account by paying 1 cent or 1 euro through a link. The link leads to a fake page that looks like iDEAL or your bank. What you enter there gives the scammer access to your account.
There is no receive-money service on Marktplaats or anywhere else that requires you to pay first. If a buyer asks you to verify anything, end the chat.

sections.heading: The fake seller with a genuine Tikkie
paragraphs: Here the link works. The seller sends a correct Tikkie for the agreed price of a shipped item, you pay, and the item never comes. The Tikkie was real, the seller was not, and the account often belongs to a money mule.

Look at the name shown on the Tikkie and in the iDEAL screen before you approve. If it does not match the seller's Marktplaats name, or it is a business you have never heard of, stop. You can also check the account number, phone number or email in the police 'Controleer handelspartij' tool before paying.

sections.heading: The lookalike payment page
paragraphs: Some scam links copy the Tikkie, Marktplaats or bank design almost perfectly. The giveaway is the web address and what the page asks for.
bullets: Domain with extra words, like a bank name plus 'secure' or 'verify'
Asks for card number, expiry date or CVC
Asks you to scan a QR code with your banking app to 'receive' money
Asks you to log in with a code from your card reader
Says the payment will expire in a few minutes

sections.heading: Safe habits with payment requests
paragraphs: Use payment requests only at a pickup, where you can see the item and the seller sees the money arrive. For shipped items, prefer a payment method that holds the money until delivery and that you start yourself from inside the app.
When in doubt, ask for the IBAN and do a normal transfer from your banking app. A genuine seller will be fine with that. A scammer will push you back to their link.

sections.heading: If you clicked or paid
paragraphs: Call your bank's fraud number straight away. Speed matters, because banks can sometimes stop or reverse a payment that has not been passed on. Block your app access or cards if they ask you to, change your passwords, and report the chat to Marktplaats. File a police report as well, online or at a station, and keep screenshots of the conversation and the link.

faq.q: Is paying with Tikkie on Marktplaats safe?
faq.a: Paying a Tikkie at a pickup, after you have seen the item, is fine. Paying a Tikkie in advance for a shipped item gives you little protection if the seller is fake.

faq.q: Why does a buyer ask me to pay 1 cent?
faq.a: That is a known scam. The link goes to a fake bank page that captures your login details. No genuine service needs you to pay to receive money.

faq.q: How can I check if a Tikkie is real?
faq.a: A genuine Tikkie shows the requester's name and sends you to your own bank to approve. It never asks for card details or login codes on its own page.

faq.q: Can I get my money back from a Tikkie scam?
faq.a: Contact your bank immediately and report it to the police. Recovery is not guaranteed, but acting within minutes improves the chance.

example_wish: Nintendo Switch OLED with games, seller I can meet in person to pay, under 220 euro, within 20 km of Amersfoort

title: Finding free stuff on Marktplaats (gratis af te halen)
meta_title: Free stuff on Marktplaats: finding gratis af te halen
description: How to find free stuff on Marktplaats: search terms like gratis af te halen, when free listings appear, what is worth taking and how to get there first.
intro: Marktplaats has a steady supply of free furniture, plants, appliances and moving boxes, listed as 'gratis' or 'gratis af te halen' (free, collect it yourself). The good items go within an hour or two, so the trick is a saved search close to home and being able to collect the same day. Expect to carry it yourself and to take it as it is.

sections.heading: What to search for
paragraphs: Filter on price type 'gratis' where the category allows it, and also search the words, because not every seller sets the price field correctly. Some list a free item for 1 euro so it shows up in price-sorted results.
Combine 'gratis' with the thing you want: 'gratis kast', 'gratis bank', 'gratis wasmachine'. Also try 'moet weg' and 'voor niks' (for nothing). Sort by newest, not by relevance.
bullets: gratis af te halen
gratis ophalen
weggeven or weg te geven
voor niks
verhuisdozen gratis (free moving boxes)
stekjes (plant cuttings, often free or 1 euro)

sections.heading: When the good free stuff appears
paragraphs: Free listings spike around moves. The last days of the month, when rental contracts end, are busy. So are the weeks when students leave in June and July, and the period around the end of the year when people clear out before visitors. Weekends see the most new listings and the most competition.

Bulky items that are hard to move, such as sofas, wardrobes, beds and pianos, are the ones most often given away. The seller would otherwise pay for a waste collection or a trip to the recycling yard, so free is cheaper for them.

sections.heading: How to be the one who gets it
paragraphs: Free listings get dozens of replies. The seller wants the item gone with the least effort, so make it easy: say you can come at a specific time today or tomorrow, that you have transport, and that you will carry it yourself.

One clear message beats ten 'still available?' ones. 'Hoi, ik kan vandaag om 18:00 ophalen met een busje. Ik draag het zelf naar beneden.' (Hi, I can collect today at 18:00 with a van. I'll carry it down myself.) Then show up on time. Sellers of free stuff get many no-shows.

sections.heading: What is worth taking, and what is not
paragraphs: Free is not free if you have to rent a van, then pay to throw it away. Ask yourself whether you would pay 20 euro for it.
bullets: Good: solid wood furniture, bookcases, desks, garden tools, plant pots, moving boxes, kids' toys in good shape
Check carefully: fridges and washing machines (ask age and whether it works), sofas (smell, stains, pets)
Skip: mattresses of unknown history, upholstered furniture from a home with a bedbug story, child car seats, bike helmets
Skip: anything 'needs a small repair' unless you know the repair

sections.heading: Etiquette at the door
paragraphs: Bring the tools to take things apart if needed (a screwdriver set and an Allen key set cover most flat-pack furniture), and blankets or straps to protect it. Do not haggle about extras or ask the seller to deliver. A small thank-you, like a bar of chocolate or 5 euro for something nice, is appreciated but not expected.
If you change your mind, tell the seller. Free-item sellers often hold a list of backups, and a quick 'sorry, I can't make it' lets the next person have it.

sections.heading: Other places for free things
paragraphs: Outside Marktplaats, local Facebook groups called 'gratis af te halen' plus a town name are active in many places, and in many neighbourhoods items left on the curb with a 'gratis' sign are fair game. Kringloop thrift shops sometimes give away items they cannot sell. When you search for a specific free item across a wide area, vindje.com can check each listing for size and condition so you only see the ones worth the trip.

faq.q: How do I find free items on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Search for 'gratis' or 'gratis af te halen' together with the item, set a small radius, and sort by newest. Save the search so you get alerts.

faq.q: Why are people giving away furniture for free?
faq.a: Usually they are moving and do not want to pay for transport or a waste collection. Free is cheaper for them than getting rid of it.

faq.q: Is it rude to ask a free-item seller to deliver?
faq.a: Generally yes. Free listings assume you collect. Offer to pick up at a time that suits them.

faq.q: Should I take a free mattress?
faq.a: Better not. You cannot check hygiene or bedbugs, and a cheap new mattress is a safer choice.

example_wish: Free bookcase or desk, solid wood, gratis af te halen, within 5 km of Utrecht Overvecht

title: Shipping vs pickup on Marktplaats: which is safer
meta_title: Shipping vs pickup on Marktplaats: which is safer
description: Shipping vs pickup on Marktplaats: why pickup is safer, when shipping makes sense, which payment options protect you and how to receive parcels well.
intro: Pickup is safer: you see the item, test it, and pay at the moment you take it. Shipping is fine for small, low-risk items or with a payment method that holds your money until delivery. Parcels rarely go missing in the post. The danger is paying a stranger before you have anything in your hands.

sections.heading: Why pickup is the default
paragraphs: At a pickup you control the moment money changes hands. You can check that the laptop boots, the blender spins and the chair does not wobble. If something is wrong, you leave with your money.
Pickup also filters out most fake listings. A scammer cannot hand over an item that does not exist, which is why they nearly always insist on shipping.

sections.heading: When shipping makes sense
paragraphs: Shipping is reasonable for small items that are hard to fake and cheap enough that the risk is acceptable: books, records, clothes, spare parts, board games. It also makes sense for rare items where the only one for sale is on the other side of the country.
It makes less sense for phones, consoles, cameras and other high-value electronics, which are the most faked and the most often swapped for a broken unit. For those, travel if you can.

Bulky items such as furniture, appliances and bikes do not fit in the normal parcel network at all. Listings for those that say 'kan verzonden worden' usually mean a courier at extra cost, so ask for the total before you agree.

sections.heading: Paying for a shipped item
paragraphs: Your options, from most to least protection:
bullets: A pay-and-ship option started from inside the Marktplaats app, where available, that holds the money until delivery
PayPal goods and services, if the seller accepts it, which has a buyer dispute process (not the 'friends and family' option)
A credit card payment through a platform with chargeback rights
A bank transfer or Tikkie to a seller with a long, consistent review history
A bank transfer to a new account with no reviews: avoid

sections.heading: Checking a seller who ships
paragraphs: Before you pay for a shipped item, ask for a photo of the item next to a piece of paper with your name and today's date. A genuine seller can do it in a minute. Check that the account is older than a few weeks, that the reviews mention completed sales, and that the seller's name matches the bank account name.
Ask how it will be packed and sent, and for the tracking number as soon as it ships. Vague answers about the courier are a bad sign.

sections.heading: Receiving the parcel
paragraphs: Film yourself opening the box, starting before you cut the tape. If the item is damaged or not as described, that video is your evidence for the seller, the platform or the payment provider. Check the item fully on the first day, not after a week.
If the parcel arrives damaged on the outside, photograph it before opening and note it with the courier if you can.

sections.heading: The in-between options
paragraphs: For large items far away there are middle routes. Courier services such as Brenger collect furniture from the seller and deliver it to you, often for 40 to 100 euro depending on size and distance; the driver sees the item before loading it. You can also ask a friend near the seller to look at it. Both still leave the payment question, so pair them with a protected payment where possible.
Some sellers offer to meet halfway, at a station or a service area. That is fine for small items and gives you the safety of a pickup.

faq.q: Is it safe to have an item shipped on Marktplaats?
faq.a: It can be, with a payment method that holds the money until delivery or a seller with a strong track record. Paying a new account by bank transfer is where most people lose money.

faq.q: Who pays shipping costs on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Usually the buyer. The seller states it in the listing or you agree it in the chat.

faq.q: Why do scammers always want to ship?
faq.a: Because a pickup would show that the item does not exist. 'Shipping only' plus a low price is the most common scam pattern.

faq.q: What if a shipped item arrives broken?
faq.a: Contact the seller with photos and an unboxing video straight away. If you used a protected payment, open a dispute through that service.

faq.q: Can I ask a seller to ship an item listed as pickup only?
faq.a: You can ask, but many sellers say no because packing is work. Offering to pay the postage plus a few euro for the box and their time helps.

example_wish: Vinyl records by Dutch bands from the 70s, can be shipped, seller with good reviews, under 15 euro each

title: How to check a Marktplaats seller before you pay
meta_title: How to check a Marktplaats seller before you pay
description: How to check a Marktplaats seller before you pay: read the profile and reviews, ask test questions, verify the bank account and spot hijacked accounts.
intro: Five minutes of checking catches most fake sellers: look at the profile age and reviews, scroll through their other listings, ask a question only the owner could answer, and run the bank account through the police check tool before any transfer. None of these alone proves anything. Together they give you a clear picture.

sections.heading: Read the profile
paragraphs: Open the seller's profile from the listing. Note how long the account has been active, how many reviews it has, and whether it is a private seller (particulier) or a business (zakelijk). A business has more legal obligations to you as a buyer than a private person does.
bullets: Account a few days old, selling expensive items: high risk
Account years old with no activity until this week: possible hijack
Reviews mention completed sales and specific items: good sign
Name on the profile fits the way they write: good sign

sections.heading: Look at the other listings
paragraphs: Most private sellers have a mix that fits one household: a bike, some kids' clothes, a lamp. A pattern of many similar expensive items, all priced low, all ship-only, is how resellers of stolen goods and scammers look.

Compare the photos. Same floor, same wall, same lighting across listings points to a person selling from home. Studio shots, watermarks or photos you can find with a reverse image search point to copied images.

sections.heading: Ask a test question
paragraphs: Ask something the owner knows and a scammer has to guess. For a bike: what size are the tyres, and is the frame number readable? For a laptop: what does the battery health show in settings? For furniture: can you send a photo of the underside or the back?
Ask for a photo of the item with a note showing your name and today's date. It takes a genuine seller a minute. A seller who refuses, or sends a photo that looks edited, has answered your question.

sections.heading: Check the bank account and phone number
paragraphs: The Dutch police run an online tool called 'Controleer handelspartij' (check a trading partner) on politie.nl. You can enter a bank account number, phone number, email address or website and see whether it has been linked to fraud reports. A clean result is not a guarantee, since new mule accounts appear daily, but a hit is a clear stop.
When you pay, your banking app may show whether the name you entered matches the account holder. If it warns about a mismatch, do not continue until you understand why.

sections.heading: Signs of a hijacked account
paragraphs: Scammers buy or steal old accounts because they look trustworthy. Things that give it away:
bullets: Many new listings in one day after months or years of silence
Listings in a completely different category than the old ones
Writing style that does not match earlier reviews or listings
Quick push to WhatsApp or email
Payment to an account in a different name, with a story about why

sections.heading: For expensive items, meet anyway
paragraphs: The best check of all is seeing the seller in person at their home with the item. If a seller with a 1,200 euro e-bike will not let you come and look, there is a reason. Paying on pickup removes most of what you would otherwise need to verify.

At the door, a few small things confirm you are dealing with the owner: the item is in the home, not in a car boot; the seller knows how it works; and for electronics or bikes they can show a receipt, a manual or a registration in their own name. For a bike, check that the seller's key fits and turns the frame lock.

faq.q: How can I see if a Marktplaats seller is reliable?
faq.a: Check the account age, reviews and other listings, ask a specific question about the item, and run the bank account through the police check tool before paying.

faq.q: What is Controleer handelspartij?
faq.a: A free tool on the Dutch police website where you can check a bank account, phone number, email or website against fraud reports.

faq.q: Can a seller with good reviews still be a scammer?
faq.a: Yes, if the account was hijacked or bought. Look for sudden new activity in categories the seller never used before.

faq.q: Does buying from a business seller give me more rights?
faq.a: Generally yes. Consumer protection rules apply to businesses that sell to consumers, not to private sellers. Check the listing for business details.

example_wish: Bosch electric drill set with two batteries and charger, private seller with reviews, under 90 euro, pickup near Zwolle

title: What to ask a seller before you go and look
meta_title: Questions to ask a Marktplaats seller before you go
description: Questions to ask a Marktplaats seller before you travel: measurements, age, faults, pets and smoke, transport and payment, with Dutch phrases you can copy.
intro: Ask the questions that would make you cancel the trip: exact measurements, age, faults not in the photos, and whether it can be carried out of the building. Two or three good questions save you a wasted afternoon, and sellers answer them faster than a vague 'still available?'.

sections.heading: Measurements first
paragraphs: Most wasted pickups come from things that do not fit: the sofa through your stairwell, the wardrobe under your sloped ceiling, the washing machine into the alcove. Ask for width, depth and height, and for sofas also the seat depth and the height of the armrests.
Then measure your side: door width, the tightest turn on the stairs, and the space in the car or van. Dutch stairs are steep and narrow, so this matters more here than in most countries.
bullets: Wat zijn de exacte afmetingen (b x d x h)?: What are the exact dimensions (w x d x h)?
Kan het uit elkaar?: Can it be taken apart?
Past het in een stationwagen?: Does it fit in an estate car?

sections.heading: Age and history
paragraphs: How old is it, where was it bought, and why are they selling? The answers tell you about wear and also about honesty. 'Bought it three years ago at IKEA, moving to a smaller place' is a normal answer. A shrug about where a nearly new laptop came from is not.
For appliances, ask for the model number. You can look up the age and original price, and check whether spare parts are still available.

sections.heading: Faults the photos do not show
paragraphs: Ask directly and specifically. 'Are there any defects?' gets 'no'. A specific question gets a specific answer.
bullets: Furniture: stains, tears, smells, wobbly legs, missing screws or shelves
Appliances: leaks, noises, error codes, last time it was used
Electronics: battery health, dead pixels, cracked corners, whether it is reset
Bikes: gears shifting cleanly, brakes, lights working, any rust

sections.heading: Smoke, pets and allergies
paragraphs: Upholstered furniture, mattresses, rugs and curtains hold smells and hair for years. If it matters to you, ask: 'Komt het uit een rookvrij en huisdiervrij huis?' (Is it from a smoke-free and pet-free home?). Many sellers put rookvrij in the listing already when it is true.

sections.heading: Logistics and payment
paragraphs: Confirm the basics before you set off, so there are no surprises at the door.
bullets: Which floor is it on, and is there a lift?
Will someone help carry it down, or should I bring a helper?
Is parking close by? Many Dutch city centres have paid or permit-only parking
Cash or bank transfer?
Can you hold it until I arrive at the agreed time?

sections.heading: Questions for specific items
paragraphs: Some categories have one question that matters more than the rest. For a fridge or freezer, ask whether it has been standing upright for a while, since one that was transported lying down needs a few hours before it is switched on. For a bike, ask whether keys for every lock come with it. For a laptop or phone, ask whether it has been removed from the seller's account. For flat-pack furniture, ask whether it has been taken apart before, since chipboard does not take many rebuilds.

sections.heading: How to ask without annoying the seller
paragraphs: Put your questions in one message, not five. Read the listing first so you do not ask what is already there. Keep it to the two or three that decide whether you will come. A seller who sees a buyer who has read the listing and asks sharp questions is more likely to hold the item for you.
If the answers are vague or the seller avoids a question, ask once more in a different way. If it is still vague, that is often your answer.

faq.q: What should I ask before buying second-hand furniture?
faq.a: Exact dimensions, whether it comes apart, any damage or smells, and whether it is from a smoke-free and pet-free home.

faq.q: How do I ask in Dutch if an item is still available?
faq.a: 'Is dit nog beschikbaar?' Add when you can collect, for example 'Ik kan morgen ophalen', to get a faster reply.

faq.q: Should I ask why someone is selling?
faq.a: Yes, it is a normal question. Moving, upgrading or a new baby are common answers. Evasive answers are worth noting.

faq.q: Is it okay to ask for more photos?
faq.a: Yes, especially of wear spots, the back or underside, and labels with model numbers. Most sellers are happy to send them.

example_wish: Washing machine 8 kg, under 6 years old, no leaks, from a ground floor or with lift, under 200 euro near Groningen

title: The best time of year to buy second hand in the Netherlands
meta_title: Best time to buy second hand in the Netherlands
description: The best time to buy second hand in the Netherlands: when bikes, furniture, garden sets and baby gear are cheapest, and why moving season matters most.
intro: Buy things when other people stop needing them: bikes and garden furniture in late autumn and winter, furniture at the end of the month and when students leave in summer, winter gear in spring. Prices on Marktplaats follow demand closely, and the gap between a busy month and a quiet one can be a third of the price.

sections.heading: Moving season is the biggest factor
paragraphs: Most good second-hand furniture comes from people moving. Rental contracts usually end at the end of a month, so the last ten days of each month bring a wave of 'wegens verhuizing' (because of moving) and 'moet weg' listings. Sellers on a deadline accept lower offers, and free listings jump.

Student cities like Utrecht, Groningen, Leiden, Delft, Amsterdam and Nijmegen see a big supply in June and July when students and expats leave, and a demand spike in August and September when the new year arrives. If you can, furnish in early summer and avoid the first weeks of September.

sections.heading: Bikes: buy in winter, avoid spring
paragraphs: Demand for bikes rises from March, peaks in spring and again in late August with incoming students. From November to February fewer people buy, and listings sit longer. That is when you have the most room to negotiate on city bikes, road bikes and e-bikes.
Cold weather is also a better test. If the lights, gears and battery behave on a wet January evening, they will in May.

sections.heading: Seasonal items, counter-cyclical
paragraphs: The pattern repeats for anything tied to a season. Look for the item in the months nobody wants it.
bullets: Garden furniture, parasols, barbecues: September to February
Lawn mowers and garden tools: autumn
Winter coats, ski gear, snow chains: April to June
Air conditioning units and fans: autumn and winter
Christmas decorations and tree stands: January
Tents and camping gear: September to November

sections.heading: Baby and kids' gear
paragraphs: Baby items follow the child, not the season, so supply is steady. Prams, high chairs and cots get listed when a family is done, often in batches. Prices dip a bit after the summer holidays, when people clear out before school starts. Skip used car seats regardless of timing: you cannot see whether one has been in a crash.
Clothes for babies and toddlers are the easiest bargain of all, often sold as a bag of 20 to 40 pieces per size for 10 to 25 euro. Search 'kledingpakket' plus the size, like 'kledingpakket maat 74'.

sections.heading: Electronics and new model releases
paragraphs: When a new phone, console or laptop generation comes out, owners of the previous one upgrade and list their old devices. The weeks after a big launch bring a good supply of the outgoing model. Around Sinterklaas and Christmas, demand for consoles and tablets rises, so buy those in January or February when unwanted gifts and upgrades appear.
Prices for previous generations fall fastest in the first months after a launch, then level out.

sections.heading: Koningsdag and other events
paragraphs: On Koningsdag (King's Day, 27 April, or the 26th when the 27th is a Sunday) the whole country turns into a flea market, the vrijmarkt. You will find books, toys, clothes and kitchen items at a euro or two, and sellers drop prices in the afternoon. It is not great for furniture, since nobody wants to carry a wardrobe to the street.
Local rommelmarkten (flea markets) and kringloop stores have their own rhythms. Kringloops restock daily, so regular visits beat any season.

sections.heading: Day and time also matter
paragraphs: Many listings go online on weekend mornings and Sunday evenings, when people have time to photograph things. Popular items are gone within hours, so a saved search with notifications beats checking once a day. Midweek, the market is quieter and sellers of older listings more willing to talk.

faq.q: When is the best time to buy a used bike in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Late autumn and winter, from November to February. Demand is low and sellers are more willing to negotiate.

faq.q: When do students sell their furniture?
faq.a: Mostly in June and July, and at the end of each month when rental contracts end.

faq.q: Is Koningsdag good for second-hand shopping?
faq.a: Yes for small things like books, toys and clothes, which go for a euro or two. It is less useful for furniture.

faq.q: When is garden furniture cheapest second hand?
faq.a: From September through the winter, when people clear their gardens and balconies before the cold.

example_wish: Wooden garden table with 4 chairs, sold before winter, under 120 euro, pickup within 20 km of Haarlem

title: Marktplaats search filters explained: radius, price, condition, sorting
meta_title: Marktplaats search filters explained, step by step
description: Marktplaats search filters explained: postcode and radius, price range, condition, delivery, category attributes, sorting and saved search alerts.
intro: The filters that matter most on Marktplaats are postcode with distance, a price range, the right category, and sorting by newest. Add a condition or delivery filter when you need it and save the search so you get a notification. The filters only check what sellers filled in, so they narrow the results but never judge the listing for you.

sections.heading: Postcode and distance
paragraphs: Enter your postcode and choose a distance. The radius is measured as the crow flies from postcode to postcode, so 10 km across the IJ or a motorway can be a long trip. In cities, start small (5 to 10 km). For rarer items, widen to 25 or 50 km and accept the travel.
If you do not have a car, set the postcode near the station you would travel to, not your home.

sections.heading: Price range
paragraphs: Set a minimum as well as a maximum. A minimum of a few euro hides 1 euro placeholder listings and many wanted ads (gezocht). A maximum keeps you honest.

Know the blind spot: listings with 'bieden', 'n.o.t.k.' or 'zie omschrijving' do not always have a number to filter on, so a strict price filter can hide them. For items where sellers often ask for offers, run the search once without a price filter as well.

sections.heading: Category and its attributes
paragraphs: Picking the right category gives you filters specific to it: brand and frame size for bikes, storage and model for phones, type and material for furniture. These come from fields sellers fill in, and many skip them. A filter on frame size 57 shows only sellers who entered 57, not every bike that is 57 cm.
Use attribute filters to narrow a big result set, but do not rely on them for completeness. If the result count drops from 300 to 6, try again with the search words instead.

sections.heading: Condition and delivery
paragraphs: Condition (conditie) usually offers options like nieuw, zo goed als nieuw and gebruikt, chosen by the seller. It is a rough sort at best. Delivery (levering) separates ophalen (pickup) from verzenden (shipping); use it to find items you can collect, which are the safer buys.

sections.heading: Sorting
paragraphs: The default order mixes relevance with paid placements. For anything popular, sort by date, newest first. The best deals go within hours and are always at the top of a date-sorted list.

Sorting by price, low to high, sounds useful but surfaces junk: parts, wanted ads, 1 euro listings and accessories. Pair it with a sensible minimum price. Sorting by distance helps when you need the item today.

sections.heading: Search tricks that help
paragraphs: The search box is literal. A few habits make it work better.
bullets: Search in Dutch, and try singular and plural
Use the option to search titles only when descriptions are cluttering results
Exclude noise by picking a narrower subcategory
Try common misspellings of brand names
Watch out for top ads and business listings mixed in with private ones

sections.heading: Saved searches and alerts
paragraphs: Save your search with notifications on (zoekopdracht opslaan). You get an alert in the app or by email when a new listing matches. For competitive items like cheap bikes and good furniture, this is how most people get them first.

Keep saved searches tight, or you will start ignoring the alerts. And remember the filters only see what sellers typed. A search for 'bank 3 zits' will not know whether a sofa has a stain or fits your stairwell. If you would rather write that kind of requirement in plain words and have each listing read for it, that is what vindje.com does.

faq.q: How do I search near me on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Enter your postcode and pick a distance in the filter options. Results then show only listings within that radius.

faq.q: Why do Marktplaats filters miss some listings?
faq.a: Filters only use the fields sellers filled in. If a seller left the brand, size or price field empty, the filter cannot match it.

faq.q: How do I get alerts for new listings?
faq.a: Save your search and turn on notifications. You will be told when new matching listings appear.

faq.q: What does 'gezocht' mean in results?
faq.a: It is a wanted ad: someone looking to buy, not sell. Setting a minimum price filters most of them out.

example_wish: Gazelle or Batavus city bike, frame 53-55 cm, with hand brakes, under 200 euro, within 10 km of Delft

title: How to transport a sofa or wardrobe you bought second hand
meta_title: How to transport a second-hand sofa or wardrobe
description: How to transport a second-hand sofa or wardrobe in the Netherlands: van rental, courier services, furniture lifts and what to measure before you pick up.
intro: For a sofa or wardrobe you have four realistic options: rent a van for a few hours, book a courier that collects from the seller, pay the seller to deliver, or take it apart and use a big car. Before any of that, measure the item and both stairwells, because getting it out and in is usually harder than the drive.

sections.heading: Measure before you book anything
paragraphs: Dutch buildings have steep, narrow stairs with tight turns. Many sofas that fit a living room will not go up a typical Amsterdam or Utrecht staircase. Measure the item's width, depth and height, the narrowest door, and the tightest point on the stairs, including the ceiling height at the turn.

Ask the seller whether the sofa legs unscrew, whether the backrest comes off, and whether a wardrobe can be taken apart. Flat-pack wardrobes like the IKEA PAX can, but chipboard furniture gets weaker every time it is disassembled, and some will not survive it.

sections.heading: Option 1: rent a van
paragraphs: A small van (bestelbus) is the cheapest way to move a big item yourself. Car rental companies, car-sharing apps and some DIY stores rent them by the hour or half day. You need a normal car licence (B) for vans up to 3,500 kg.
Book a van, not a car with a trailer, unless you are used to trailers. Bring two straps, a few old blankets and a helper. Check the cargo length: a three-seat sofa often needs about 2.2 m.
Mind parking. In city centres, loading in front of the seller's door can mean a paid zone or a permit area. A quick stop for loading is common, but check the signs and keep someone with the van.

sections.heading: Option 2: a courier for second-hand items
paragraphs: Courier services such as Brenger specialize in collecting items bought online and delivering them, often with one or two people to carry. You enter both addresses and the size, and get a price. Ask whether carrying up stairs is included or costs extra.

The courier collects from the seller, so you need to pay the seller in advance or have them accept payment on delivery. Agree this in writing. A seller with good reviews who will let you see the item on a video call first is the safer setup.

sections.heading: Option 3: the seller delivers
paragraphs: Some sellers have a van or a friend with one and offer delivery for a fee, often written as 'bezorgen mogelijk' (delivery possible). It is the easiest route, since they carry it out and you only carry it in. You pay on delivery, so the gelijk oversteken principle still holds.

sections.heading: Option 4: furniture lift and hoisting beam
paragraphs: When something will not go up the stairs, the Dutch answer is through the window. Many older canal houses have a hijsbalk (hoisting beam) at the top of the facade, and you can rent a verhuislift (furniture lift) with an operator for a few hours. You may need a parking or permit arrangement with the municipality for the lift on the street, so check that in advance.
It costs more than the sofa in many cases. That is a good moment to reconsider a modular or smaller model.

sections.heading: Small and medium items
paragraphs: Not everything needs a van. A chair, side table, lamp or small cabinet fits in an estate car with the seats folded, and many Dutch people move items like that on a bakfiets or with a bike trailer, which you can rent in most cities. A taxi with a large boot also works for a single chair or a box of kitchenware.

sections.heading: Pickup day checklist
bullets: Tape measure, screwdriver set, Allen keys, a few zip bags for screws
Blankets, straps and stretch wrap to protect corners
A helper with gloves
Exact address, floor, and where to park
Payment ready, cash or banking app
Photo of the item before you move it, in case of damage questions

price_guide.item: Van rental, a few hours, short distance
Courier for a sofa within the same region
Courier across the country, large item
Furniture lift with operator, half day

faq.q: How do I move a sofa without a car in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Book a courier that collects from the seller, rent a van by the hour, or ask the seller whether they deliver for a fee.

faq.q: Can I take a sofa on the train?
faq.a: No, large furniture is not suitable for public transport. Small items like a chair or lamp are a different story.

faq.q: What licence do I need to rent a van?
faq.a: A normal car licence (category B) covers vans up to 3,500 kg total weight.

faq.q: Will a sofa fit up Dutch stairs?
faq.a: Often not. Measure the narrowest turn and ceiling height on the stairs and compare with the sofa's depth and height before you buy.

example_wish: Three-seat sofa with removable legs, depth under 90 cm so it fits narrow stairs, under 250 euro, within 15 km of Amsterdam

title: Furnishing a whole apartment second hand in the Netherlands
meta_title: Furnish an apartment second hand in the Netherlands
description: Furnish an apartment second hand in the Netherlands: what to buy used and what new, a realistic budget, the order to buy in and how to batch pickups.
intro: You can furnish a one-bedroom apartment second hand for around 800 to 1,500 euro if you are patient and have transport for a weekend or two. Buy the bulky, durable things used (sofa, table, wardrobe, appliances), buy the mattress new, and start with what you need to sleep, cook and work.

sections.heading: Start with an inboedel listing
paragraphs: An inboedel is a household's contents. People moving abroad or into care sometimes sell everything at once, as 'complete inboedel' or 'inboedel wegens verhuizing'. You can get a sofa, table, chairs, kitchenware and a bed in one pickup for a few hundred euro.
The catch: you take what they have, and you need a van. Check what you do not want before agreeing, and whether you are expected to take everything.

sections.heading: Buy in this order
paragraphs: Furnishing takes weeks if you do it one listing at a time. Get the basics first so you can live there, then fill in.
bullets: Week 1: bed frame (new mattress), fridge, a table and two chairs, curtains
Week 2: washing machine, sofa, wardrobe or rail
Week 3: desk and office chair, bookcase, lamps
Later: rug, side tables, plants, art

sections.heading: What to buy used, what to buy new
paragraphs: Used is best for things that are built to last, expensive new and easy to check at a pickup. New is best for anything where hygiene or hidden wear matters.
bullets: Used: solid wood tables, bookcases, dressers, office chairs from known brands, washing machines under 6 years, fridges, lamps, kitchen tools
Inspect hard: sofas (smell, springs, stains), beds (squeaks, broken slats)
New: mattress and pillows, and if you can afford it, the bed linen
Skip used: cheap chipboard furniture that has already been moved twice

sections.heading: Batch your pickups
paragraphs: Transport is where the budget goes. Rent a van for one afternoon and plan four or five pickups in the same part of town. Message all the sellers in advance with a time slot. Even with a delay or two, a single van day costs less than three separate couriers.
Small things, such as lamps, kitchen items, cushions and chairs, fit on a bike or in a backpack and are easier to collect one at a time.

sections.heading: Measure the apartment first
paragraphs: Before you buy anything, measure each room, the wall space for a wardrobe, the height under sloping ceilings, the stairs and the door widths. Note the alcove size for the washing machine; many Dutch apartments have a narrow space and a standard 60 cm machine needs a few extra centimetres. Take photos with the tape measure in frame, so you can check them later while scrolling listings.

Writing all your requirements into one search per item (size, condition, distance, budget) saves a lot of scrolling. vindje.com reads every listing against a plain description like that and drops the ones that do not fit.

sections.heading: Kringloop stores as a backup
paragraphs: Thrift stores (kringloopwinkels) have fixed prices and you can see everything in one place. Prices are often a bit above the best Marktplaats deals, but you skip the messaging and some stores deliver for a fee. They are good for kitchenware, lamps, plates and small furniture.

Some cities also have repair cafes, where volunteers help fix a lamp, a toaster or a wobbly chair for free or a small donation. That makes cheap broken items worth a second look if the fault is simple.

sections.heading: A realistic budget
paragraphs: A sensible split for a one-bedroom place: about a third on the bed and sofa, a third on appliances, and the rest on tables, storage and small items. Leave 100 to 150 euro for van rental and the bits nobody thinks of, such as curtain rails, light fittings, an extension lead and a toolbox. A new mattress adds 150 to 400 euro on top, depending on size and type.

faq.q: How much does it cost to furnish an apartment second hand in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Roughly 800 to 1,500 euro for a one-bedroom apartment, plus van rental. Doing it fast or picky pushes it up.

faq.q: Should I buy a used mattress?
faq.a: Better not. You cannot check hygiene, bedbugs or sagging properly. Buy the mattress new and the bed frame used.

faq.q: What is an inboedel?
faq.a: The contents of a household. A 'complete inboedel' listing means someone is selling all their furniture and household goods together.

faq.q: Where can I buy cheap second-hand furniture besides Marktplaats?
faq.a: Kringloop thrift stores, local Facebook groups, and curbside giveaways around the end of the month.

example_wish: Complete inboedel or several furniture items from one seller moving out: sofa, dining table and bed, under 500 euro total, near Rotterdam

title: How to buy a used bike in the Netherlands
meta_title: How to buy a used bike in the Netherlands
description: How to buy a used bike in the Netherlands: which brands hold up, what to test at the pickup, how to avoid stolen bikes, and fair used prices in 2026.
intro: A good used city bike in the Netherlands costs about 120 to 300 euro, from a private seller who can show you the keys for every lock and lets you ride it around the block. Stick to Dutch city bike brands like Gazelle, Batavus, Sparta and Cortina, check the frame number against the police Stop Heling register, and walk away from anything cheap offered on the street.

sections.heading: Pick the type of bike
paragraphs: Most people need a city bike (stadsfiets): upright position, mudguards, chain guard, rack, lights and a frame lock. It works for commuting, groceries and rain. Choose between a herenfiets (men's frame, top tube) and damesfiets (women's or step-through, easier in a skirt or with a child seat). Anyone can ride either.

Gears: a single speed with coaster brake (terugtraprem) is fine for flat cities and the cheapest to maintain. A 3, 7 or 8 speed hub gear (Shimano Nexus, Sturmey Archer) handles bridges and wind. Hub gears are sealed and last for years; derailleur gears on a city bike need more care.

sections.heading: Brands and what they cost
paragraphs: Dutch city bike brands are built for daily use outdoors and parts are easy to find. Gazelle, Batavus, Sparta, Cortina, Union, Azor and Workcycles all keep their value. Cheap supermarket or webshop bikes under 300 euro new are worth very little used and rust fast.

Frame size matters more than brand. Typical sizes: 49 to 53 cm for 160 to 170 cm tall, 53 to 57 cm for 170 to 182 cm, 57 to 61 cm above that. You should be able to stand over the frame and reach the ground on tiptoes from the saddle.

sections.heading: Avoiding stolen bikes
paragraphs: Bike theft is common in Dutch cities, and many stolen bikes are resold online. Buying one, even unknowingly, can cost you the bike without a refund. Clear signs: a price far below similar bikes, no key for the frame lock, a seller who wants to meet on the street instead of at home, or a lock that has been cut.
