Ask for the frame number (framenummer) before you go and check it in the police Stop Heling register. At the pickup, check that the number on the frame matches, usually stamped under the bottom bracket or on the rear dropout. A receipt or a registration card in the seller's name is a strong plus.

sections.heading: Test ride checklist
paragraphs: Ride it at least two minutes. These checks take about five more.
bullets: Brakes stop firmly, front and back, without scraping
Gears shift through every step without jumping or slipping
Wheels spin straight, no wobble, no grinding in the hubs
Grab the saddle and handlebars: no play in the headset or seat post
Chain not rusty orange or stretched, no skipping under load
Tyres not cracked on the sides, valves not leaking
Lights work, front and back, dynamo or battery
Frame lock and any chain lock open with the keys you get

sections.heading: What repairs cost
paragraphs: Factor small repairs into your offer. At a Dutch bike shop, new tyre and tube is roughly 30 to 50 euro per wheel, a new chain 25 to 50 euro fitted, a brake service 20 to 40 euro, and a new rear wheel with hub gear can be 150 euro or more. A bike that needs both wheels redone is rarely a bargain.
Squeaks and a dull chain are normal. A bent rear wheel, a seized hub gear or rust holes in the frame are reasons to skip.

sections.heading: Where else to look
paragraphs: Bike shops sell used bikes with a few months of warranty, usually 50 to 100 euro above private prices. For students and new arrivals, that can be worth it. Local refurbishers and social projects also sell checked bikes at fair prices. For private listings, the trick is to search for size and gear type together, not only 'fiets'. Something like 'herenfiets 57 cm 7 versnellingen' cuts out most of the noise.

price_guide.item: Gazelle or Batavus city bike, 3-8 gears
Hybrid or trekking bike with derailleur gears

faq.q: How much should I pay for a used bike in the Netherlands?
faq.a: A decent used city bike from a private seller is usually 120 to 300 euro. Under 60 euro is either a project or a warning sign.

faq.q: How do I check if a used bike is stolen?
faq.a: Ask for the frame number and check it in the police Stop Heling register. Make sure the seller has keys for every lock and lets you see it at their home.

faq.q: What size bike do I need?
faq.a: Roughly 53 to 57 cm frame for people between 170 and 182 cm tall. You should reach the ground on tiptoes from the saddle.

faq.q: Should I buy a cheap bike from someone on the street?
faq.a: No. Bikes offered on the street for 20 or 30 euro are very often stolen, and buying one is a crime.

example_wish: Gazelle or Batavus women's city bike, 7 gears, frame 53-55 cm, with lights and frame lock key, under 250 euro, within 10 km of Utrecht

title: Buying a used e-bike: battery, motor and price checks
meta_title: Buying a used e-bike: battery, motor and price checks
description: Buying a used e-bike in the Netherlands: how to check battery health, mid or hub motor, charger and keys, theft risk, and what a fair price looks like.
intro: The battery decides what a used e-bike is worth. A replacement costs roughly 450 to 800 euro, so ask for proof of its health before you agree a price, and make sure the charger and both keys come with it. A 3 to 5 year old e-bike with a mid-motor from Bosch, Shimano or Yamaha and a healthy battery usually sells for 900 to 1,600 euro.

sections.heading: Mid-motor or hub motor
paragraphs: A mid-motor sits at the pedals and drives the chain. Bosch, Shimano Steps and Yamaha are the common ones on Dutch brands like Gazelle, Batavus, Sparta, Stromer and Riese and Muller. They feel natural, handle hills and wind well, and are easy to service at almost any bike shop.

A hub motor sits in the front or rear wheel. It is cheaper and quieter, common on budget brands and older models, and fine for flat commutes. Parts and diagnostics for lesser-known hub systems can be hard to find, which hurts resale value.

sections.heading: Checking the battery
paragraphs: Batteries lose capacity with charge cycles and age. A typical lithium battery is in good shape until roughly 500 to 1,000 full cycles, depending on the brand and how it was stored. Capacity is printed on it in Wh: 400, 500 or 625 Wh are common.

Ask the seller for a diagnostic printout from a bike shop, or a screenshot from the brand's app. Bosch and Shimano systems can show charge cycles and remaining capacity this way. No proof means you price in the risk of a new battery. On the test ride, start full, ride a few minutes in the highest assist and watch whether the charge indicator drops unusually fast.

sections.heading: At the pickup
paragraphs: Test it the way you will use it, including a short hill or bridge.
bullets: Motor assists smoothly in every level, no clicking or grinding
Display works, no error codes
Battery locks into the frame and comes out with the key
Two keys for the battery and frame lock, or at least one plus a code
Original charger included and matches the battery brand
Brakes strong: e-bikes are heavier and faster, hydraulic or roller brakes in good shape
Chain and cassette not worn; e-bikes wear drivetrains faster
Frame number checked in the Stop Heling register

sections.heading: Theft and tuning
paragraphs: E-bikes are among the most stolen items in the Netherlands, so the stolen goods checks matter even more than for a normal bike. No charger, no battery key, or a battery from a different brand are red flags.

Avoid bikes advertised as 'opgevoerd' (tuned) to go faster than 25 km/h. A tuned bike is no longer legal as a normal e-bike on the road. A speed pedelec, which assists up to 45 km/h, is a separate category that needs a yellow number plate, insurance and a helmet, so check the paperwork if you buy one.

sections.heading: Battery tips that affect price
paragraphs: A bike stored in a cold shed with a flat battery all winter may have a damaged battery even with low mileage. Ask where it was kept. Also ask about the warranty: some brands extend the battery warranty for the first owner only, so it may not transfer.
If the battery is weak but the bike is otherwise good, a lower price can still make it a fair buy. Do the math: asking price plus a new battery should stay well below a new bike of the same quality.

sections.heading: Fair prices in 2026
paragraphs: Prices depend most on motor, battery, age and brand. Listings from 2019 and earlier with weak batteries are plentiful and should be cheap. Lease bikes returned after a contract sometimes appear in good condition with dealer service history. Search the brand, the motor and a year, for example 'Gazelle Bosch middenmotor 2022', to compare like with like.

price_guide.item: Older e-bike with front hub motor
Premium mid-motor (e.g. Gazelle, Riese and Muller), 1-3 years

faq.q: How do I check the battery of a used e-bike?
faq.a: Ask for a bike shop diagnostic or the brand app screenshot showing charge cycles and remaining capacity. On the test ride, watch how fast the charge drops in high assist.

faq.q: How long does an e-bike battery last?
faq.a: Usually several years and many hundreds of full cycles, depending on brand and storage. A weak battery is the most expensive part to replace.

faq.q: Is a used e-bike worth buying?
faq.a: Yes, if the battery is healthy and the price reflects its age. Compare the price plus a possible new battery with a new bike.

faq.q: What is a speed pedelec?
faq.a: An e-bike that assists up to 45 km/h. In the Netherlands it needs a number plate, insurance and a helmet, and it cannot use every bike path.

example_wish: Gazelle or Batavus e-bike with Bosch mid-motor, battery at least 500 Wh, from 2021 or newer, with charger and two keys, under 1,400 euro, within 25 km of Amersfoort

title: Buying a second-hand bakfiets (cargo bike)
meta_title: Buying a second-hand bakfiets: models, checks, prices
description: Buying a second-hand bakfiets: two wheels or three, which brands hold value, what to check on the box, steering and motor, recalls, and fair used prices.
intro: A used bakfiets is a good buy if the frame, steering and box are sound, and an expensive mistake if they are not. Decide first between a two-wheeler (faster, narrower, harder to learn) and a three-wheeler (stable when stopped, wide, slower in corners), then check the box floor, steering play and, on electric models, the battery. Expect 500 euro for an older non-electric model and 2,000 euro or more for a recent electric Urban Arrow.

sections.heading: Two wheels or three
paragraphs: Two-wheel bakfietsen (Urban Arrow, Bakfiets.nl Cargobike, Workcycles Kr8, Riese and Muller Load) ride much like a long bike once you have practiced for an afternoon. They fit through bike path gates and are faster.

Three-wheelers (Christiania, Babboe Big and Curve, many Johnny Loco and Nihola models) stand on their own, which is easy with toddlers climbing in. They lean the wrong way in corners, are wide on narrow paths and are heavier. Test ride both before you decide which type to buy.

sections.heading: Check the box and seats
paragraphs: Wooden boxes rot at the floor and corners if the bike stood outside under a rain tent for years. Press the floor with your thumb; soft spots mean a new box. Foam boxes (Urban Arrow) can crack or dent. Check the bench, the seat belts and their buckles, and whether a rain tent (huif) comes along, since a new one costs 150 to 300 euro.

sections.heading: Steering, frame and brakes
paragraphs: Most two-wheelers steer the front wheel through a rod under the box. Hold the front wheel between your knees and turn the handlebar: any clunk or free play means worn joints. Three-wheelers turn the whole box; check the pivot for play and rust.

Look closely at welds around the head tube and where the box meets the frame. In 2024 Babboe recalled a large number of its cargo bikes after reports of frame breakage. If you look at a Babboe built before then, ask whether it was inspected or repaired under the recall and ask for proof. Brakes should be hydraulic disc or roller brakes in good shape; a loaded bakfiets is heavy.

sections.heading: Electric models
paragraphs: Most bakfietsen sold today are electric, and the better ones use a mid-motor, most often from Bosch or Shimano. Ask for a battery diagnostic and the charger, and test the bike on a bridge with someone in the box if you can. Front hub motors on budget three-wheelers can struggle with a full load and wind.
Cargo bike batteries work hard, so a five-year-old battery used for a daily school run may be near the end. Budget 500 to 900 euro for a replacement.

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
bullets: Box floor solid, no soft or black wood
No play in steering rod or pivot
No cracks at welds, especially around the head tube and box mounts
Kickstand holds the bike stable with the box loaded
Brakes stop a loaded bike firmly
Battery diagnostic, charger and two keys
Recall status for Babboe models
Frame number checked in the police Stop Heling register

sections.heading: Where the good ones turn up
paragraphs: Families sell when the youngest is around five or six, often in late summer before school starts. That is a good moment to buy. Specialist cargo bike shops also sell used ones with a check and a short warranty, for a few hundred euro more. Search the brand name plus 'elektrisch' and narrow by distance, since you need to test ride it and riding one home can take a while.

Accessories add up, so note what is included: rain tent, child seats with belts, a baby seat adapter (maxi-cosi houder), a lock and a cover. A listing with all of them can be worth 300 to 500 euro more than the bare bike. A good frame lock plus a heavy chain lock is the minimum for something this expensive and this easy to spot.

price_guide.item: Electric Urban Arrow Family, 2-5 years old

faq.q: How much is a used bakfiets in the Netherlands?
faq.a: From about 500 euro for an older non-electric model to 2,000 to 4,000 euro for a recent electric Urban Arrow or Riese and Muller.

faq.q: Is a two-wheel or three-wheel bakfiets better?
faq.a: Two-wheelers are faster and narrower, three-wheelers stand still without tipping and are easier for nervous riders. Test both.

faq.q: What was the Babboe recall about?
faq.a: In 2024 Babboe recalled many cargo bikes over frame breakage. When buying a used Babboe, ask whether it was inspected or repaired under the recall.

faq.q: Can I transport a bakfiets in a car?
faq.a: Usually not. Plan to ride it home, or use a van or a courier that handles large bikes.

example_wish: Two-wheel electric bakfiets, Urban Arrow or similar with Bosch mid-motor, with rain tent, under 2,500 euro, within 30 km of Utrecht

title: Used road bike (racefiets): sizing and what to check
meta_title: Used road bike sizing and checks: buying a racefiets
description: Buying a used road bike (racefiets): how to pick the right frame size, which groupsets to look for, how to spot carbon damage and wear, and fair prices.
intro: Get the size right first, then judge the groupset and the wear. Most riders between 172 and 182 cm fit a 54 to 56 cm frame, but brands measure differently, so compare stack and reach and do a test ride. An aluminium road bike with Shimano 105 in good order sells for about 400 to 750 euro used, and carbon bikes need a careful look for cracks.

sections.heading: Frame size
paragraphs: Road bike sizes are usually given in cm, sometimes as S, M, L. As a starting point:
bullets: 160 to 167 cm tall: 49 to 52 cm frame
167 to 174 cm: 52 to 54 cm
174 to 182 cm: 54 to 56 cm
182 to 189 cm: 56 to 58 cm
Above 189 cm: 58 to 61 cm

sections.heading: Beyond the number
paragraphs: A 56 from one brand can ride like a 54 from another, because the cm figure is measured along the seat tube in different ways. Look up the geometry of the exact model and year and compare two numbers: stack (how high the handlebars sit) and reach (how far forward). If your current bike fits, compare with that.

On the test ride, you should be able to reach the brake hoods with a slight bend in your elbows, without locking your arms or feeling cramped. Saddle height can be set, and a stem swap can fix a centimetre or two of reach, but not a wrong frame. A rough saddle height is your inseam times 0.883, measured from the centre of the bottom bracket to the top of the saddle.

sections.heading: Groupsets and what they tell you
paragraphs: The groupset (gears and brakes) says a lot about the bike's quality and value. Shimano's road ranges from entry to top are Claris, Sora, Tiagra, 105, Ultegra and Dura-Ace. SRAM and Campagnolo have their own lines. A 105 bike is the sweet spot for most riders: durable, light enough and cheap to maintain.

Disc brakes are now standard on newer bikes and stop better in the wet. Older rim-brake bikes are cheaper and lighter, and plenty of riders still prefer them, but check the rims for wear: many have a small indicator groove or dot that disappears when the rim is worn.

sections.heading: Checking a carbon frame
paragraphs: Carbon is strong but can hide damage after a crash. Look and feel carefully, ideally in daylight.
bullets: Cracks or lifted paint around the head tube, bottom bracket and seat clamp
Scratches or dents on the top tube from a handlebar swinging round
Damage to the rear dropouts and derailleur hanger area
Tap gently with a coin: a dull, flat sound in one spot can mean delamination
Ask directly whether it has been crashed, and why it is for sale

sections.heading: Wear on any road bike
paragraphs: Chains, cassettes and chainrings wear together. A chain checker tool costs a few euro; if the chain is stretched, the cassette is probably worn too, which adds 60 to 150 euro to your costs. Shift through every gear on the stand and on the ride. A rear derailleur that sits crooked usually means a bent hanger from a fall.
Spin the wheels: they should run straight and quietly, and the hubs should feel smooth. Check the tyres for cuts, and ask when the bar tape and cables were last replaced.

sections.heading: Vintage steel racefietsen
paragraphs: Older steel racefietsen from Dutch and Italian brands, such as Gazelle Champion Mondial, Batavus, Koga Miyata, Peugeot and Bianchi, are popular and often affordable. Many need new tyres, cables and brake pads. Check for rust inside the frame, a stuck seat post and stretched chains. Vintage bikes use older standards, so replacement parts can take some hunting. Searching for frame size and groupset together saves a lot of scrolling, since many listings bury the size in the description.

faq.q: What size road bike do I need for my height?
faq.a: As a start: 52 to 54 cm for 167 to 174 cm, 54 to 56 cm for 174 to 182 cm, 56 to 58 cm for 182 to 189 cm. Check the model's stack and reach before buying.

faq.q: Is a used carbon road bike safe?
faq.a: Usually, if it has not been crashed. Inspect the head tube, bottom bracket and top tube for cracks and ask about crash history.

faq.q: What is a good groupset on a used road bike?
faq.a: Shimano 105 is the best value for most riders. Tiagra is fine for occasional rides, Ultegra adds lighter weight and finer shifting.

faq.q: What is a racefiets?
faq.a: Dutch for road bike: drop handlebars, narrow tyres and a light frame, built for speed on tarmac.

example_wish: Road bike with Shimano 105, frame 56 cm, aluminium or carbon, not crashed, under 800 euro, within 25 km of Eindhoven

title: Kids bike sizes by age and height, and buying them used
meta_title: Kids Bike Sizes by Age and Height: Used Buying Guide
description: Kids bike sizes by age and height in inches, which Dutch brands last, what to check on a used kinderfiets and fair prices for 12 to 24 inch bikes.
intro: Kids bikes are sized by wheel diameter in inches, and height matters more than age: a child of about 105-120 cm fits a 16 inch bike, 115-135 cm a 20 inch, 130-150 cm a 24 inch. Because children outgrow a bike in two or three years, buying used makes a lot of sense, and Marktplaats is full of sturdy Dutch kids bikes that have already been through one owner.

sections.heading: Size chart: wheel size by height and age
paragraphs: Use inseam and height first, age second. Two six year olds can be 110 cm and 128 cm tall, and they need different bikes. When the child sits on the saddle, both feet should reach the ground with the balls of the feet. For a first bike with pedals, flat feet on the ground is better because it gives confidence.
Dutch sellers list size in inches (inch or the quote mark), and sometimes the frame size in cm. Wheel size is what you search on.
bullets: Loopfiets (balance bike), 10-12 inch: roughly 2-4 years, 85-100 cm
12 inch: roughly 3-4 years, 90-105 cm
14 inch: roughly 3-5 years, 95-110 cm
16 inch: roughly 4-6 years, 105-120 cm
18 inch: roughly 5-7 years, 110-125 cm
20 inch: roughly 6-9 years, 115-135 cm
22 inch: roughly 8-10 years, 125-140 cm
24 inch: roughly 8-12 years, 130-150 cm
26 inch or small adult frame: from about 145 cm

sections.heading: Growing room without overdoing it
paragraphs: Parents love to buy one size up so the bike lasts longer. A little room is fine: the seatpost can go up 8-10 cm on most kids bikes. But a bike that is too big is heavy and hard to stop, and a nervous child on a bike they can't control will ride less. If your child is between sizes, pick the smaller one for a first or second bike and the bigger one for a confident rider.
Check how far the seatpost can still extend. It has a minimum insert line, and if the seller's photo already shows it near that line, the bike has less life left in it than you think.

sections.heading: Coaster brake, hand brakes and gears
paragraphs: Most Dutch kids bikes in 12-16 inch have a terugtraprem (coaster brake): you pedal backwards to stop. Many Dutch children learn this way and it works well, but if your child learned on a balance bike, a bike with two hand brakes can feel more natural. From 20 inch up you often see a 3-speed hub (Shimano Nexus 3) plus a coaster brake, and from 24 inch some bikes have 7 gears.
Gears on a 20 inch bike are nice in a hilly town, but in most of the Netherlands a single speed or 3-speed hub is plenty and has less to go wrong.

sections.heading: Which brands hold up
paragraphs: Kids bikes from Dutch brands are built heavy and simple, which is exactly what you want after years of being dropped in a schoolyard. Batavus, Gazelle, Cortina, Alpina, Popal, Loekie and Volare are common on Marktplaats. Alpina and Cortina have a good name for durability. Lightweight bikes like Woom are pricier new and hold their value well used, so a used Woom is rarely a bargain but is often worth it for a smaller child, since a 16 inch Woom weighs a lot less than a steel Dutch bike.
Supermarket and discount bikes with plastic parts and caliper brakes tend to wear out after one child. Fine for 25 euro, not for 90.

sections.heading: Checklist at the pickup
paragraphs: Bring your child if you can. Fit is everything and a two minute test ride tells you more than any photo.
bullets: Coaster brake: lift the rear wheel, pedal backwards, the wheel should lock hard
Hand brakes: squeeze, the lever must not touch the handlebar
Chain: no rust flakes, no stiff links, the chain guard (kettingkast) not cracked
Wheels: spin them, look for wobble and loose spokes
Tyres: cracks on the sidewall mean new tyres, budget EUR 15-25 each
Seatpost and stem: loosen and move them, seized parts are a pain
Bell and reflectors: required on the road and cheap to add if missing
Frame: look under the bottom bracket for cracks and heavy rust

sections.heading: Searching on Marktplaats
paragraphs: Search the wheel size with the Dutch word: kinderfiets 16 inch, meisjesfiets 20 inch, jongensfiets 24 inch. Many listings are labelled by gender but the frames are close to identical, so search both and you double your choice. The best time to look is late summer and around birthdays in spring, when families sell the outgrown bike. On vindje.com you can type something like a 20 inch bike with hand brakes and 3 gears within 10 km, and it reads the listings for the brake type and gears so you don't have to open each one.

faq.q: What size bike for a 5 year old?
faq.a: Most 5 year olds ride a 16 inch bike. A tall 5 year old around 115 cm can manage an 18 inch, a small one is better on a 14 inch.

faq.q: What size bike for a 7 or 8 year old?
faq.a: Usually a 20 inch bike, which suits children from about 115 to 135 cm. A tall 8 year old may already fit a 24 inch.

faq.q: Is it better to buy a kids bike used?
faq.a: Usually yes. Children outgrow bikes in two or three years, Dutch kids bikes are built to last, and a used 16 inch costs a third of a new one.

faq.q: Should a kids bike have a coaster brake?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Coaster brakes are common in the Netherlands and work fine, but many children who learned on a balance bike find hand brakes easier.

example_wish: 20 inch kids bike with hand brakes and 3 gears for a 7 year old, good condition, under 120 euro, within 10 km

title: How to avoid buying a stolen bike on Marktplaats
meta_title: How to Avoid Buying a Stolen Bike in the Netherlands
description: How to avoid buying a stolen bike in the Netherlands: check the frame number, spot red flags in the listing and at the meetup, and know what to ask.
intro: The safest way to avoid buying a stolen bike is to check the frame number, ask for the original keys and receipt, and walk away from deals that are too cheap or too rushed. Bike theft is common in the Netherlands, and buying a bike you should have suspected was stolen can get you into legal trouble, not just lose you the bike.

sections.heading: Why it matters to you as a buyer
paragraphs: Under Dutch law, buying goods you knew or could reasonably have suspected were stolen counts as heling. The police do check bikes, and if a bike you bought turns out to be stolen it can be taken back and returned to the owner, without you getting your money back. So the question is not only whether you feel the seller is honest, it is whether a reasonable person would have asked more questions at that price.
The good news: most bikes on Marktplaats are sold by ordinary people moving house or upgrading. A few checks separate them from the rest.

sections.heading: Check the frame number
paragraphs: Every bike has a framenummer, usually stamped under the bottom bracket (turn the bike over or look between the pedals), sometimes on the rear dropout or the seat tube. Ask the seller to send a photo of it before you travel. A seller who refuses, or a frame number that looks filed, scratched or painted over, is a reason to stop right there.

With the frame number you can check the police-backed register at stopheling.nl, which lists bikes and other goods reported stolen. A clean result does not prove the bike is legit (not every theft is reported with the number), but a hit is a clear answer. Many newer bikes also have an AXA or similar lock key with a registration code, and e-bikes often have a registered battery and key.

sections.heading: Red flags in the listing
paragraphs: Most stolen bikes are sold fast and cheap. Read the listing like a detective.
bullets: Price far below the going rate: a recent Gazelle e-bike for EUR 300, a VanMoof for EUR 200
Stock photos or photos taken on a street instead of in a hallway, shed or garden
Vague text: no model name, no frame size, no history
A brand new account, or one account selling several similar bikes at once
Wants to meet at a train station or on a street corner, never at home
Asks for payment upfront or wants to send the bike by courier

sections.heading: Red flags at the meetup
paragraphs: Questions do more work than inspection here. An owner knows their bike: where they bought it, roughly when, why the left brake squeaks. Ask a few and listen.
bullets: No key for the frame lock (ringslot), or the lock is missing or freshly cut
Only one key, with a story about the other being lost
Seller doesn't know the frame size, gears or year
The seat is set for someone much shorter or taller than the seller
Rush: 'I need to go now, cash only, no time for a test ride'
Fresh spray paint or stickers covering the frame

sections.heading: What to ask for
paragraphs: The original aankoopbon (receipt) is the best proof. Many sellers don't have it for an older bike, which is normal, but for anything above a few hundred euro, or any e-bike, you should expect it, or at least a bank statement or warranty card. Both keys of the ringslot should come with the bike. For e-bikes, also the battery key, the charger and, for brands with an app, a proper transfer of the bike to your account.

Write down the seller's name, phone number and the frame number, and take a photo of the bike with the seller's ID if they offer it. Pay by bank transfer or Tikkie at the handover rather than cash: it leaves a trace, and honest sellers rarely object.

sections.heading: If you think it might be stolen
paragraphs: Don't buy it, and don't try to play police. If you have a strong suspicion, for example the frame number shows up in the register, you can report it to the police at 0900-8844 or via politie.nl. If you already bought a bike and later find out it was stolen, contact the police yourself. Being open about it is much better than being found with it.

faq.q: How do I check if a bike is stolen in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Ask for the frame number and check it at stopheling.nl, the register used by the Dutch police. Also ask for both lock keys and the original receipt.

faq.q: Where is the frame number on a bike?
faq.a: Usually stamped under the bottom bracket, between the pedals. On some bikes it is on the rear dropout or the seat tube.

faq.q: Is it illegal to buy a stolen bike without knowing?
faq.a: If you could reasonably have suspected it was stolen, for example because of a very low price or no keys, it can count as heling under Dutch law. The bike can also be taken back without compensation.

faq.q: Is a bike without a receipt always stolen?
faq.a: No. Many people lose receipts for older bikes. Combine it with the other checks: keys, frame number, price and how well the seller knows the bike.

example_wish: Gazelle or Batavus city bike, frame size 57, with both keys and receipt, under 300 euro, within 15 km

title: Omafiets, opafiets or city bike: which used Dutch bike to buy
meta_title: Omafiets vs City Bike: Which Used Dutch Bike to Buy
description: Omafiets, opafiets or city bike? How the classic Dutch bikes differ in weight, gears and brakes, and what a fair used price is in the Netherlands.
intro: An omafiets is the classic upright Dutch bike with a low step-through frame, often one gear and a coaster brake. An opafiets is the same idea with a men's frame and a top tube. A city bike (stadsfiets) is lighter, usually has 3 to 8 gears and hand brakes, and is the better pick if you ride more than a few kilometres a day.

sections.heading: What the names mean
paragraphs: These words are used loosely on Marktplaats, so read the specs, not just the title. In general:
bullets: Omafiets: step-through frame, very upright, heavy (often 20-25 kg), single speed or 3-speed hub, coaster brake and sometimes rod brakes, full chain guard and skirt guard
Opafiets: the same build with a straight top tube, often a bit stiffer and taller
Stadsfiets or city bike: modern frame, 3, 7 or 8 gears in a hub, roller or V-brakes, dynamo lights, usually 16-20 kg
Transportfiets: an oma or opa bike with a sturdy front carrier, built for groceries and crates
Damesfiets and herenfiets: just ladies and gents frame, can be any of the above

sections.heading: Which one fits how you ride
paragraphs: If you ride 2-3 km to the station or the supermarket on flat streets, an omafiets is great. You sit upright, see traffic, and there is almost nothing to maintain. It looks the part too.

If you ride 5-10 km each way, face wind on open roads, or have a bridge or two, get a city bike with at least 7 gears. Wind is the Dutch hill, and pushing a 24 kg single speed into a headwind gets old fast. If you carry kids or heavy shopping, a transportfiets or a city bike with a strong rear rack (draagvermogen 25 kg or more) is worth seeking out.

sections.heading: Brands and models to look for
paragraphs: Gazelle, Batavus, Sparta and Union are the mainstream Dutch brands and parts are easy to get at any bike shop. The Gazelle Tour Populair and Batavus Old Dutch are the classic omafiets models. For city bikes, look at the Gazelle Chamonix or Esprit, Batavus Mambo or Diva, and Sparta Pick-Up. Cortina and Azor (and Workcycles, which builds on Azor frames) are known for heavy transport bikes that last decades.
Many cheap omafietsen from webshops look the same in photos but use thin steel, weak spokes and plastic hubs. They rust quickly and are not worth more than about EUR 75 used.

sections.heading: Checks for a used Dutch bike
paragraphs: These bikes are simple, which makes them easy to judge in five minutes.
bullets: Hub gears: shift through all gears while riding, no slipping or clicking under load
Coaster brake: pedal backwards hard, it should stop you without a delay
Roller brakes (front): they can be weak by design, but should not squeal like metal on metal
Rust: surface rust on the rims and chain is normal, rust bubbling under the paint on the frame is not
Chain guard: a closed kettingkast should not rub on the chain
Frame size: for the upright Dutch position most adults ride 53-61 cm, measure seat tube or ask

sections.heading: Buying from a shop or a private seller
paragraphs: Bike shops and refurbishers sell checked used bikes with a short warranty for roughly EUR 75-150 more than a private sale. For a first bike in the Netherlands that premium can be worth it, since they will sort the lights, brakes and tyres. From a private seller you pay less but take the risk, so ask for the keys and check the frame number. On vindje.com you can ask for a step-through bike with 7 gears and hand brakes and it filters out the listings that only say omafiets in the title but have one gear.

price_guide.item: Gazelle Tour Populair or Batavus Old Dutch
Refurbished city bike from a shop

faq.q: What is the difference between an omafiets and an opafiets?
faq.a: The frame. An omafiets has a low step-through frame, an opafiets has a horizontal top tube. Both are upright, heavy and simple.

faq.q: Is an omafiets good for commuting?
faq.a: For short flat trips, yes. For more than about 5 km each way or with headwind, a city bike with 7 or 8 gears is much easier.

faq.q: How much should I pay for a used omafiets?
faq.a: A decent used omafiets from a known Dutch brand costs about EUR 150-350. Very cheap ones under EUR 75 are often webshop bikes or need work.

faq.q: What frame size Dutch bike do I need?
faq.a: As a rough guide, riders around 165-175 cm fit a 53-57 cm frame and 175-190 cm a 57-61 cm frame. Test ride if you can.

example_wish: Ladies city bike with 7 gears and hand brakes, frame size 53 or 54, lights working, under 250 euro, within 10 km

title: Buying a used Gazelle bike: models and prices
meta_title: Used Gazelle Bike: Models, Prices and What to Check
description: Buying a used Gazelle bike: which models are common on Marktplaats, what fair prices look like for city and e-bikes, and what to check before you pay.
intro: Gazelle is the most common Dutch bike brand on Marktplaats, and a used one is usually a safe buy because they last and every bike shop can fix them. Expect to pay about EUR 150-350 for a good non-electric city bike and EUR 800-1800 for a recent e-bike, depending on model, age and battery.

sections.heading: The models you will see most
paragraphs: Gazelle uses model names for years, so check the year too. A few names to know:
bullets: Tour Populair: the classic black omafiets or opafiets, often with rod brakes, built to last decades
Chamonix, Esprit, Paris, Primeur: everyday city bikes, 3 to 8 gears, often from the 2000s and 2010s
Orange (C7, C8, C7 HMB): comfortable city and touring bike, popular as both normal and electric
Miss Grace and Heavy Duty NL: stylish city and transport bikes
Arroyo, Grenoble, Ultimate, Medeo: e-bikes, Arroyo being the comfortable low-step option

sections.heading: Reading the model code
paragraphs: Gazelle names often end in a code. C7 or C8 means a Shimano Nexus hub with 7 or 8 gears, and HMB means hydraulic rim brakes (Magura). A plus sign or 'HMB Elite' usually marks an electric version. Frame sizes are in cm, typically 46, 49, 53, 57 and 61. If you are 1.70 m, 53 is a common pick on a ladies frame, 57 on a gents frame.
The year is often on a sticker or can be found with the frame number at a Gazelle dealer. Sellers sometimes guess, so a 'recent' bike might be eight years old.

sections.heading: Electric Gazelles: the battery decides the price
paragraphs: Most Gazelle e-bikes from the last several years use a Bosch motor (Active Line or Performance Line), either in the middle or in the front hub on cheaper models. Bosch parts and diagnosis are widely available, which is a big reason Gazelle e-bikes hold their value. Older Gazelle e-bikes can have systems where parts are harder to find, so be more careful with anything around ten years old.

A new battery for a Bosch system costs several hundred euro. Ask the seller how far it goes on one charge and how many charge cycles it has had. A Gazelle dealer can read out cycles and capacity with the Bosch diagnostic tool, so offer to meet at a shop if the bike is expensive.

sections.heading: Checklist for a used Gazelle
bullets: Ask for both frame lock keys and, for e-bikes, the battery key and charger
Ride it: shift through every gear, the Nexus hub should not jump
Hydraulic brakes (HMB): the lever should feel firm, not spongy
Front fork and headset: hold the front brake and rock the bike, no clunk
E-bike: check the display for error codes, test all assist levels on a short ride
Battery: no cracks in the casing, clicks firmly in place, charger matches
Frame number: photo before you travel, check it on stopheling.nl

sections.heading: Where the good deals are
paragraphs: Gazelles hold value well, so a 'too good' price on a recent e-bike is a warning sign, not luck. The better deals are older non-electric bikes from people who switched to an e-bike, and e-bikes sold with a weaker battery at an honest discount. If you want a specific model and size, describing it in plain words on vindje.com (say, an Orange C7 in 57 cm under 300 euro) saves opening dozens of listings that just say Gazelle fiets.

Avoid paying near-new prices for an e-bike without a receipt, and don't let a shiny frame distract you from a tired battery. Dealers sell used Gazelle e-bikes with a battery check and warranty, which is the fair benchmark.

price_guide.item: Gazelle Arroyo or Grenoble e-bike, 3-6 years old

faq.q: Is a used Gazelle bike worth it?
faq.a: Usually yes. They are built to last, parts are easy to get, and any Dutch bike shop can service one.

faq.q: How much is a second hand Gazelle e-bike?
faq.a: A 3 to 6 year old Arroyo or Grenoble usually sells for about EUR 900-1800. The battery condition matters more than the paint.

faq.q: What does C7 mean on a Gazelle?
faq.a: It means a Shimano Nexus hub with 7 gears. C8 is 8 gears, and HMB means hydraulic rim brakes.

faq.q: How do I know how old my Gazelle is?
faq.a: A Gazelle dealer can look up the year with the frame number. Some bikes also have the year on a sticker on the frame.

example_wish: Gazelle Orange C7 or Chamonix, gents frame 57 cm, non-electric, good brakes, under 300 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used VanMoof: what to check after the bankruptcy
meta_title: Buying a Used VanMoof: What to Check in 2026
description: Buying a used VanMoof S3, X3, S5 or A5: how to check the digital key, ownership transfer, known faults and repair options, and what prices are fair now.
intro: A used VanMoof can be a good deal, but only if the bike's digital key is properly transferred to you and the known weak points work. VanMoof went bankrupt in 2023 and the brand was taken over by Lavoie, so service exists again, but many S3 and X3 bikes depend on the app and on parts that are not cheap. Prices have dropped a lot, which also attracts stolen and broken bikes.

sections.heading: The models you will see
paragraphs: The S3 (large frame) and X3 (compact frame) from 2020 are by far the most common on Marktplaats. The S5 and A5 came in 2023, just before the bankruptcy, and are less common and more expensive. Older Electrified S2 and X2 bikes and non-electric models still turn up too. Under the new owner newer models have followed, but those are rarely cheap used.

All of them are designed around the app: opening the lock, settings and diagnostics go through your phone, and the bike is tied to an account. That is the core difference with any other used e-bike: you are buying hardware plus an account link, and both need to work.

sections.heading: The digital key is the first check
paragraphs: Without the digital key, a VanMoof is hard to use and can lock itself. After the bankruptcy, owners were urged to export their keys, and third-party apps made that possible. Today the seller should transfer ownership to you through the VanMoof app or account, so the bike appears in your app.

Do this transfer at the handover, before you pay. If the seller says the bike works fine 'without the app', can't log in, or wants to sort it out later, walk away. A VanMoof that can't be transferred is either stolen or a project.

sections.heading: Known weak points on the S3 and X3
paragraphs: The S3 and X3 had a reputation for faults, and a bike that has been fixed under warranty in the past is not necessarily a lemon. Test these specifically:
bullets: E-shifter: the automatic 4-speed hub sometimes got stuck in one gear, ride it until it shifts up and down
Kick lock: lock and release it several times, it should engage cleanly
Motor and controller: error codes on the matrix display, sudden cut-outs under load
Battery: built into the frame, ask for range on a full charge, 60 km+ claimed when new
Boost button and front light: both should respond instantly
Brakes: hydraulic discs, firm lever, no squealing grind

sections.heading: Repairs and parts
paragraphs: Many VanMoof parts are proprietary, so a normal bike shop often can't help with electronics. Independent VanMoof repair specialists appeared after the bankruptcy, especially in Amsterdam and the larger cities, and the brand's own service network has been rebuilding. Before buying, find out where you would take this bike and what common repairs cost there. A failed motor controller or battery can cost more than the bike is worth used.
If the seller has receipts for repairs, ask to see them. A recent new battery or controller is a plus.

sections.heading: Stolen VanMoofs and fair prices
paragraphs: VanMoofs are popular with thieves, and a working bike with a bad digital story is the typical stolen listing. Check the frame number and insist on the in-app transfer. A cheap price plus 'no app' is the full warning.

On vindje.com you can ask for a VanMoof S3 or X3 with the app transfer included and recent battery, and skip listings that are parts-only or locked. Expect to pay noticeably more for bikes sold with proof of a recent service, and that premium is usually worth it.

Last tip: check whether the bike still has its original charger. The S3 and X3 charger is specific to the bike, and a replacement is another cost to factor into your offer. Also look at the tyres and brake pads, as they are cheap to replace but give you room to negotiate.

price_guide.item: VanMoof S3 or X3, working, with app transfer

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a used VanMoof?
faq.a: It can be, if the seller transfers the bike to your account in the app at the handover and the e-shifter, lock and motor work on a test ride.

faq.q: Can you use a VanMoof without the app?
faq.a: Partly, depending on the model and setup, but you need the digital key to open the lock and change settings. A bike without a transferable key is risky.

faq.q: Who repairs VanMoof bikes now?
faq.a: The brand's service network under its new owner and independent VanMoof specialists, mostly in larger Dutch cities. Normal bike shops can do brakes and tyres.

faq.q: How much is a used VanMoof S3 worth?
faq.a: Roughly EUR 450-950 depending on condition, battery and whether the app transfer works. Locked or faulty ones sell for parts.

example_wish: VanMoof S3 or X3 with working e-shifter, ownership transfer in the app, under 800 euro, within 20 km of Amsterdam

title: Shimano and SRAM groupsets explained for used road bike buyers
meta_title: Road Bike Groupsets Explained: Shimano and SRAM
description: Shimano and SRAM road groupsets explained: Claris to Dura-Ace, Apex to Red, model codes, wear checks and what each level means for a used road bike price.
intro: The groupset is the set of shifters, derailleurs, brakes, crank and cassette, and it tells you more about a used road bike's level than the frame colour. For most buyers Shimano 105 or SRAM Rival is the sweet spot: reliable, easy to service and not overpriced used. The model code also tells you the age and whether the bike has 9, 10, 11 or 12 gears.

sections.heading: Shimano road groupsets, from entry to top
paragraphs: Shimano's hierarchy has been stable for years. Gears per cassette went up over time, so the same name can mean different generations.
bullets: Claris: 8 speed, entry level, fine for commuting
Sora: 9 speed, entry level
Tiagra: 10 speed (4700 series), a decent all-rounder
105: 11 speed (5800, R7000), and 12 speed in the newer R7100 series, the sensible choice
Ultegra: 11 speed (6800, R8000), 12 speed (R8100), lighter and smoother
Dura-Ace: race level (9000, 9100, 9200), expensive to replace
Di2: electronic shifting, available on 105, Ultegra and Dura-Ace

sections.heading: SRAM road groupsets
paragraphs: SRAM uses a different shift logic (one lever for both up and down, DoubleTap) on its mechanical groups, and wireless shifting on AXS.
bullets: Apex: entry level, often 1x (single chainring)
Rival: roughly the level of Shimano 105
Force: roughly the level of Ultegra
Red: top level
eTap AXS: wireless 12 speed, needs charged batteries in each derailleur

sections.heading: Reading a listing
paragraphs: Dutch sellers often write the groupset in the title: racefiets Shimano 105 or Ultegra 2x11. Check the code if they give it, because 105 5700 (10 speed, around 2010) is a different bike from 105 R7000. A mixed groupset is common on older bikes: a 105 rear derailleur on a Tiagra bike makes it a Tiagra bike. Look at the shifters and crank in the photos; they tell you more than the rear derailleur that the seller probably upgraded.

Also check the crank and cassette sizes. A compact crank (50/34) with an 11-32 cassette is friendly for a beginner and for the hills in Limburg or abroad, while a 53/39 with 11-25 is a racing setup that will feel heavy on a long climb. Rim brakes versus disc brakes also matters for value. Disc brake bikes hold their price better, rim brake bikes are cheaper and lighter, and still perfectly good for dry rides. Campagnolo also turns up on older Italian frames; it is good kit, but parts are less common in Dutch shops than Shimano.

sections.heading: Wear checks at the pickup
paragraphs: Drivetrain parts wear, and replacing them can add EUR 100-300 to the price.
bullets: Chain: use a chain checker if you have one, or try lifting the chain off the front chainring, a big gap means it is stretched
Cassette and chainrings: shark-fin shaped teeth mean they are worn
Shifting: go through every gear on both chainrings, it should click in cleanly
Shifter hoods: torn or worn hoods hint at a crash, look at the levers for scrapes
Di2 or AXS: check battery level and that the charger is included
Brakes: disc pads and rotors not glazed, rim brake tracks not concave

sections.heading: What it means for price
paragraphs: The groupset sets roughly the price band, the frame material and condition do the rest. An aluminium bike with Claris or Sora is a commuter. Aluminium with 105 is the best value for someone starting out. Carbon with Ultegra is a serious bike, and electronic shifting adds a few hundred euro used. Size matters more than any of it, and in the Netherlands there is plenty of choice, so don't settle: racefiets frames run in cm (52, 54, 56, 58) or S/M/L, and a perfect groupset on the wrong size is a bad buy. With vindje.com you can ask for a 56 cm aluminium racefiets with 105 11 speed under 700 euro and it drops the listings that are the wrong size or groupset.

price_guide.item: Aluminium road bike, Claris or Sora
Carbon, Ultegra Di2 or SRAM AXS

faq.q: Is Shimano 105 good enough?
faq.a: Yes. 105 is what most amateur riders use, it shifts well and parts are cheap and everywhere. Ultegra is lighter and smoother but not a must.

faq.q: What is the SRAM equivalent of Shimano 105?
faq.a: SRAM Rival is roughly the same level. Apex sits below it and Force is comparable to Ultegra.

faq.q: Is an 11 speed groupset outdated?
faq.a: No. 11 speed 105 and Ultegra are still widely used and parts are easy to find. 12 speed is newer but not needed for most riders.

faq.q: Should I buy a used road bike with electronic shifting?
faq.a: It can be good value, but check that the batteries hold charge, the charger is there and every gear works.

example_wish: Aluminium road bike with Shimano 105 11 speed, frame size 56, rim or disc brakes, under 700 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used mountain bike: suspension, frame and wear
meta_title: Buying a Used Mountain Bike: Suspension, Frame, Wear
description: Buying a used mountain bike in the Netherlands: how to check the fork, rear shock, frame and drivetrain, hardtail or full suspension, and fair used prices.
intro: A used mountain bike is a good buy if the suspension still works, the frame has no cracks and the drivetrain isn't worn out. Those three checks take ten minutes. In the Netherlands, where most riding is on forest trails in the Veluwe, Utrechtse Heuvelrug or the dunes, a decent hardtail is enough for most people and costs a lot less to keep running than a full suspension bike.

sections.heading: Hardtail or full suspension
paragraphs: A hardtail has a suspension fork at the front and a rigid rear. It is lighter, cheaper, and has fewer parts to wear out. For Dutch trails, which are flowing, sandy and rooty rather than steep and rocky, a hardtail with 100-130 mm of fork travel covers almost everything.

A full suspension bike (a fully, as Dutch riders say) adds a rear shock and pivot bearings. It is more comfortable and faster on rough ground, and more expensive to service. A cheap used fully is often a worse buy than a good hardtail at the same price, because the rear shock and bearings on a budget fully tend to be worn.

sections.heading: Checking the fork and shock
paragraphs: Suspension is where a used MTB hides its biggest costs. A fork service runs from roughly EUR 80 for a lower leg service to EUR 200 or more for a full damper service at a shop.
bullets: Stanchions (the shiny upper tubes): no deep scratches or pitting, a scratch you can feel with a nail will eat the seals
Seals: oil residue or dirt rings on the stanchions mean leaking seals
Push down hard on the bars: smooth travel, no clunk, returns at a steady speed
Lockout and rebound dials: turn them, they should change how the fork feels
Rear shock: same stanchion check, then bounce on the saddle and listen for knocking
Air forks: ask what pressure the seller ran, a fork that won't hold air will sag overnight

sections.heading: Frame and bearings
paragraphs: Look at every weld and tube junction, especially around the head tube, the bottom bracket and the rear dropouts. Paint cracks in a line can be frame cracks. On carbon frames, tap gently around any chip with a coin, a dull sound compared to the rest means damage under the surface. Carbon is fine used, but a crashed carbon frame is not worth buying without an inspection.
On a fully, lift the rear wheel and try to move it side to side. Any play means worn pivot bearings, which is fixable but adds cost. Also grab the front brake and rock the bike to check the headset.

sections.heading: Drivetrain and brakes
paragraphs: Modern mountain bikes mostly run 1x drivetrains (one chainring) with 11 or 12 speeds. Shimano Deore and SRAM SX/NX are the common entry groups, SLX and GX the step up. Worn cassettes and chainrings on 12 speed are not cheap, so check for shark-fin shaped teeth and a chain that skips under hard pedalling. Hydraulic disc brakes should feel firm at the lever and not sink to the bar. A spongy lever needs a bleed, which is a normal service item but negotiable.

sections.heading: Size, wheels and what to search
paragraphs: Wheel size is 27.5 or 29 inch on bikes from the last ten years; older bikes run 26 inch and are cheaper but parts like forks are getting harder to match. Frame sizes are S, M, L, XL. At 1.75-1.85 m most people ride an M or L, but geometry varies a lot between brands, so test ride.

Dutch listings use mountainbike, MTB, hardtail and fully. Watch out for ATB, which in the Netherlands often means a hybrid or trekking bike with knobby tyres rather than a trail bike. On vindje.com you can ask for a 29 inch hardtail in size L with a 1x12 drivetrain and air fork, and it skips the ATB city hybrids and kids bikes.

price_guide.item: Trail fully, Shimano SLX or SRAM GX

faq.q: Is it worth buying a used mountain bike?
faq.a: Yes, if the fork and shock work, the frame is crack free and the drivetrain is not worn out. Mountain bikes lose value fast, so used is good value.

faq.q: Do I need a full suspension bike in the Netherlands?
faq.a: For most Dutch trails, no. A hardtail with 100-130 mm fork travel is lighter, cheaper and handles the Veluwe and Heuvelrug well.

faq.q: How do I check a used mountain bike fork?
faq.a: Look for scratches and oil on the stanchions, push down hard and feel for smooth travel without clunks, and turn the dials to check they work.

faq.q: What size mountain bike do I need?
faq.a: Most riders of 1.75-1.85 m ride M or L, but geometry differs per brand. A test ride beats any size chart.

example_wish: 29 inch hardtail mountainbike, size L, air fork, 1x12 Shimano Deore or SRAM, under 700 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying a used fatbike: legality, speed and battery checks
meta_title: Buying a Used Fatbike: Legality, Speed and Battery
description: Buying a used fatbike in the Netherlands: how to spot a tuned bike, why throttles cause trouble, battery checks and what Ouxi, Phatfour and Knaap cost.
intro: A used fatbike is only a good buy if it is legal as a normal e-bike: pedal assist up to 25 km/h, no throttle that drives the bike on its own, and an unmodified motor. Many fatbikes for sale in the Netherlands have been tuned (opgevoerd), and riding one can mean a fine and the bike being impounded. Check that first, then the battery.

sections.heading: What makes a fatbike legal
paragraphs: In the Netherlands an electric bike counts as a normal bicycle when the motor only helps while you pedal, assistance stops at 25 km/h, and the continuous motor power is limited to 250 W. A fatbike that goes faster on assist, or has a throttle that moves the bike without pedalling, falls outside that. It then counts as a moped-class vehicle, which needs registration, a licence plate, insurance and in most cases a helmet, and most fatbikes can't meet those rules at all.

Police in several cities have been checking fatbikes on test benches, and the rules around fatbikes (like age limits and helmets) have been under discussion. Check the current situation on government sites before buying for a teenager.

Also think about insurance and theft. A legal fatbike is a bicycle, so normal bike insurance can cover it, but insurers usually won't pay out for an accident on a modified bike. Fatbikes are also stolen a lot, so a solid chain lock or an approved ART-rated lock is worth budgeting for.

sections.heading: Spotting a tuned or illegal fatbike
paragraphs: Sellers rarely write 'illegal' in a listing. Read between the lines.
bullets: Words like opgevoerd, 35 km/h, 45 km/h, snelheid ontgrendeld or 'kan sneller'
A thumb throttle (gashendel) on the handlebar, especially one that works from standstill
Display settings that let you change the speed limit or wheel size
Motor stickers of 500 W, 750 W or 1000 W
A seller who offers to 'put it back to 25' after you pay

sections.heading: Brands you will see
paragraphs: Ouxi V8 and similar cheap imports dominate the listings. They are the bikes most often tuned, have generic parts and modest build quality, and are fine for short trips if legal and in good shape. Phatfour is a Dutch brand with better finish and dealer support. Knaap and Lacros make heavier, more premium models. A known brand costs more used, but you can get parts and service, which matters more on a heavy bike that eats brake pads and tyres. Ask the seller for the original receipt: it shows the model, the original speed setting and where you can go for warranty or parts, and a seller who can't produce one for a bike under two years old deserves extra questions.

sections.heading: Battery and electrical checks
paragraphs: The battery is most of the value on a fatbike. Cheap batteries degrade fast, and a replacement for an import brand can be hard to find or costs EUR 200-450.
bullets: Ask how many km it does on a full charge now, and how old the battery is
Look for swelling, cracks or a battery that doesn't sit flush in the frame
Bring the bike to full and watch the bars drop on a 5-minute ride
Original charger only, a mismatched charger is a fire risk
Check every assist level, the lights and the brakes cut-off sensors
Never buy a fatbike with a damaged or wet-looking battery, they can catch fire

sections.heading: Mechanical checks
paragraphs: Fatbikes weigh 30-40 kg, which wears brakes and tyres quickly. Test the disc brakes hard, look at pad thickness, and check the fat 20x4 inch tyres for cracks and bulges. Check the rear suspension and front fork for clunks, and the folding hinge (if it has one) for play. Most fatbikes use a cheap 7-speed derailleur, so expect some wear there. On vindje.com you can ask for a fatbike without throttle, limited to 25 km/h, with receipt, and it filters out listings that mention tuning or 45 km/h.

price_guide.item: Ouxi V8 or similar import, legal setup

faq.q: Is a fatbike legal in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Yes, if it only assists while you pedal, stops assisting at 25 km/h and the motor is 250 W. Tuned bikes or bikes with a free throttle are not legal as a bicycle.

faq.q: What happens if I ride a tuned fatbike?
faq.a: Police can fine you and impound the bike, and your insurance may not cover accidents. It is treated as an unregistered moped.

faq.q: How long does a fatbike battery last?
faq.a: A good battery holds up for several hundred charge cycles, often a few years of normal use. Cheap import batteries can lose range faster.

faq.q: Is an Ouxi V8 worth buying used?
faq.a: For short trips it can be, if it is untuned, has the original charger and the battery still gives a decent range. Don't pay near new prices.

example_wish: Fatbike with pedal assist up to 25 km/h, no throttle, original charger, battery under 2 years old, under 800 euro, within 15 km

title: How to buy a used sofa without regrets
meta_title: How to Buy a Used Sofa Without Regrets
description: How to buy a used sofa: measure stairs and doors, check the frame, foam, smell and pests, and know what IKEA, Leolux and leather sofas cost used.
intro: A used sofa is one of the best second hand buys, as long as it fits through your door, the frame is solid and it doesn't smell or carry pests. Measure first, sit on it in person, and lift the cushions. Sofas lose most of their value in the first few years, so a three year old Montel or Bolia can cost a third of new.

sections.heading: Measure before you message
paragraphs: Dutch homes have narrow hallways and famously steep stairs, and the most common sofa regret is not the colour, it is that it won't go up. Measure the sofa's width, depth and height, and then your front door, hallway corners and staircase. The key number is usually the sofa's depth and height combined with the tightest turn.

If it doesn't fit the stairs, ask whether the legs and backrest come off (many modern sofas have removable legs and bolt-on backs). Otherwise you are looking at hoisting it through a window, which movers do with a verhuislift for roughly EUR 100-200.

sections.heading: Frame and springs
paragraphs: Sit on every seat, bounce a bit and listen. Creaks, cracks or a seat that dips more on one side point to a broken frame or slats. Lift one front corner off the floor about 15 cm: on a solid frame the other front leg lifts quickly too. If it twists, the frame is weak. Under the cushions, press the seat base, you want even resistance from springs or webbing, not a hollow.

sections.heading: Cushions, covers and leather
paragraphs: Foam goes soft over time. Cushions that stay flat after you stand up, or that have lumps, will need new foam, which costs EUR 30-80 per cushion from a foam shop (schuimrubber op maat). Removable covers you can wash are a big plus on a used sofa.

With leather, check the seat edges and arms for cracks and peeling. Peeling usually means bonded or PU leather, which can't be repaired. Light scuffs on full grain leather are normal and can be treated.

sections.heading: Smell, pets and pests
paragraphs: Smoke, pet and damp smells sink deep into foam and don't come out with a clean. Ask directly if there are pets or smokers in the house and smell the cushions up close. Use your phone torch along the seams, under the cushions and under the frame: tiny dark spots, shed skins or live insects can mean bedbugs. It is rare, but the cost of being wrong is high, so walk away if you see anything. Cat hair and scratches on the sides are easy to spot in person and often missing from the photos.

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
bullets: Your measurements on your phone, plus a tape measure
Phone torch for seams and underside
Ask if the legs or back unscrew, bring an Allen key and screwdriver
Blankets and straps for the van, sofas scuff on the way
A second person: even a 2-seater is a two-person lift
Plan transport: a rental van, or a courier like Brenger who does Marktplaats pickups

sections.heading: What to search and what to pay
paragraphs: Dutch sellers use bank, 3-zitsbank, 2,5-zitsbank, hoekbank (corner sofa), loungebank, slaapbank (sofa bed) and chesterfield. Good used brands include Leolux, Montel, Gelderland, Bolia and Design on Stock; IKEA Kivik and Söderhamn are everywhere and have replaceable covers. On vindje.com you can describe the size, fabric and maximum depth you can get up your stairs, and it reads the listings for the measurements so you only see ones that might fit.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a used sofa?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Check for smells, pet damage and signs of bedbugs along the seams with a torch, and test the frame by sitting and lifting a corner.

faq.q: How do I check a used sofa for bedbugs?
faq.a: Look along seams, under cushions and on the underside of the frame for small dark spots, shed skins or insects. If you see any, don't buy it.

faq.q: How do I get a sofa up narrow Dutch stairs?
faq.a: Check if the legs and back come off. If not, movers can hoist it through a window with an outside lift.

faq.q: How much is a used sofa worth?
faq.a: Most sofas sell for 20 to 40 percent of the new price after a few years. Design brands like Leolux hold value better.

example_wish: Grey fabric 3-seater sofa, max 85 cm deep, removable covers, no pets or smoking, under 300 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used dining table: wood, size and stability
meta_title: Buying a Used Dining Table: Wood, Size, Stability
description: Buying a used dining table: how to tell solid wood from veneer, which size seats how many, how to test stability and what oak and design tables cost used.
intro: For a used dining table, check three things: whether it is solid wood or veneer, whether it fits your room with chairs pulled out, and whether it wobbles. Solid oak tables are common on Marktplaats, last decades and can be sanded back to look new, so they are often the best second hand value.

sections.heading: Size: how many people and how much room
paragraphs: Count about 60 cm of table edge per person, and leave at least 75-90 cm between the table edge and a wall or cabinet so people can sit and get past. A 140 cm table seats 4 comfortably and 6 tightly. 180-200 cm seats 6, 220-240 cm seats 8. Round tables of 110-120 cm seat 4, 140 cm seats 6.
Measure the room before you search, then write the maximum length in your search. Dutch living rooms tend to be long and narrow, which favours a rectangular table or an extendable one.
bullets: 4 people: 120-140 x 80 cm, or round 110-120 cm
6 people: 180-200 x 90 cm, or round 140 cm
8 people: 220-240 x 100 cm
Height: standard is 74-76 cm, check if you have existing chairs

sections.heading: Solid wood, veneer or MDF
paragraphs: Look at the edge of the tabletop and the underside. On solid wood the grain on the edge continues from the top, and the underside is the same wood, often rougher. Veneer shows a thin layer on top of a different core, usually visible as a line on the edge or at a chip. MDF or particle board with foil feels lighter and the underside looks uniform and smooth.

Solid wood can be sanded and oiled many times, so stains, rings and scratches are fixable for an afternoon of work. Veneer can be sanded lightly once, maybe. Foil can't be repaired. That is why a scratched solid oak table is often a better buy than a pristine veneer one.

sections.heading: Testing stability
paragraphs: Push the table sideways at the tabletop, then lean on one corner. Slight movement is normal on long tables, but wobble that comes back with a knock means loose joints or legs. Many modern tables have bolted legs you can tighten; antique and older tables with mortise joints may need glue. Check under the top for cracks along the boards and for splits around the bolt holes.

For extendable tables (uitschuiftafel), open and close it twice. Runners should slide without force, leaves should line up flush, and leaf storage should still work. Missing leaves happen often, so count them.

sections.heading: Common table types on Marktplaats
bullets: Boomstamtafel: thick slab top with natural edge, heavy and popular, check for deep cracks
Eiken eettafel: solid oak, the classic, often with a steel U or V leg
Industriële eettafel: wood top with metal frame, check welds and the bolts
Rond or ovaal: good for small rooms, check the central pedestal for wobble
Teak and mango: often from interior chains, mango is softer and dents easily
Design: Pastoe, Arco and Hay hold value, older Ikea tables usually don't

sections.heading: Transport and price
paragraphs: A solid oak table of 200 cm can weigh 60-100 kg. Ask whether the legs come off, bring the right tools, and plan for two or three people plus a van. Wrap the top in blankets, as the edges dent easily. With vindje.com you can ask for a solid oak table between 180 and 200 cm with removable legs, and it reads the listing text so you skip veneer tables and ones that are too long.

faq.q: How big a dining table do I need for 6 people?
faq.a: About 180-200 cm long and 90 cm wide, or a 140 cm round table. Leave 75-90 cm around it for chairs.

faq.q: How can I tell if a table is solid wood?
faq.a: Look at the edge and underside. On solid wood the grain continues over the edge and the underside is the same wood. Veneer shows a thin top layer on a different core.

faq.q: Can you refinish a scratched oak table?
faq.a: Yes. Solid oak can be sanded and oiled several times, which removes most scratches, rings and stains.

faq.q: How do I fix a wobbly dining table?
faq.a: First tighten the leg bolts underneath. If the wobble stays, the joints may need regluing or a carpenter.

example_wish: Solid oak dining table 180-200 cm for 6 people, removable legs, under 400 euro, within 20 km

title: Used office chairs: Herman Miller, Steelcase and what to check
meta_title: Used Office Chairs: Herman Miller, Steelcase Guide
description: Buying a used office chair: Herman Miller Aeron and Embody, Steelcase Leap and Gesture, how to spot fakes, what to test and fair second hand prices.
intro: A used high-end office chair is one of the smartest second hand buys: a Steelcase Leap or Herman Miller Aeron costs over EUR 1000 new and often EUR 250-600 used, and they are built to last well over ten years. Check the gas cylinder, tilt, armrests and mesh or foam, and make sure it is the original and not a copy.

sections.heading: The chairs worth looking for
paragraphs: Companies replace whole floors of chairs when they move or downsize, so Marktplaats has a steady supply of office chairs from refurbishers and private sellers.
bullets: Herman Miller Aeron: mesh seat and back, comes in sizes A (small), B (medium) and C (large). The newer Remastered version has a better lumbar pad
Herman Miller Embody: very adjustable, holds its price well
Herman Miller Mirra and Sayl: cheaper and lighter, still good
Steelcase Leap (V1 and V2): many people's favourite, foam seat, V2 is the one to get
Steelcase Gesture and Think: Gesture has very flexible arms, Think is simpler
Haworth Zody and Interstuhl, Sedus, Dauphin: common in Dutch and German offices, solid and cheaper

sections.heading: Spotting copies
paragraphs: Cheap 'Aeron style' and 'Embody style' chairs are sold everywhere, and a few are listed as the original. Genuine chairs have the brand logo cast or printed on the back and a label with a model and serial number under the seat. An Aeron copy often has a plain plastic frame without the Herman Miller logo, a different mesh pattern, and a price under EUR 150. Ask for a photo of the label underneath before you travel.

sections.heading: What to test in person
paragraphs: Sit in it for at least five minutes and go through every lever.
bullets: Gas cylinder: set the seat high, sit down with your full weight, it should not sink over a minute
Tilt: lean back, the tension knob should change resistance, lock in each position
Armrests: move up and down, in and out, no loose wobble at the top
Mesh (Aeron, Mirra): no tears, sagging or loose edges at the frame
Foam seat (Leap, Gesture): no thin spots or crushed front edge
Wheels: roll smoothly, hard floor or carpet casters, check you have the right type
Base: no cracks in the star base around the cylinder

sections.heading: Refurbisher or private seller
paragraphs: Dutch office furniture refurbishers sell checked chairs with new cylinders, cleaned upholstery and sometimes a one or two year warranty. You pay about EUR 50-150 more than private, but you can test several chairs in one visit, which is useful for finding your Aeron size. Private sellers are cheaper and often sell lightly used home office chairs from the pandemic years. For bulk office clearouts, chairs are sometimes sold in lots, and you can ask to buy just one.

sections.heading: Parts and repair
paragraphs: Both Herman Miller and Steelcase use parts that are easy to find, and standard gas cylinders fit most chairs. A new cylinder costs EUR 25-50 and takes ten minutes with a pipe wrench and a rubber mallet. Armrest pads and casters are also cheap. That makes a used chair with one worn part a fair bargain if you price the fix in.
On vindje.com you can search for a Steelcase Leap V2 or Aeron size B with adjustable arms under 400 euro, and it reads the listings to skip copies and chairs in the wrong size.

faq.q: Is a used Herman Miller chair worth it?
faq.a: Yes, if it is genuine and the cylinder, tilt and mesh are fine. They last well over a decade and parts are easy to replace.

faq.q: Which Aeron size do I need?
faq.a: Size B fits most adults. Size A suits smaller people up to about 1.65 m, size C taller and heavier people.

faq.q: How can I tell if an Aeron is fake?
faq.a: Look for the Herman Miller logo on the back and a label with model and serial number under the seat. Copies often have plain plastic frames and cost under EUR 150.

faq.q: Can I replace the gas cylinder on an office chair myself?
faq.a: Yes. Most chairs use a standard cylinder that costs EUR 25-50. You need a pipe wrench or rubber mallet to remove the old one, and it takes about ten minutes.

faq.q: Is the Steelcase Leap V1 or V2 better?
faq.a: The V2 is the newer model with a more refined seat and arms. A V1 in good condition is still a good chair at a lower price.

example_wish: Steelcase Leap V2 or Herman Miller Aeron size B, adjustable arms, no sinking cylinder, under 400 euro, within 25 km

title: Which IKEA furniture is worth buying second hand
meta_title: Which IKEA Furniture Is Worth Buying Second Hand
description: Which IKEA furniture is worth buying second hand: Kallax, Billy, Ivar, Pax, Hemnes and Poäng, what survives moving, what to skip and fair used prices.
intro: IKEA furniture is worth buying second hand when it is solid wood or built to be taken apart and rebuilt, like Ivar, Hemnes and Poäng, or so common that you can buy it already assembled and carry it home, like Kallax and Billy. Particleboard pieces that have been dismantled several times are often not worth the effort. The rule: the cheaper it was new, the less sense it makes used.

sections.heading: Good buys
paragraphs: These hold up well, are easy to find on Marktplaats, and sell for a fraction of new.
bullets: Ivar: solid pine shelves and cabinets, survives endless moves, easy to paint
Hemnes: solid pine dressers, beds and cabinets, much sturdier than the price suggests
Poäng: bentwood armchair, covers are replaceable and cheap, a classic
Kallax: particleboard, but sturdy as a unit, often sold already assembled
Billy: same story, buy one that is assembled and doesn't need to come apart
Stockholm and Ekenäset ranges: better materials, hold value
Kitchen trolleys and stools (Råskog, Bekväm), indestructible and cheap

sections.heading: Think twice
paragraphs: Some IKEA items lose a lot when they are taken apart, or are so cheap new that used makes little sense.
bullets: Cheaper particleboard ranges like Malm and Brimnes: fine assembled, but cam lock holes wear after one or two moves
Lack tables: EUR 10-15 new, not worth a trip
Pax wardrobes: worth it, but only if you can dismantle carefully and have the exact height
Mattresses and sofa beds: hygiene risk and hard to check
Kitchens: possible, but measuring and missing parts make it a project
Anything with water damage: swollen particleboard edges never recover

sections.heading: What to check on particleboard IKEA
paragraphs: Particleboard holds screws and cam locks well the first time and worse every time after. Look closely at the holes for the cam locks and dowels: crumbled edges or holes that are oval mean the joint won't be tight. Check the back panel (the thin hardboard sheet nailed on). If it is missing or torn, the unit will wobble, though you can buy a replacement sheet at any hardware store. Look for swollen edges near the floor, a sign of a wet basement or a leak.

Ask for the assembly instructions or the article name, so you can download the manual from IKEA's site. Most parts and screws can be ordered through IKEA's spare parts service, sometimes free for small items.

sections.heading: Assembled or flat
paragraphs: If you can, buy assembled and transport it in one piece. A Kallax 4x4 fits in most estate cars lying down. Billy at 202 cm tall needs a van. If it has to come apart, take photos at each step, bag and label the screws, and keep each panel's orientation. Dutch stairs are narrow, so check whether an assembled Pax or Hemnes dresser will make the turn before you decide not to dismantle it.

sections.heading: Prices and how to search
paragraphs: IKEA furniture typically sells for 30 to 60 percent of the current new price in good condition, less if you need to dismantle it yourself. Check IKEA's current price first, since some items got more expensive and some cheaper, and sellers often use the price they paid. Dutch sellers usually use the IKEA name in the title, so searches are easy. On vindje.com you can ask for a Kallax 2x4 in white oak effect, already assembled, within 5 km, and it skips listings with missing shelves or the wrong size.

faq.q: Is IKEA furniture worth buying second hand?
faq.a: Solid wood ranges like Ivar and Hemnes and sturdy items like Kallax and Poäng are. Cheap particleboard that needs to be dismantled often is not.

faq.q: Can you take IKEA furniture apart and rebuild it?
faq.a: Yes, but particleboard gets weaker each time. Check that cam lock and dowel holes are not crumbled.

faq.q: How do I get spare parts for IKEA furniture?
faq.a: IKEA has a spare parts service where you can order screws and fittings with the article number from the manual, often for free.

faq.q: Is it worth buying an IKEA Pax second hand?
faq.a: Often yes, a Pax with doors costs a lot new. Make sure the height fits your ceiling, all hinges and rails are included, and you can dismantle it carefully.

faq.q: How much does used IKEA furniture sell for?
faq.a: Usually 30 to 60 percent of the current new price, depending on condition and whether you need to dismantle it.

example_wish: IKEA Kallax 2x4 white, already assembled, all shelves present, under 40 euro, within 5 km

title: Buying a used wardrobe (kledingkast): measure, dismantle, move
meta_title: Buying a Used Wardrobe: Measure, Dismantle, Move
description: Buying a used wardrobe (kledingkast): measure ceiling height and stairs, dismantle a Pax or old linnenkast safely, move it and know fair used prices.
intro: A used wardrobe is cheap to buy and expensive in effort: the price is low because it has to come apart, go down stairs and fit under your ceiling. Measure the height, the tilt-up diagonal and your stairs first, check the doors and back panel, and plan how you will dismantle and transport it before you agree a time.

sections.heading: Measure three things, not one
paragraphs: Height alone isn't enough. A wardrobe is assembled lying down and tilted up, so its diagonal (depth and height) must fit under your ceiling. A 236 cm Pax needs at least about 240 cm of ceiling height to tilt up. In older Dutch homes and attic rooms, ceilings and sloped roofs often decide what is possible.
bullets: Height and width of the wardrobe, plus the space you have
Tilt-up diagonal: the square root of depth squared plus height squared, or ask the seller
Stairs and doors: width of the narrowest point, and whether panels fit in the turn
Skirting boards (plinten): they push the wardrobe out from the wall by 1-2 cm

sections.heading: Types you will see
bullets: Kledingkast 2 deurs or 3 deurs: freestanding wardrobe with hinged doors
Hanglegkast: half hanging rail, half shelves
Schuifdeurkast: sliding doors, needs less space in front, check the rails
Linnenkast: traditional Dutch linen cabinet, often oak, very solid
IKEA Pax: modular, the most common, with many door and interior options
Kabinetkast: antique, heavy, collectors' piece, comes apart in sections

sections.heading: Checks before you dismantle
paragraphs: See it standing and closed before anything comes apart. Open and close every door, check the hinges line up and the doors don't sag or rub. On sliding doors, slide each door end to end and check the top and bottom rails for bent sections and missing wheels. Look inside at the back panel and shelves for moisture stains and mould smell, especially if it stood against an outside wall. On particleboard wardrobes, check the cam lock holes, as a well used Pax can be loose after a second move.

sections.heading: How to dismantle it
paragraphs: Agree with the seller who dismantles. Many sellers prefer you do it, and that is better anyway: you learn how it goes back together.
bullets: Bring a drill with bits, Phillips and flat screwdrivers, an Allen key set and a hammer
Take photos from all sides before you start, and of each hinge
Remove doors first, then shelves and rails, then the back panel
Bag and label the screws per part, tape small bags to the panels they belong to
Mark panels with tape: left side, right side, top, bottom
Download the IKEA manual by article number if it is a Pax

sections.heading: Moving and rebuilding
paragraphs: Panels of a 2 metre wardrobe need a van, not a car. Carry panels flat on stairs and protect the corners with blankets. When rebuilding, put it up near its final place, tilt it up with two people, and secure it to the wall with the included bracket. A tall wardrobe without wall anchoring can tip over, which matters a lot with children in the house.

Old solid wood linnenkasten usually come apart in two or three sections and a top cornice, which is easier than it sounds but heavy. On vindje.com you can ask for a wardrobe no higher than 220 cm with sliding doors, and it reads the measurements in each listing so you only see ones that fit your room.

price_guide.item: IKEA Pax 200 cm with sliding doors

faq.q: How do I know if a wardrobe will fit under my ceiling?
faq.a: Check the tilt-up diagonal, not just the height. A wardrobe is built lying down and tilted up, so it needs a few extra cm of ceiling height.

faq.q: Can you dismantle and rebuild an IKEA Pax?
faq.a: Yes, it is designed for it. Photograph each step, label the parts and check the cam lock holes are not crumbled.

faq.q: How much does a used wardrobe cost?
