faq.a: A simple 2-door wardrobe costs EUR 20-80, a Pax with sliding doors EUR 150-350 depending on size and doors.

faq.q: Should I buy a wardrobe already dismantled?
faq.a: It saves time, but you can't check doors and hinges in use, and missing screws are common. Ask for photos of it standing and a bag count before you travel.

faq.q: Do I need to anchor a wardrobe to the wall?
faq.a: Yes. Tall wardrobes can tip over, especially when children climb or pull drawers. Use the wall bracket it came with.

example_wish: White wardrobe with sliding doors, max 200 cm wide and 220 cm high, already dismantled or easy to take apart, under 200 euro, within 10 km

title: Buying a used bed frame, and why to think twice about the mattress
meta_title: Buying a Used Bed Frame (and Skipping the Mattress)
description: Buying a used bed frame in the Netherlands: Dutch bed sizes, slatted bases, how to check joints and bedbugs, and why a used mattress is usually a bad idea.
intro: A used bed frame is a good buy: solid wood and metal frames last for decades and are easy to check. A used mattress is a different story, with hygiene, bedbugs and sagging you can't see in photos. Buy the frame second hand, and in most cases buy the mattress new.

sections.heading: Dutch bed sizes
paragraphs: Beds in the Netherlands use metric sizes, and mattresses must match exactly. The common ones are 90x200 (single), 140x200, 160x200 and 180x200 (double). Long sizes of 210 or 220 cm are popular because Dutch people are tall. Ask the seller for the mattress size, not the outside size of the frame, since those differ by several cm.
A 140 cm bed is fine for one person and tight for two. 160 is the most common double, and 180 is comfortable for two adults.

sections.heading: Frame and slatted base
paragraphs: Most Dutch bed frames (ledikant or bedframe) use a lattenbodem, a slatted base that the mattress sits on. Check each slat: cracked or missing slats are cheap to replace, but a broken frame rail is not. Adjustable slatted bases (verstelbaar) should move smoothly; electric ones need a working motor and remote.

Push and pull the assembled frame at the corners. Creaking usually comes from loose bolts, which you can tighten. A wobble that remains points to stripped threads or cracked joints. Check the metal brackets that hold the side rails for bends.

sections.heading: Check for bedbugs, every time
paragraphs: Bedbugs travel with furniture, and beds are their favourite place. They hide in joints, screw holes, under the slats and in the seams of headboards. Use your phone torch and look for small dark spots (droppings), tiny pale shed skins, or live brown insects about the size of an apple seed. A sweet, musty smell can also be a sign. If you see anything, don't buy it. Treating an infestation costs far more than any bed frame.

sections.heading: Why skip the used mattress
paragraphs: A mattress takes years of sweat and skin, and you can't wash the core. Even if it looks clean, it may be sagging in the middle, and you only feel that after a few nights. Mattress life is roughly 8-10 years, and you rarely know the exact age of a used one. It is also hard to check for bedbugs inside. For a guest bed or a short stay, a mattress that is clearly very new, still in its protective cover, with the receipt, can be fine. Otherwise budget for a new one, and look at the frame as the second hand saving.

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
bullets: Mattress size of the frame (90, 140, 160, 180 x 200 or 210)
Torch check of joints, slats and headboard for bedbugs
All bolts, brackets and the slatted base included
Tools: Allen keys, screwdrivers, a ratchet for bed bolts
Measure your stairs for the headboard, which usually doesn't come apart
For a hoogslaper (loft bed): check the ladder and guard rail are solid

sections.heading: Brands and searching
paragraphs: Auping is the Dutch bed brand that holds value, and its frames and bases last very long. IKEA Malm and Hemnes beds are everywhere and cheap. Solid oak or pine beds and simple metal frames are good finds. On vindje.com you can ask for a 160x200 wooden bed frame with slatted base, without mattress, and it filters by size so you don't wade through 140 cm beds.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a used bed frame?
faq.a: Yes, if you check joints and slats and look for bedbugs with a torch. Solid wood and metal frames last for decades.

faq.q: Should I buy a used mattress?
faq.a: Usually not. You can't clean the core, can't see sagging or bedbugs inside, and you rarely know its age. Buy the frame used and the mattress new.

faq.q: What are standard bed sizes in the Netherlands?
faq.a: 90x200 for a single, and 140x200, 160x200 and 180x200 for doubles. Long versions of 210 or 220 cm are common too.

faq.q: Can I put any mattress on a slatted bed frame?
faq.a: Most foam and pocket spring mattresses, yes, but check the slat spacing. Gaps wider than about 7 cm can let a foam mattress sag between the slats.

faq.q: How do I check a bed for bedbugs?
faq.a: Look in joints, screw holes and seams for small dark spots, pale shed skins or brown insects the size of an apple seed.

example_wish: Solid wood double bed frame 160x200 with slatted base, no mattress, headboard included, under 200 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used boxspring: hygiene, springs and transport
meta_title: Buying a Used Boxspring: Hygiene, Springs, Transport
description: Buying a used boxspring: which parts to replace, how to test springs and electric bases, moving the heavy halves, and fair prices.
intro: A used boxspring can be a good deal if you buy the sprung bases second hand and replace the topper, and ideally the mattresses too. The bases hold up for many years and cost the most new, while the parts you sleep on are where the hygiene problems sit. Test the springs, check for stains and pests, and plan for a van and two strong people.

sections.heading: How a boxspring is built
paragraphs: A boxspring has three layers: the box (the sprung base on legs), a mattress on top, and a thin topper. On a 160 or 180 cm bed the base and mattress are usually two separate halves of 80 or 90 cm each, with one topper over both. A headboard is often a separate panel bolted to the bases or the wall.

Knowing this helps you buy smart. The bases are the expensive, durable part. The topper is the cheapest to replace and the part that touches you most. Many buyers keep the bases, maybe the mattresses, and always buy a new topper.

sections.heading: Hygiene and what to replace
paragraphs: Ask how old the bed is and whether it was used with a mattress protector. Look at the mattresses and topper in daylight for stains, yellowing and body dips. A topper costs roughly EUR 100-300 new, so factor that in. Mattresses in a boxspring set are often pocket spring with a foam layer, and the same rule applies as for any used mattress: unknown age and history means risk.

Check for bedbugs along the piping, seams and the underside of the bases, where the fabric is stapled to the frame. Use a torch and look for dark spots, shed skins or small brown insects. If in doubt, walk away; bedbugs love boxsprings because of all the fabric.

sections.heading: Testing springs and electric bases
bullets: Press the base surface in several places, the resistance should be even with no dead spots or clunks
Sit on the edge of each half, a strong edge (edge support) shouldn't collapse
Lie on it if the seller allows, feel for dips where someone always slept
Electric (elektrisch verstelbaar): run head and foot up and down, both halves, with the remote
Listen to the motors, grinding or one side lagging means a worn motor
Check the legs and their fittings, a missing leg is fixable but annoying

sections.heading: Size, weight and transport
paragraphs: Dutch boxsprings come in 140x200, 160x200 and 180x200, plus long versions of 210 and 220 cm, and height is often 60-70 cm including topper. Each base half can weigh 30-50 kg, electric ones more. They don't bend, so measure your stairs carefully: a 90x200 base needs to make the turn upright or on its side. The mattresses are flexible but heavy.
You need a van and two people. A courier for Marktplaats pickups or a moving service is a good option if you don't have help.

sections.heading: Brands and searching
paragraphs: Auping, Swiss Sense, Beter Bed (and its house brands), Eastborn and Emma are common in Dutch listings. Auping holds its value best, and Auping bases are often sold separately from the rest of the bed. Price matters less than condition here: a cheap boxspring with a stained base is no bargain, while a well kept mid-range set from a non-smoking home is. Many sellers list a boxspring only by size, so filtering is slow. On vindje.com you can ask for an electric boxspring 180x200 with a headboard, no mattress and topper needed, and it reads which parts each listing includes.

price_guide.item: Boxspring 160 or 180x200, Swiss Sense or similar

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a used boxspring?
faq.a: The bases are usually fine if there are no stains or signs of bedbugs. Replace the topper, and consider new mattresses as well.

faq.q: How heavy is a boxspring?
faq.a: Each base half often weighs 30-50 kg, and electric versions more. You need two people and a van to move one.

faq.q: Can I buy just the base of a boxspring?
faq.a: Yes, many sellers sell the bases and headboard without mattresses and topper, which is often the smartest used buy.

faq.q: How long does a boxspring last?
faq.a: The bases can last 15 years or more. Mattresses and toppers wear out sooner, often after 8-10 years for mattresses and less for toppers.

faq.q: What is the difference between a boxspring and a bed with a slatted base?
faq.a: A boxspring has a sprung base under the mattress, a bed with a lattenbodem uses wooden slats. Boxsprings are higher and softer, slatted bases more adjustable.

example_wish: Electric boxspring 180x200 with headboard, Auping or Swiss Sense, bases in good condition, under 600 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used bookcase or open shelving unit
meta_title: Buying a Used Bookcase or Open Shelving Unit
description: Buying a used bookcase: shelf sag, depth for books, wall anchoring, String and Pastoe versus Billy and Kallax, and fair second hand prices.
intro: A good used bookcase has shelves that don't sag, a depth that fits your books, and a way to fix it to the wall. Solid wood and modular systems like String last forever and resell well, while particleboard units are best bought assembled and close by. Measure your wall and your biggest books before you look.

sections.heading: Depth and shelf height
paragraphs: Most paperbacks need about 20 cm of depth, hardbacks and art books 25-35 cm. An IKEA Billy is 28 cm deep, a Kallax 39 cm, which is good for records and boxes but wastes space on paperbacks. Shelf height of 25-30 cm fits most books; adjustable shelves give you room for large formats.
If the unit is also a room divider, check that it looks good from both sides and has no back panel, or a finished one.

Measure the wall too, including skirting boards, sockets and radiators. A 40 cm deep Kallax in front of a radiator blocks heat, and many older Dutch houses have walls that aren't quite straight, so leave a centimetre or two of space.

sections.heading: Shelf sag
paragraphs: Long shelves sag under books. Particleboard shelves start to bow on spans over about 80 cm, and a sagging shelf rarely straightens again. Look along each shelf at eye level in the listing photos or in person. Solid wood and metal shelves sag less. A bowed shelf can be flipped or replaced with a cut board from a hardware store, so it is a reason to negotiate, not always to walk away. Thicker shelves (25 mm or more) and shelves with a metal or solid wood front strip hold up much better than thin 16 mm board.

sections.heading: Types you will find
bullets: IKEA Billy and Kallax: cheap and everywhere, best bought assembled
IKEA Ivar: solid pine, easy to take apart and extend
String shelf: Swedish design with wall panels or floor panels, sold in parts, holds value
Vitsoe 606: wall-mounted track system, rare and expensive used
Pastoe and Montana: modular cabinets, Dutch and Danish design
Industrial metal and wood shelves: heavy, check welds and wobble
Ladder shelves: decorative, light loads only

sections.heading: Checks at the pickup
bullets: Shelf pins or brackets: all present, they are easy to lose in a move
Back panel: intact and attached, it keeps the unit square
Wobble: push the top sideways, a tall unit should feel rigid
Wall anchors: ask if the fixings come with it, and plan your own
Water damage: swollen edges at the bottom on particleboard
For String: count the side panels, shelves and clips against the listing

sections.heading: Anchoring and moving
paragraphs: Any bookcase taller than about 1 metre should be fixed to the wall, because a full one can tip forward. Most come with a strap or bracket; for Dutch walls you need the right plug for brick, concrete or plasterboard. A loaded 2 metre bookcase weighs well over 100 kg, so empty it fully before moving.
Tall units like a Billy at 202 cm need a van if they stay assembled. Modular systems like String and Ivar come apart in minutes and fit in a car.

sections.heading: Searching and price
paragraphs: Dutch listings use boekenkast, open kast, vakkenkast (cube shelf), wandkast and roomdivider. Brand names like String, Pastoe and Montana help a lot. On vindje.com you can ask for a solid wood bookcase at least 30 cm deep and no wider than 100 cm, and it checks measurements in the listing text so you don't have to.

Prices for IKEA bookcases are low and fixed by how easy they are to get new. Design systems are the opposite: a String set with the right panels sells quickly and often for a good share of the new price, so expect less room to haggle there.

price_guide.item: String shelf set, a few shelves

faq.q: How deep should a bookcase be?
faq.a: About 20-25 cm for paperbacks and novels, 30-35 cm for art books and large hardbacks. Billy is 28 cm deep.

faq.q: How do I stop bookshelves from sagging?
faq.a: Keep spans under about 80 cm on particleboard, use solid wood or metal shelves, or add a support in the middle. Flip a lightly bowed shelf.

faq.q: Do I need to fix a bookcase to the wall?
faq.a: Yes for anything taller than about 1 metre. A full bookcase can tip forward, especially if children climb it.

faq.q: Is a used String shelf worth it?
faq.a: Usually yes. String parts are standard, easy to extend and hold their value, so you can resell them later.

example_wish: Solid wood bookcase, 30 cm deep, max 100 cm wide and 200 cm high, adjustable shelves, under 150 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used standing desk (zit-sta bureau)
meta_title: Buying a Used Standing Desk: What to Check
description: Buying a used standing desk (zit-sta bureau): dual or single motor, height range, wobble, controller and fair prices for IKEA, Flexispot and office models.
intro: A used electric standing desk is good value if both motors run smoothly, it reaches the heights you need, and it doesn't wobble at standing height. Office clearouts and post-pandemic home offices put plenty of them on Marktplaats, often at less than half the new price. Run it up and down at least twice before you take it apart.

sections.heading: Types of standing desks
bullets: Electric dual motor: one motor per leg, smoother, stronger, the one to look for
Electric single motor: one motor drives both legs via a shaft, cheaper, slower
Hand crank (slinger bureau): no electronics, cheap, slow to adjust, fine if you rarely switch
Three-stage legs: bigger height range, good for tall people
Desk converters: sit on a normal desk, usually wobbly, not covered here

sections.heading: Why the motors matter most
paragraphs: The frame is the expensive part of a standing desk, and the motors and control box are the parts that fail. A replacement control box or motor for a known brand is usually available, but for a cheap no-name frame you may never find one. That is why a well known frame with a tired top is often a better buy than a pretty desk on a frame you can't identify. Ask for the brand and model, and look for a sticker under the crossbar or on the control box.

sections.heading: Height range and size
paragraphs: Most desks go from about 65-70 cm to 115-125 cm. Check the range against your own height: standing, your elbows should be at about 90 degrees with the desktop at elbow height. Very tall people (1.90 m+) need a frame that goes up to about 125-130 cm, which usually means three-stage legs. Short people should check the lowest height, as many desks can't go below 70 cm.
Desktops are commonly 120x60, 140x70, 160x80 or 180x80 cm. Frames with telescopic width can take a bigger top, so you can buy a frame and a separate top.

sections.heading: Tests at the pickup
paragraphs: Do these with the desk assembled and a bit of weight on it.
bullets: Run it fully up and down twice, both legs should move evenly without jerking
Listen: a steady hum is normal, grinding or clicking is not
At standing height, push the desk sideways and forward, some sway is normal, a rocking desk is tiring to work at
Controller: test the up, down and memory buttons, check the display
Ask for the reset procedure, many desks need one after being moved
Check the power cable and the control box under the desk are all there

sections.heading: Brands you will see
paragraphs: IKEA Bekant and Idåsen are very common. Idåsen uses a Linak system, known for reliability. Flexispot (E5, E7, E7 Pro) is popular in home offices and good value used. Fully Jarvis and Steelcase Ology or Migration come from offices and are solid. Office refurbishers sell checked desks with a short warranty, which is worth it if you are unsure about the electronics. Cable trays, monitor arms and anti-collision sensors are nice extras; check if they are included, since sellers often keep them.

sections.heading: Transport and assembly
paragraphs: Electric desks weigh 30-60 kg with the top, and the frame is long. Take the top off the frame (usually 8-12 screws) and keep the legs and crossbar together if possible. Label the cables. Don't carry the desk by the top while assembled, the legs are heavy and can bend the brackets. On vindje.com you can ask for a dual motor standing desk with a 160x80 top and memory buttons under 300 euro, and it skips hand crank models and frames without a top.

price_guide.item: Flexispot E5 or E7 with top

faq.q: Is a used standing desk worth buying?
faq.a: Yes, if both motors run evenly, it reaches the height you need and it is stable at standing height. They often sell for less than half of new.

faq.q: Single or dual motor standing desk?
faq.a: Dual motor is smoother and carries more weight. Single motor is cheaper and fine for a light setup.

faq.q: How tall should a standing desk go?
faq.a: The desktop should be at elbow height when you stand. For most adults that is 100-120 cm, tall people need up to 125-130 cm.

faq.q: What breaks on a used electric desk?
faq.a: Usually the control box, a motor or the hand controller. For known brands like Linak-based IKEA desks and Flexispot, replacements are available, for no-name frames often not.

faq.q: What does zit-sta bureau mean?
faq.a: It is Dutch for sit-stand desk. Search zit-sta bureau or elektrisch bureau on Marktplaats.

example_wish: Electric dual motor standing desk with 160x80 top, memory buttons, up to 125 cm high, under 300 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying used dining chairs: sets, joints and upholstery
meta_title: Buying Used Dining Chairs: Sets, Joints, Upholstery
description: Buying used dining chairs: how to check joints and seats, spot Eames, Cesca and Series 7 replicas, buy a full matching set and what fair prices are.
intro: Used dining chairs are cheap and plentiful, and good ones last generations. Check each chair separately, because one wobbly chair in a set of six is normal and fixable, a whole set with loose joints is not. Watch for replicas of design classics, which are fine to buy as long as you pay replica prices.

sections.heading: Buy the set, or mix on purpose
paragraphs: Complete matching sets of 4, 6 or 8 are worth more than single chairs, and finding a fifth matching chair later is hard. If you need six, look for a set of six, or decide to mix: four of one style plus two at the table ends, or the same chair in different colours. Mixed chairs can look great if they share a seat height (usually 45-47 cm) and a material.
Check the seat height against your table. A 75 cm table needs a seat around 45-48 cm, and armchairs need their arms to slide under the tabletop.

sections.heading: Joints and frames
paragraphs: Sit on each chair and rock gently side to side and back to front. Listen for creaks and feel for movement at the joints where legs meet the seat. On wooden chairs, loose joints can be reglued, which is a fair DIY job but takes clamps and time, so price it in. Look for screws added by previous owners, often a sign of a bad repair. Metal chairs: check welds, and on tubular chairs check the tube ends and feet for cracks and missing glides.
bullets: Wobble when you rock: loose joint, fixable with glue
Cracked leg or split seat: walk away unless it's a valuable chair
Mismatched legs or extra screws: earlier repair
Missing floor glides: cheap to replace, protects your floor

sections.heading: Seats and upholstery
paragraphs: Fabric seats on dining chairs take spills and stains, and smell can stay in the foam. Press the seat: foam that bottoms out needs replacing. Most dining chair seats are a board with foam and fabric stapled underneath, easy to redo with a staple gun for about EUR 15-30 a chair. Rush seats (biezen) and cane webbing (Weens vlechtwerk, as on Thonet and Cesca chairs) can be rewoven by specialists, but that costs more than a cheap chair is worth, so check for holes and sagging.

sections.heading: Design classics and copies
paragraphs: Some of the most common chairs on Marktplaats are copies of famous designs. They are not bad chairs, but they are worth much less than the originals.
bullets: Eames DSW or DSR (plastic shell): originals by Vitra or Herman Miller have a stamp underneath, copies cost EUR 20-40 each
Cesca (Marcel Breuer): genuine Thonet or Knoll versions are marked, many are unbranded
Series 7 (Arne Jacobsen): Fritz Hansen stamp under the seat, copies are common
Thonet bentwood (no. 14, no. 18): old originals have a stamp or label, also made by other makers
Tulip chair (Saarinen): Knoll originals are heavy and marked

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
bullets: Count the chairs, check each one separately
Rock each one, look under the seat for stamps, repairs and cracks
Seat height and armrest height against your table
Smell the upholstery up close
Stackable? Check that they stack without scratching
Bring blankets, chairs scuff easily in a car

sections.heading: Searching and price
paragraphs: Search eetkamerstoelen, set van 4 or set van 6, and specific names: Thonet, Pastoe, Cesca, kuipstoel (bucket chair). On vindje.com you can ask for a set of six wooden dining chairs with upholstered seats under 200 euro, and it filters out single chairs and replicas sold as originals.

price_guide.item: Cesca chair, Thonet or Knoll original, each

faq.q: How do I fix wobbly dining chairs?
faq.a: Take the loose joint apart if you can, clean off old glue, apply wood glue and clamp it for a day. Screws alone rarely hold.

faq.q: How can I tell if an Eames chair is original?
faq.a: Look under the seat for a Vitra or Herman Miller stamp or label. Copies are often unmarked, lighter and cost far less.

faq.q: What seat height do dining chairs need?
faq.a: For a standard 74-76 cm table, a seat height of about 45-48 cm works for most people.

faq.q: Are replica design chairs worth buying?
faq.a: They can be, as long as you pay replica prices. They are usually lighter and less durable than the originals and have little resale value.

faq.q: Can you reupholster dining chair seats yourself?
faq.a: Yes. Most seats unscrew from below. Replace the foam, staple new fabric underneath and screw it back on.

example_wish: Set of 6 solid wood dining chairs with upholstered seats, seat height around 46 cm, no wobbly joints, under 250 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying used garden furniture: teak, aluminium, rattan
meta_title: Buying Used Garden Furniture: Teak, Aluminium, Rattan
description: Buying used garden furniture: how teak, aluminium and polyrattan age outdoors, what to check, when to buy, and fair prices for tables and lounge sets.
intro: Used garden furniture is a good deal when the material ages well: teak and aluminium last for decades, while cheap polyrattan and plastic get brittle in the sun. Check the frame, the joints and the cushions, and buy in autumn or winter, when sellers have no use for it and prices are lowest.

sections.heading: Teak
paragraphs: Good teak is dense and oily and lasts for decades outside. It turns silver grey if left untreated, which is only colour, not damage. A grey teak table can be sanded or cleaned back to honey brown in an afternoon. Look for cracks along the grain, especially at the ends of boards, and loose joints in chairs. Bolted tables should be tightened each season.

Not all teak is equal. Grade A heartwood from established brands like Jati & Kebon, Traditional Teak or Borek feels heavy and has tight grain. Cheap teak with lots of light sapwood, knots and wide grain weathers faster. If a table feels light for its size, it may not be teak at all, and acacia or other hardwoods are sometimes sold as teak look.
Extendable teak tables have runners and leaves that can swell after wet winters. Open and close the table fully before you buy, and check the leaves aren't warped.

sections.heading: Aluminium
paragraphs: Aluminium doesn't rust, which makes it a good used buy. Check the powder coating for chips and blisters, especially at joints and the feet. Look at the welds and bolts: aluminium chairs can crack at the welds after years of rocking. Textilene or rope seats (common on aluminium chairs) should be taut, without tears or sun-faded brittleness. Fermob Bistro chairs and tables are steel, not aluminium, and can rust where the paint is chipped.

sections.heading: Rattan, polyrattan and wicker
paragraphs: Most outdoor lounge sets labelled wicker or rattan are polyrattan: a synthetic weave over an aluminium or steel frame. Good polyrattan (flat or round fibre from brands like 4 Seasons Outdoor, Hartman, Life Outdoor Living) lasts many years. Cheap sets fade, crack and unravel within a few seasons. Check corners and the edge of seats, where the weave breaks first, and press the fibre: if it cracks or feels like dry plastic, it's at the end of its life.
Natural rattan and wicker are indoor materials. A natural rattan chair that has been outside will rot and loosen.

sections.heading: Cushions
paragraphs: Cushions are often the worst part of a used set. Check for mould spots, mildew smell and flattened foam. Removable covers that can go in the wash help a lot. New cushions for a lounge set easily cost EUR 100-300, so a set with good cushions is worth more and a set with ruined ones should be priced lower. Ask where the cushions were stored over winter: a dry shed or attic is a good sign, a garden box with condensation often means mould inside the foam.

sections.heading: Checks at the pickup
bullets: Sit on every chair and lean back, listen for cracks
Push the table at the corners for wobble
Teak: look for cracks along the board ends
Aluminium: chips in the coating at joints and feet
Polyrattan: brittle or broken fibres at corners and seat edges
Cushions: mould, smell, flat foam, covers removable
Size: measure your terrace or balcony, lounge sets are bigger than photos suggest

sections.heading: When and what to search
paragraphs: Prices fall from September and are lowest in winter, when people clear their sheds or move. In spring, the first sunny weekend sends prices up. Search tuinset, loungeset, teak tuintafel, tuinstoelen, aluminium tuinset. On vindje.com you can ask for a teak garden table for 6 with chairs, within 20 km, and it filters out polyrattan sets and loose chairs.

faq.q: When is the best time to buy used garden furniture?
faq.a: Autumn and winter. People sell when they clear the shed or move, and demand is low. Prices go up in spring.

faq.q: Can you restore grey teak?
faq.a: Yes. Clean it with a teak cleaner or sand it lightly, then oil it if you want the warm colour back. The grey is only on the surface.

faq.q: Is polyrattan garden furniture durable?
faq.a: Good quality polyrattan lasts many years. Cheap sets can crack and unravel after a few summers in the sun.

faq.q: How do I know if garden furniture is genuine teak?
faq.a: Teak is heavy, slightly oily to the touch and has a tight, straight grain. A light table with wide grain is probably another wood or low grade teak.

faq.q: Can aluminium garden furniture stay outside in winter?
faq.a: It won't rust, so yes, but covers or a shed protect the coating and the cushions.

example_wish: Teak garden table 180-200 cm with 6 chairs, solid and no cracks, under 500 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying a used chest of drawers (ladekast)
meta_title: Buying a Used Chest of Drawers (Ladekast)
description: Buying a used chest of drawers (ladekast): test drawer runners, joints and veneer, why to anchor it, and fair prices for IKEA, vintage and antique.
intro: A used chest of drawers is a good second hand buy when the drawers run smoothly, the joints are tight and the carcass is square. Pull every drawer all the way out before you agree a price. And whatever you buy, fix it to the wall: chests of drawers are the piece of furniture most likely to tip over onto a child.

sections.heading: Test every drawer
paragraphs: The drawers are the whole point, so open each one fully, close it and push it in again. It should run smoothly without catching or dropping when fully extended.
bullets: Wooden runners: should glide, waxing them with candle wax helps, but deep grooves mean wear
Metal ball-bearing runners: smooth, quiet, check they don't rattle or stick
Drawer bottoms: no sagging or cracks, they carry the weight
Fronts: lined up evenly when closed, a crooked row means a twisted carcass
Handles: all present, matching replacements for vintage pieces can be hard to find
Smell: musty or mothball smell in drawers is hard to remove

sections.heading: Joints and construction
paragraphs: Pull a drawer out and look at the corners. Dovetail joints (interlocking fingers) mean good, solid construction and are typical of older and better furniture. Stapled or glued corners on particleboard drawers are found on cheaper modern pieces and can come apart. Rock the whole chest gently: it should not twist. On older pieces check the back panel and feet for woodworm, small round holes with fine dust. Old holes without dust are usually inactive.

Check the top as well. Ring marks and scratches on solid wood can be sanded out, but on veneer you only get one careful attempt. A glass plate on top is a common way sellers hide damage, so lift it or ask about it.

sections.heading: Vintage, antique and modern
paragraphs: Dutch and Danish teak dressers from the 1960s and 70s are popular and priced accordingly. Look for veneer that is lifting at the edges or bubbled from water, which is repairable but fiddly. Antique oak and mahogany chests are heavy and solid, and often cheaper than vintage teak because they are less fashionable.

Modern chests from IKEA (Malm, Hemnes, Brimnes) are everywhere. Hemnes is solid pine and holds up. Malm is particleboard and fine for a bedroom, but loses strength after dismantling. Dutch design pieces from Pastoe and Spectrum hold value.

Watch for the word dressoir in listings. In Dutch that usually means a sideboard with doors and a few drawers, not a chest of drawers, so search ladekast or commode to get what you want, and check the width and depth against the spot in your bedroom.

sections.heading: Anchor it to the wall
paragraphs: A chest of drawers with heavy drawers pulled out becomes front-heavy and can tip. IKEA recalled millions of Malm and other chests in the United States and Canada after fatal tip-over accidents, and the advice since then has been simple: always anchor it. Most chests come with a wall fixing kit; if it's missing, a hardware store sells anti-tip straps for a few euro. Use plugs that suit your wall type.
This applies to vintage pieces too. A solid oak commode is heavy, but with three drawers full and open it can still tip.

sections.heading: Moving it
paragraphs: Take the drawers out and move them separately, it makes the carcass much lighter and stops them sliding out on the stairs. Tape the drawers' order on the back. Carry the carcass upright and protect corners and veneer with blankets. On vindje.com you can ask for a vintage teak ladekast up to 120 cm wide with smooth drawers, and it reads the listings for width and condition.

faq.q: How do I fix sticking drawers?
faq.a: Rub candle wax or paraffin on wooden runners. If drawers still stick, check for a loose runner or a drawer bottom that sags.

faq.q: Is a vintage teak dresser worth the price?
faq.a: Often yes if the veneer is intact and the drawers run well, as they resell easily. Be careful with lifted or water damaged veneer, which is costly to restore properly.

faq.q: Should a chest of drawers be anchored to the wall?
faq.a: Yes, always. With open drawers it becomes front-heavy and can tip over, especially if a child climbs it.

faq.q: How can I tell if a dresser is solid wood?
faq.a: Look at drawer sides and the back. Solid wood shows grain on the edges and inside, and old ones often have dovetail joints. Veneer has a thin top layer over a different core.

faq.q: What is the difference between a ladekast and a commode?
faq.a: In Dutch both mean a chest of drawers. Commode is often used for a lower, wider piece, sometimes with a changing top for babies.

example_wish: Vintage teak chest of drawers, max 120 cm wide, smooth running drawers, under 350 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used armchair (fauteuil) on Marktplaats
meta_title: Buying a used armchair (fauteuil): what to check
description: How to buy a used armchair in the Netherlands: Dutch search terms, frame and cushion checks, fair prices for a fauteuil, and which ones to skip.
intro: A used armchair is one of the best second-hand buys in the Netherlands: they are bulky to move, so sellers price them low just to clear space. Search for fauteuil rather than armchair, check the frame and the seat foam at pickup, and expect to pay EUR 30-150 for a solid everyday chair.

sections.heading: Search in Dutch, and use more than one word
paragraphs: Dutch sellers almost never write armchair. The main word is fauteuil, with leunstoel for a more upright chair with arms and oorfauteuil for a wingback. A recliner is usually a relaxfauteuil or sta-op stoel (a powered lift chair, often from elderly households). Swivel chairs are draaifauteuil.
Add a material or style to cut the noise: fauteuil leer, fauteuil velours, fauteuil teddy, fauteuil vintage. Colour words help too: groen, cognac, okergeel.

sections.heading: Check the frame before the fabric
paragraphs: Fabric can be cleaned or reupholstered. A wobbly or cracked frame is much harder to fix. Sit down, rock side to side and lean back hard against the backrest. Listen for creaks and feel for movement at the arm joints.
bullets: Tip the chair over and look at the underside: staples, glue blocks and webbing should be intact
Press the seat with your fist: elastic webbing or springs should push back evenly
Look at the legs where they meet the frame, that is where cheap chairs crack
For a recliner, run the mechanism several times and check both end positions
For a swivel chair, turn it fully and listen for grinding in the base

sections.heading: Cushions, foam and smell
paragraphs: Seat foam is what wears out first. If you sink in and feel the frame, the foam is finished. New cut-to-size foam for one seat cushion costs roughly EUR 40-90 at an upholstery supply shop, so factor that in.

Smell the chair up close, including under the seat cushion. Smoke, pets and damp all soak into foam and do not come out with a spot cleaner. A chair that lived in a smoking household is rarely worth taking home, however cheap it is.

sections.heading: Which armchairs hold up second hand
paragraphs: Solid wood frames with removable covers last for decades. Older Dutch and Scandinavian lounge chairs from the 1960s and 1970s often have teak or oak frames with loose cushions you can replace. IKEA's Poang and Strandmon show up constantly and are fine buys at the right price, since covers are still sold new.
Be wary of very cheap chairs with fixed fabric and a particleboard frame. They looked good in the shop photo but loosen quickly, and you cannot fix them properly.

sections.heading: Getting it home
paragraphs: Measure your door and stairwell before you go. Most armchairs are 75-95 cm wide, and a wingback can be taller than you expect. Many fit in a hatchback with the seats down; otherwise a rental van by the hour or a courier platform like Brenger is a common option for single items.

If you are hunting for something specific, a plain-language search on vindje.com can handle details like a velvet swivel chair under 100 euro within 15 km, so you are not scrolling through hundreds of dining chairs.

sections.heading: Pickup checklist
paragraphs: Use this when you are standing in someone's living room.
bullets: Sit in it for at least a minute
Rock it, lean back, check the arms for play
Lift cushions, look and smell underneath
Check the underside for broken webbing or loose staples
Ask if it came from a smoke-free and pet-free home
Measure it against the numbers you wrote down for your door

price_guide.item: IKEA Poang or similar basic armchair
Vintage teak lounge chair, original cushions

faq.q: What is an armchair called in Dutch?
faq.a: Fauteuil is the most common word. Leunstoel and oorfauteuil (wingback) are also used, and relaxfauteuil means a recliner.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a used upholstered chair?
faq.a: Usually yes, if you inspect it. Check for smells, stains and any sign of bugs in the seams, and skip anything that smells of smoke or damp.

faq.q: Is it worth reupholstering an old armchair?
faq.a: Professional reupholstery of an armchair often costs several hundred euro, so it only makes sense for a chair with a good solid frame or a design piece. For a cheap chair, a new seat cushion or a loose cover is the better fix.

faq.q: How do I transport an armchair without a car?
faq.a: Rent a van by the hour, ask the seller if they can deliver for a small fee, or book a courier platform that handles single furniture items.

example_wish: Green velvet armchair or swivel fauteuil in good condition, no smoke or pets, under 120 euro, within 15 km of Utrecht

title: Buying a used leather sofa: genuine vs bonded leather
meta_title: Used leather sofa: genuine vs bonded leather
description: Buying a used leather sofa? How to tell genuine from bonded or PU leather in a listing and at pickup, what to check, and fair second-hand prices.
intro: A used leather sofa can last another 15 years or fall apart in two, and the difference is almost always the material. Genuine full-grain or top-grain leather ages well; bonded leather and PU (polyurethane) peel within a few years. Learn to tell them apart before you pay, because sellers often do not know either.

sections.heading: The three materials you will see
paragraphs: Genuine leather (echt leer, rundleer, volnerf leer) is a hide. It wrinkles a little, warms up under your hand and develops a patina. Top-grain has a sanded and coated surface but is still a hide.

Bonded leather (gerecycled leer, bonded leer) is leather scraps glued to a fabric backing with a polyurethane coat on top. PU leather or kunstleer is plastic on fabric with no leather at all. Both look fine for a year or two, then crack and flake in sheets. Once that starts it cannot be repaired.

sections.heading: Reading the listing
paragraphs: Listings that say leren look, lederlook or kunstleer are not leather. Listings that say leer without more detail could be anything. Look closely at photos of the seat edges and armrests: small flakes or white fabric showing through means bonded or PU.

Ask the seller for the brand and model. A sofa from Leolux, Montel, Gelderland, de Sede or Natuzzi is almost certainly genuine leather. A no-name sofa from a big furniture chain sold as leer for very little money new is often partly leather (seat and backrest) with split leather or PU on the sides and back.

sections.heading: Tests at the pickup
paragraphs: You can usually tell in a minute with your hands and eyes.
bullets: Look at a cut edge or underneath a cushion zip: genuine leather has a fibrous suede-like back, bonded and PU show woven fabric
Press a thumb into the seat: genuine leather wrinkles in fine, irregular lines
Check the pore pattern: genuine leather has uneven pores, PU repeats a stamped pattern
Smell it: genuine leather smells like leather, PU smells faintly of plastic
Inspect armrests and headrests for peeling, the first places bonded leather fails
Sit, recline, and test any electric mechanism on every seat

sections.heading: Frame, cushions and size
paragraphs: Leather sofas are heavy, and the frame takes a lot of stress when people drop into them. Lift one end a few centimetres: it should feel rigid, with no twisting. Unzip a seat cushion if you can and look at the foam. Grey crumbling foam means the seat will sag soon.

Measure doors, stairwells and your car. A three-seater is often 200-230 cm long, and a hoekbank (corner sofa) usually comes apart in two or three pieces. Ask the seller how it splits before you arrive with a small van.

sections.heading: Cracks, scratches and colour loss
paragraphs: Dry, faded genuine leather is often recoverable with a cleaner and conditioner, and light cat scratches blend in over time. Deep cracks in the surface of a genuine leather seat can be recoloured by a specialist but cost money. Peeling bonded leather is a write-off: price it as if you will replace the sofa in a year.
Aniline leather (soft, no protective coat) marks easily and shows every drop of water. Some people love that look; if you have small children, a pigmented leather is easier to live with.

sections.heading: First week at home
paragraphs: Before it goes into your living room, vacuum the seams and under the cushions with a brush nozzle. Clean the whole surface with a pH-neutral leather cleaner and a damp cloth, then apply a conditioner, testing both on a hidden spot first. Keep the sofa out of direct afternoon sun and at least a metre from a radiator, since heat dries leather and makes it crack.

If the seat cushions feel flat, an upholsterer can add a layer of new foam or a wrap of polyester fibre inside the existing leather cover. That is usually far cheaper than replacing the leather, and it makes an older sofa feel firm again.

price_guide.item: Leolux, Montel or de Sede leather sofa

faq.q: How can I tell if a sofa is real leather?
faq.a: Look at the underside or a seam: genuine leather has a suede-like fibrous back, while bonded and PU leather show a woven fabric. Irregular pores and fine wrinkles when you press it also point to a hide.

faq.q: Can peeling bonded leather be repaired?
faq.a: Not in a lasting way. The coating separates from the backing, and patches or paint only hide it for a short time.

faq.q: Is a used leather sofa hygienic?
faq.a: Leather is easier to clean than fabric and does not hold dust mites the same way. Wipe it with a mild leather cleaner and check the cushion foam for smells.

faq.q: What does lederlook mean on Marktplaats?
faq.a: It means leather look, so imitation leather. It is not leather.

example_wish: Genuine leather 3-seater sofa in cognac or dark brown, not bonded or PU, no peeling, under 400 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used coffee table (salontafel)
meta_title: Buying a used coffee table (salontafel) second hand
description: Find a good used coffee table in the Netherlands: Dutch search terms, solid wood versus veneer, glass and marble checks, sizes and fair prices.
intro: Coffee tables are some of the cheapest furniture on Marktplaats, and plenty are given away for free. Search for salontafel, decide on size and material first, then check the top for damage you cannot sand out and the legs for wobble.

sections.heading: Start with the size you need
paragraphs: A coffee table usually works best at about two thirds the length of your sofa and 5-10 cm lower than the seat. For a standard sofa that means roughly 90-120 cm long and 40-45 cm high. Round tables of 70-90 cm suit small Dutch living rooms because you do not bump into corners.
Write your measurements down before you search. Sellers often list dimensions in the description, and a table that looks small in a photo can be 140 cm long.

sections.heading: Solid wood, veneer and particleboard
paragraphs: Massief means solid wood. Fineer means veneer, a thin layer of wood over a board. Both can be good. Solid oak or teak can be sanded and oiled again and again. Veneer can be lightly sanded once, if at all, and deep scratches will go through it.

Melamine or foil-wrapped particleboard (spaanplaat) is the cheap end. It is fine at EUR 10, but water damage makes it swell at the edges and that cannot be fixed. Look at the edges of the top and the bottom of the legs for swelling.

sections.heading: Glass, marble and travertine
paragraphs: Glass tables should have tempered glass (gehard glas). Look for chips along the edge, which can spread into cracks. Ask whether the glass is loose on the frame and take blankets for transport.

Marble and travertine tables are popular and heavy. A 100 cm marble top can weigh 60 kg or more, so bring a second person. Check for cracks running through the stone rather than surface marks, and look for rings from glasses: marble etches with wine, lemon and cleaning products and needs polishing to remove them. Many marble look tables are ceramic or laminate, so ask.

sections.heading: Checks at the pickup
paragraphs: A coffee table is simple, so the checks are quick.
bullets: Push on a corner to see if the table wobbles or the legs flex
Look under the top at screws and brackets, tighten what you can
Run your hand over the surface for scratches deeper than the finish
Check drawers and lift-up tops open and close smoothly
Look for white rings and dark water stains on wood
Measure it yourself if the size matters

sections.heading: Vintage and design tables
paragraphs: Mid-century teak tables from Danish and Dutch makers turn up often and can be good value at EUR 60-200 if the veneer is intact. Noguchi style glass tables are almost always copies when cheap; the Vitra original is far more expensive new. Treat a designer name in a listing as a claim to check, not a fact.

If you want something specific, like a round oak table under 80 cm wide with a shelf, describing that in plain words on vindje.com saves going through hundreds of results that only match the word salontafel.

sections.heading: Free tables and quick upgrades
paragraphs: Search with the price filter set to gratis or sort by price and you will find plenty of tables offered for nothing, mostly when people move house. They are a good base for a project: a pine table with an orange lacquer can be sanded and finished with a matt hardwax oil in an afternoon, and swapping dated legs for new hairpin or turned legs costs EUR 20-40 for a set.
Skip free tables with swollen particleboard, broken glass or a top that is coming apart in layers. Those are moving-day leftovers, not projects.

price_guide.item: IKEA Lack or similar basic table
Solid oak or pine coffee table
Glass coffee table with metal frame

faq.q: What is a coffee table called in Dutch?
faq.a: Salontafel. A small side table is a bijzettafel, and a set of nesting tables is a mimiset or set bijzettafels.

faq.q: Can I refinish a used wooden coffee table?
faq.a: Solid wood can be sanded and oiled or varnished again. Veneer is thin, so only sand it lightly by hand or use a refresher product instead.

faq.q: How do I remove white rings from a wood table?
faq.a: White rings are moisture in the finish and sometimes fade with gentle heat from a hair dryer or a little furniture polish. Dark rings have gone into the wood and usually need sanding.

faq.q: Is a cheap marble coffee table real marble?
faq.a: Often not. Ask the seller, look at the edge for a uniform layer that suggests laminate or ceramic, and check the weight, since solid stone is very heavy.

example_wish: Round solid oak coffee table, 70-90 cm across, no water damage, under 80 euro, within 10 km of Amsterdam

title: Buying a used rug (vloerkleed): wool, hand-knotted and cleaning
meta_title: Buying a used rug (vloerkleed): wool and hand-knotted
description: How to buy a used rug in the Netherlands: tell hand-knotted from tufted or machine-made, spot moths and latex rot, clean it, and pay a fair price.
intro: Second-hand rugs are great value if you buy wool and avoid the two big problems: moths and rotting latex backing. Flip the rug over before anything else. The back tells you how it was made, what it is worth and whether it will last.

sections.heading: Search terms that find the good ones
paragraphs: Vloerkleed is the general word, tapijt is also used for rugs as well as wall-to-wall carpet. For handmade rugs, sellers write Perzisch tapijt, Oosters tapijt, handgeknoopt (hand-knotted) or name a type: Berber, kelim (flat-woven, no pile), Gabbeh, Heriz, Kazak. Wollen vloerkleed finds wool rugs of all kinds.
Many good rugs are listed by people clearing out a parent's house with titles like oud tapijt or groot kleed. Those can be the best buys because nobody looked closely at them.

sections.heading: Flip it over: knotted, tufted or machine-made
paragraphs: On a hand-knotted rug the pattern on the back is a clear, slightly less sharp copy of the front, with tiny individual knots you can see. The fringes are the ends of the warp threads and run through the whole rug.

A hand-tufted rug has a canvas or fabric backing glued over the back, often with a stiff layer of latex under it. You will not see the pattern. A machine-made rug shows a very regular grid on the back and its fringes are often sewn on as a separate strip. Tufted and machine-made rugs can be nice, but they are worth much less used.

sections.heading: The problems to look for
paragraphs: Unroll the rug fully, ideally outside or in a well lit room, and go over it slowly.
bullets: Moths: bald patches where the pile is eaten down to the knots, small white casings or sandy grit, mostly in corners and under where furniture stood
Latex rot: on tufted rugs, a back that crumbles into powder, cracks when folded or smells sour
Dry rot: on old knotted rugs, bend a section gently and listen for cracking, which means the cotton foundation is brittle
Colour run: dyes bleeding into white areas, usually after a bad wash
Pet urine: yellow stains and a sharp smell, worse when damp
Holes and worn edges: the side cords (selvedge) and fringes take the most wear

sections.heading: Cleaning a used rug
paragraphs: Vacuum both sides first, then hang it or lay it pile down and beat the back to get grit out. For wool, do not soak it in a bathtub with regular detergent. A professional rug washer is the safe choice for anything valuable, and they usually charge per square metre, with prices that make sense for a good wool rug but not for a cheap synthetic one.

For moths, a professional wash kills larvae and eggs. Freezing small rugs for a few days in a sealed bag works too. Bring anything that might have moths home in a bag and keep it away from your other rugs and wool clothes until it is treated.

sections.heading: Value: what is and is not worth money
paragraphs: Most used Persian style rugs in Dutch homes are ordinary decorative pieces, not antiques. A hand-knotted rug in good condition is a solid buy at a few hundred euro but rarely a hidden treasure. Machine-made rugs with Persian patterns are common and should be cheap.

If you know what you want, for example a wool rug of at least 200 by 300 cm with low pile in muted colours, a search on vindje.com can read the descriptions for size and material instead of only matching the word vloerkleed.

price_guide.item: Hand-knotted Persian style rug, 200x300, good condition
Vintage Berber or Beni Ouarain style rug

faq.q: How can I tell if a rug is hand-knotted?
faq.a: Turn it over. A hand-knotted rug shows the pattern on the back with visible individual knots, and the fringes are part of the rug rather than sewn on.

faq.q: How do I know if a used rug has moths?
faq.a: Look for bare patches where the pile is eaten away, tiny white casings and sandy debris, especially near the edges and under furniture spots. Moth damage is often worse on the back side.

faq.q: Can I wash a wool rug myself?
faq.a: Small wool rugs can be cleaned carefully with cold water and a wool detergent, then dried flat quickly. Larger or valuable rugs are better sent to a professional rug washer.

faq.q: Why does the back of my rug crumble?
faq.a: That is degraded latex on a tufted rug. It cannot be repaired and will keep shedding powder, so these rugs are usually not worth buying.

example_wish: Wool rug at least 200x300 cm, hand-knotted or kelim, muted colours, no moth damage, under 300 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying a used bunk bed (stapelbed) safely
meta_title: Buying a used bunk bed (stapelbed) safely
description: How to buy a used bunk bed safely in the Netherlands: guardrails, gaps, ladders, missing parts, which brands last, and fair stapelbed prices.
intro: A used bunk bed is a sensible buy, since children outgrow them long before they wear out. The things to check are safety ones: guardrails high enough above the mattress, no gaps a child's head can get through, a solid ladder and every original bolt.

sections.heading: Stapelbed, hoogslaper or halfhoogslaper
paragraphs: A stapelbed has two beds above each other. A hoogslaper is a loft bed with one high bed and space underneath, often for a desk. A halfhoogslaper is a mid-height loft bed for younger children. Many brands sell beds that convert between these, so search all three terms.

Note the mattress size. Most Dutch children's beds take 90x200, but some, including several IKEA models, take 90x190 or 80x200. Buy a new mattress that fits exactly, since a gap at the side is a trapping hazard.

sections.heading: Safety checks on the top bunk
paragraphs: Bunk beds sold new in Europe are made to the EN 747 standard, and a well made used bed will match it. You cannot run a lab test in someone's bedroom, but you can check the main points.
bullets: Guardrails on all four sides of the top bed, with an opening only where the ladder is
The top of the guardrail should stand well above the mattress; many beds have a line marking the maximum mattress height, so keep to it
No openings between rails, or between rail and bed, where a child's head or neck could get stuck
No bolts or corner posts sticking up that could catch clothing
Ladder rungs flat and firm, ladder fixed to the frame, not hooked loosely
Shake the assembled bed hard: it should not sway or creak at the joints

sections.heading: Missing parts and assembly
paragraphs: Most used bunk beds are sold taken apart, or you take them apart together with the seller. Do it together if you can, and put all bolts and small parts in labelled bags. Ask for the assembly manual or download it, since most brands keep them online.

Check that the bolt holes are not stripped or split. Pine beds that have been taken apart several times often have worn holes, and a bed that cannot be bolted tight should not be used as a bunk. Replacement bolts for well known brands can often be ordered, but count on the parts being complete.

sections.heading: Brands that hold up
paragraphs: Flexa (Danish) and Life Time are the brands people look for: solid wood, modular, and spare parts exist. They keep their value well. IKEA bunk beds like Mydal, Tuffing and the Kura loft bed are everywhere on Marktplaats and are fine when complete and undamaged, at low prices.
Be more careful with old no-name pine beds and anything clearly home made. They can be perfectly sturdy, but there is no manual and no way to check how they were designed.

sections.heading: What not to buy used
paragraphs: Skip the old mattresses. You do not know their history, and children's mattresses are cheap new. Also skip beds with cracked slats or rails, beds with a broken or improvised ladder, and fabric tents or slide add-ons that are torn.
The usual advice printed on bunk beds is that children under six should not sleep in the top bed. Keep that in mind when choosing between a bunk and a lower halfhoogslaper.

sections.heading: Searching smarter
paragraphs: Bunk beds are bulky and most people want one within driving distance. If you describe the size and features you need, like a wooden bunk for 90x200 mattresses with a storage drawer within 20 km, vindje.com can filter out the doll beds, mattresses and single beds that crowd the normal results.

price_guide.item: IKEA Mydal or Tuffing bunk bed
Life Time loft or bunk bed

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a second-hand bunk bed?
faq.a: Yes, if it is complete, assembled tight, has guardrails on all sides of the top bed and no gaps where a head could get stuck. Buy new mattresses.

faq.q: What age is a top bunk suitable for?
faq.a: The common guidance on bunk beds sold in Europe is from six years. Younger children are safer in the bottom bed or a low loft bed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stapelbed and a hoogslaper?
faq.a: A stapelbed has two sleeping places stacked. A hoogslaper is a single raised bed with space underneath for a desk, sofa or play area.

faq.q: Can I get spare parts for a used Flexa bed?
faq.a: Flexa parts are often available through their dealers and online, and there is a busy second-hand market for Flexa parts on Marktplaats too.

example_wish: Wooden bunk bed for two 90x200 mattresses, complete with ladder and guardrails, Flexa or similar solid wood, under 300 euro, within 20 km

title: Eames chairs on Marktplaats: original vs replica
meta_title: Eames chair original vs replica: how to tell
description: How to tell an original Eames chair from a replica on Marktplaats: Vitra and Herman Miller marks, lounge chair checks, plastic chairs and fair prices.
intro: Most chairs listed as Eames on Marktplaats are replicas, and many sellers use the name for any plastic chair with wooden legs. Originals are made by Vitra (for Europe) and Herman Miller (for North America), and they carry marks you can check. If the listing has no photo of the underside, ask for one before you travel.

sections.heading: How the name gets used
paragraphs: Charles and Ray Eames designed a set of chairs that have been copied for decades. In listings, Eames style, Eames look, inspired by and replica are honest signs of a copy. Plain Eames stoel with a price of EUR 25 is also a copy, the seller just did not say so.
Only Vitra and Herman Miller are licensed to make them. A listing that says origineel should be backed by photos of labels and, ideally, a receipt.

sections.heading: Plastic side chairs (DSW, DSR, DAW)
paragraphs: These are the chairs you see most. DSW has wooden dowel legs, DSR has a metal Eiffel base, DAW is the armchair on wooden legs. Vitra's current shells are polypropylene with a matt, slightly textured surface. Turn the chair over and look under the seat.
bullets: A Vitra original has moulded markings under the shell, including the Vitra name, the Eames name and production details
The legs on an original fit cleanly to the shell with neat mounts, no wobble
The wooden legs and metal cross wires on a copy are often thinner or rougher, with visible welds
Copies tend to be glossier plastic and sometimes have a seat that flexes more
Vintage fibreglass shells (older Herman Miller and Zenith production) have a visible fibre texture and are a separate collector market

sections.heading: The lounge chair and ottoman
paragraphs: The Eames Lounge Chair (670) with ottoman (671) is the most copied design chair there is. A new original costs many thousands of euro, so a listing at EUR 600 is a replica, however convincing the photos are.

On an original, look for a Vitra or Herman Miller label under the seat, plywood shells with even veneer, and armrests and backrest connected through rubber shock mounts. Ask for the purchase receipt and the label photo. Replicas often have thicker, clumsier aluminium parts, a different angle and recline, and leather that creases in flat folds. If the seller dodges the underside photo, walk away.

sections.heading: Office chairs and other models
paragraphs: The Aluminium Group chairs (EA 117, EA 119 and similar) are used in offices and turn up when companies clear out. Originals are Vitra or Herman Miller with marks on the base and under the seat. The Soft Pad versions have thick cushions. Copies of these exist too but are less common than with the lounge chair.
The Eames Hang It All coat rack, House Bird and Elephant are Vitra products too and widely copied at low prices.

sections.heading: Are replicas worth buying?
paragraphs: A replica plastic chair at EUR 20-40 can be a fine kitchen chair. What you should not do is pay original money for one. Replica lounge chairs vary a lot in build quality; some fall apart at the shock mounts within a few years.

Resale also differs: an original Vitra chair keeps most of its value, while a copy is worth little second hand. If you want only originals, a plain-language search on vindje.com can ask for a Vitra Eames chair with a photo of the label and skip listings that say stijl or replica.

price_guide.item: Vitra DSW or DSR, original, good condition
Original Eames Lounge Chair with ottoman

faq.q: How do I know if my Eames chair is original?
faq.a: Look under the seat for Vitra or Herman Miller markings or labels, and compare the base, mounts and plastic finish with photos on the maker's site. No marks at all usually means a copy.

faq.q: Is a Vitra Eames chair worth buying second hand?
faq.a: Yes, they are durable and hold their value. Check that the shell is not cracked around the mounts and that the legs are original.

faq.q: Why are there so many cheap Eames chairs on Marktplaats?
faq.a: Because replicas are mass produced and sold cheaply online, and sellers often list them under the Eames name.

faq.q: Is it legal to sell an Eames replica?
faq.a: Design rights in the EU are complex and we will not give legal advice here. As a buyer, the main rule is to pay replica money for a replica.

example_wish: Original Vitra Eames DSW chair in white or black, with photo of the Vitra marks underneath, no replica, under 250 euro, within 40 km

title: Vintage design lamps worth looking for second hand
meta_title: Vintage design lamps worth buying second hand
description: Which vintage design lamps are worth finding on Marktplaats: Dutch makers like Hala and Raak, Danish and Italian classics, copies, wiring and prices.
intro: Lamps are one of the best categories for finding vintage design second hand, because many good ones are listed as oude lamp without a brand. Dutch makers from the 1950s to 1970s are common and still affordable, while Danish and Italian classics are worth knowing but heavily copied.

sections.heading: Dutch makers to know
paragraphs: The Netherlands had a busy lighting industry, and its lamps are all over Marktplaats. These names are worth searching on their own.
bullets: Hala Zeist: desk and wall lamps, often designed by H. Busquet, recognisable by sturdy hinged arms
Anvia Almelo: desk and floor lamps with slim arms and conical shades
Raak Amsterdam: pendants and wall lights from the 1960s and 1970s, glass and metal
Dijkstra: pendants and floor lamps, many in teak and glass
Philips: from Bauhaus style desk lamps to space age pendants
Herda and Gepo: pendant lamps in metal and acrylic, good value

sections.heading: Danish and Italian classics
paragraphs: Louis Poulsen (PH5, PH Artichoke), Le Klint pleated shades and Fog & Morup glass pendants are the Danish names that come up most. Le Klint shades in good condition are still affordable.

From Italy, the Flos Arco floor lamp, Artemide Tizio desk lamp and the Guzzini acrylic mushroom lamps are popular. The Arco is one of the most copied lamps: an original has a heavy single block of Carrara marble and the Flos name, while a copy's base is often lighter or composite. The PH5 and Panton Flowerpot are also widely copied, so ask for labels and close-up photos.

sections.heading: Finding unbranded pieces
paragraphs: Many sellers do not know what they have. Search for descriptive words instead of brands: hanglamp messing (brass pendant), bureaulamp knikarm (desk lamp with hinged arm), glazen bol lamp, teak lamp, opaline. Look at the shapes in the photos and compare with what you know.

This is where vindje.com helps: you can describe the shape and era you want, like a 1960s brass and opaline glass pendant, and the AI reads the photos and descriptions instead of needing a brand in the title.

sections.heading: Wiring and safety
paragraphs: Old lamps often have cracked cloth or rubber cable, no earth wire on metal bodies, and brittle sockets. Plan to rewire anything you buy older than the 1980s, especially metal lamps. Cable, plug and an E27 socket cost little; if you are not confident doing it, a lamp shop or electrician will rewire a lamp for a modest fee.
Test the lamp at the pickup if possible, but do not take a working bulb as proof of safe wiring. Look for brown, stiff or taped cable.

sections.heading: Condition and value
paragraphs: Original paint and finish matter for value. A Hala lamp with original paint and some patina is worth more than a repainted one. Dented shades, missing diffusers and replaced glass lower the price a lot, especially for pendants where the glass is the design.
Check that all parts are there: springs on hinged desk lamps, shade rings, ceiling cups on pendants. Missing parts are hard to find for older Dutch lamps.

sections.heading: Getting fragile lamps home
paragraphs: Glass pendants and opaline shades break more often on the way home than in forty years of use. Bring a box, towels or bubble wrap, take the glass off the fitting before moving it, and carry the shade on your lap rather than in the boot. For a lamp further away, ask the seller whether they ship; many collectors do, packed well, for a reasonable fee.
For a big floor lamp like an Arco copy or original, bring a second person and check that it fits in your car diagonally before driving across the country.

price_guide.item: Hala or Anvia desk lamp, working
Flos Arco, original with marble base

faq.q: How can I tell if a vintage lamp is valuable?
faq.a: Look for maker marks or labels on the base, under the shade ring or on the socket, and compare the shape with known designs. Brand, original condition and completeness drive most of the value.

faq.q: Is a vintage lamp safe to use?
faq.a: Only if the wiring is in good condition. Most lamps over 40 years old benefit from new cable, plug and socket.

faq.q: How do I know if an Arco lamp is a copy?
faq.a: An original Flos Arco has a solid Carrara marble base weighing tens of kilos, a Flos marking and a specific hole through the marble for lifting. Light bases and missing marks point to a copy.

faq.q: What does space age mean in lamp listings?
faq.a: Usually 1960s and 1970s designs with round shapes, acrylic or chrome. It describes a style, not a brand.

example_wish: Vintage 1960s Dutch desk lamp with hinged arm, Hala or Anvia or similar, original paint, working, under 150 euro, within 50 km

title: Pastoe furniture second hand: how to recognise it and what it's worth
meta_title: Pastoe furniture second hand: recognise and value it
description: How to recognise vintage Pastoe furniture on Marktplaats, from Cees Braakman's 1950s birch and teak pieces to later cabinets, with fair second-hand prices.
intro: Pastoe is the Utrecht furniture maker behind many of the best Dutch modernist pieces, and its furniture turns up on Marktplaats both correctly labelled and listed as just an old cabinet. Learn the main design periods, look for the label and check the veneer, and you can buy well at fair prices.

sections.heading: A short history that helps you identify pieces
paragraphs: Pastoe started in Utrecht in the early twentieth century, and early pieces carry the name UMS (Utrechtsche Meubelfabriek) or UMS Pastoe. After the Second World War, in-house designer Cees Braakman created the work most collectors look for: light birch furniture, the Japanese series in teak and birch, wire chairs and modular cabinets.

From the 1970s onward Pastoe moved toward clean, lacquered cabinets in bright colours and white, including tambour door cabinets such as the Amsterdammer. Later modular systems are still made today, which means a second-hand Pastoe cabinet can be a recent piece rather than vintage.

sections.heading: Finding the label
paragraphs: Most Pastoe furniture has a mark, but it is not always easy to find.
bullets: Look inside doors and drawers, on the back panel and under the top
Older pieces may have a metal plate, a printed paper label or a stamp reading UMS Pastoe
Later pieces often have a sticker or plate with the Pastoe name and sometimes a production code
Labels fall off: an unlabelled piece can still be Pastoe if construction and design match known models
Ask the seller for photos of the back and inside before you travel

sections.heading: Recognising the designs without a label
paragraphs: Braakman's birch series is pale, with rounded edges, slim tapered legs and simple recessed grips. The Japanese series combines teak or dark wood with lighter frames and sliding doors. 1950s Pastoe wire chairs have thin black steel frames with wooden or upholstered seats.

Look at the details. Pastoe used good joinery, solid edges on veneered panels and consistent hardware. Lots of Dutch furniture from the 1950s and 1960s copied the look, often in cheaper materials, so a birch sideboard alone does not make it Pastoe.

sections.heading: Condition checks
paragraphs: Veneer is the main thing. Look along the edges for lifting or chipped veneer, and at the top for water rings and sun bleaching. Birch yellows with age, which is normal. Light damage can be repaired by a furniture restorer, but large missing areas on a top reduce value a lot.

Open every door and drawer. Sliding doors should run smoothly in their tracks; missing sliders and keys are common. On later lacquered cabinets, chips in the paint and scratches show clearly and are harder to touch up than wood.

sections.heading: What sells and what to pay
paragraphs: The most wanted pieces are Braakman's 1950s birch and teak cabinets and sideboards, the wire chairs, and complete modular wall units. Single small pieces like a nightstand or a side table are more affordable. Recent white or coloured Pastoe cabinets sell well too, but as quality used furniture rather than vintage collectibles.

Prices vary a lot with condition and completeness. If you are hunting for a specific piece, a search on vindje.com can look for Pastoe furniture described in words, including listings where the seller only wrote berken kast jaren 50 and mentioned the label in the description.

sections.heading: Pieces often mistaken for Pastoe
paragraphs: Several other Dutch makers worked in a similar spirit, and their furniture is regularly listed as Pastoe by hopeful sellers. 't Spectrum (with designs by Martin Visser), Fristho, Webe and Topform all made good modernist cabinets and chairs. These are worth buying in their own right, often for less than Pastoe, but pay for the maker that is on the label.
Danish teak sideboards are another frequent mix-up. If the piece has a Danish control label or a Danish maker's mark, it is not Pastoe, whatever the title says.

price_guide.item: Pastoe birch side table or nightstand

faq.q: How do I know if my furniture is Pastoe?
faq.a: Look for a Pastoe or UMS Pastoe label, plate or stamp inside drawers, on the back or underneath. Without a label, compare design details and construction with documented pieces.

faq.q: Who designed Pastoe furniture?
faq.a: Cees Braakman designed most of the well known 1950s and 1960s pieces. Later designers include Aldo van den Nieuwelaar and others for the lacquered cabinets.

faq.q: Is Pastoe still made?
faq.a: Yes, Pastoe still makes furniture, mostly cabinet systems. That is why some second-hand pieces are recent rather than vintage.

faq.q: Can damaged Pastoe veneer be repaired?
faq.a: Small chips and lifting veneer can be repaired well by a furniture restorer. Large missing areas on visible surfaces are expensive and lower the value.

example_wish: Pastoe sideboard in birch or teak from the 1950s or 60s, Cees Braakman design, label visible, veneer in good shape, under 900 euro, anywhere in the Netherlands

title: Gispen tube chairs: originals, reissues and copies
meta_title: Gispen chairs: originals, reissues and copies
description: How to tell original vintage Gispen tube chairs from reissues and copies on Marktplaats, what to check on the chrome and seat, and fair prices.
intro: Gispen is the best known Dutch maker of tubular steel furniture, and the name gets attached to almost every chrome chair on Marktplaats. Original pre-war and postwar Gispen chairs exist in good numbers, the company makes reissues today, and there are countless look-alikes. Labels, construction and the seat tell them apart.

sections.heading: Three kinds of Gispen listings
paragraphs: Vintage originals: chairs made by Gispen in the 1930s through the 1970s, designed by W.H. Gispen himself and later by designers like André Cordemeyer and Wim Rietveld. These range from elegant cantilever chairs to sturdy office and school chairs.

Reissues: Gispen still exists and has reissued classic tube designs. These are official, well made and expensive new, so a used reissue is a legitimate buy. Look-alikes: tubular chairs by other makers, plus listings saying Gispen stijl or Gispen look. Some are good vintage chairs in their own right, they are just not Gispen.

sections.heading: Labels and marks
paragraphs: Many Gispen chairs have or had a label: a metal plate, a sticker or a stamp, often under the seat or on the frame. Labels were easily lost, so a missing one does not rule out an original, but its presence helps a lot. Ask the seller for a photo underneath before you arrange a pickup.
Reissues usually carry current Gispen branding and sometimes a reference to the original design year. A chair with a modern label is a reissue, not a 1930s piece, and should be priced that way.

sections.heading: Construction details to check
paragraphs: Bring a small torch and look closely.
bullets: Tube: originals use solid, evenly bent steel tube; bends should be smooth with no flat spots or kinks
Chrome: pitting and rust spots are normal on old chairs, but flaking chrome over large areas means rechroming, which is costly
Seat and back: original upholstery is often worn and replaced; check whether the shell or wood underneath is sound
Cantilevers: sit down and bounce gently, the frame should spring back evenly and not creak at welds
Feet: look for original glides or caps, and for cracks in the tube near the floor
Screws and fixings: mismatched modern screws suggest repairs

sections.heading: Is it worth restoring?
paragraphs: Reupholstering a seat and back is affordable and often improves a chair. Rechroming the frame costs much more and is only worth it for a desirable model. Light surface rust can usually be removed with fine steel wool and a chrome polish; deep pitting stays.
Price a damaged chair on what it will cost to make it usable, not on the name. A Gispen label does not make a bent or cracked frame a good deal.

sections.heading: Where the bargains are
paragraphs: Postwar Gispen office and canteen chairs are the most common and the most affordable. Offices, schools and churches cleared them out by the hundred, and they turn up in sets. Pre-war cantilever chairs and armchairs are rarer and priced accordingly.

Sellers often list them as oude buisstoelen without a brand. A plain-language search on vindje.com for something like a set of four chrome tube chairs with original Gispen labels can pick these out of the descriptions.

sections.heading: Common look-alikes
paragraphs: Thonet made the Breuer and Stam cantilever chairs (S32, S64 and relatives) that many people call Gispen. Kembo, another Dutch maker, produced tubular chairs and tables that look very similar to Gispen's postwar work. Ahrend office chairs, including Friso Kramer's Result chair, are also often mislabelled.

None of these are fakes. They are separate makers, and several are collectible. Just check that the price matches the chair you are buying, and ask the seller where the Gispen name came from: a label, a receipt, or a guess.

price_guide.item: Postwar Gispen office or canteen chair

faq.q: How do I recognise an original Gispen chair?
faq.a: Look for a Gispen label, plate or stamp under the seat or on the frame, and check that the tube work and construction match documented models. Without any mark, treat it as unconfirmed.

faq.q: Who designed Gispen chairs?
faq.a: W.H. Gispen founded the company and designed the early tube furniture. Later Gispen designs came from designers including André Cordemeyer and Wim Rietveld.

faq.q: Is rust on a Gispen chair a problem?
faq.a: Small rust spots and light pitting are normal and can be cleaned. Large areas of flaking chrome or rust through the tube are expensive to repair.

faq.q: Does Gispen still make chairs?
faq.a: Yes, Gispen is still in business and has reissued several of its classic designs alongside modern office furniture.

example_wish: Set of 4 vintage Gispen tube chairs, chrome frames, original label, upholstery can be worn, under 400 euro, within 60 km

title: Vintage Danish design furniture on the Dutch second-hand market
meta_title: Vintage Danish design furniture: buy it second hand
description: Buying vintage Danish design furniture in the Netherlands: makers and designers to know, labels, teak versus rosewood, Deens design copies and fair prices.
intro: Danish mid-century furniture is everywhere on Marktplaats, but the label Deens design is used for almost any teak piece from the 1960s. Much of it was made in the Netherlands, Germany or England in a Danish style. Genuinely Danish pieces carry makers' marks and better joinery, and they cost more, so check before paying the premium.

sections.heading: What Deens design means in a listing
paragraphs: Dutch sellers use Deens design for a look: teak, slim legs, rounded edges, sliding doors. It says nothing certain about where a piece was made. Plenty of good Dutch furniture from makers like Topform and Fristho looks very similar, and many German and British sideboards were made for export in the same style.
That is fine if you just want a teak sideboard. It matters when the price is set as if a known Danish designer made it.

sections.heading: Names worth knowing
paragraphs: These designers and makers show up regularly on the Dutch market.
bullets: Hans J. Wegner: the Wishbone chair (CH24, Carl Hansen & Son, still in production) and many others
