Many infant seats like the Maxi-Cosi Pebble 360 or Cybex Cloud T click onto an Isofix base. Check that the base and seat are a matching pair, and test that the base legs and Isofix arms lock with a green indicator.

sections.heading: Bases, boosters and safer used buys
paragraphs: An Isofix base has no foam or harness and takes less of the force in a crash than the seat itself, but the same history rule applies. A booster cushion (zittingverhoger) without a back offers little side protection, so a high-back booster is better. In the Netherlands, children shorter than 1.35 m need a child seat, so most kids will use two or three seats in total.
Rear-facing seats for toddlers are expensive new. If you find one from a trusted source with a known history, that is where a used buy saves the most.

sections.heading: Test the fit in your own car
paragraphs: Not every seat fits every car. Before you pay, ask to try it in your car, or at least check the manufacturer's vehicle fit list for your model. Install it the way the manual says, then grab the seat at the belt path and push it side to side: it should move no more than a couple of centimetres. With a belted infant seat, check that your car's belt is long enough to reach around the shell.

sections.heading: When to walk away
paragraphs: Skip any seat with missing labels, a production date you cannot find, a replaced or knotted harness, or a seller who does not know where it came from. Listings with several identical seats or 'from a deceased estate' type stories leave too many questions. A seat at EUR 20 that turns out to be crashed is the most expensive bargain on the site.

price_guide.item: Maxi-Cosi Pebble 360 or Cybex Cloud T infant seat (no base)
Toddler i-Size seat, forward or rear facing

faq.q: Is it legal to sell or buy a used car seat in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Yes, buying and selling used seats is allowed. What matters is that the seat has a valid approval label and is fit for your child.

faq.q: How long does a car seat last?
faq.a: Most manufacturers give a lifespan of roughly 6 to 10 years from production. The exact figure is in the manual, and the production date is stamped on the shell.

faq.q: Can I still use an R44 car seat?
faq.a: Yes, using an R44/04 seat you own is still allowed. New R44 seats are no longer sold in EU shops, so used ones will only get older.

faq.q: Should I buy a used car seat after an accident?
faq.a: No. Manufacturers advise replacing a seat after any crash, even if it looks fine.

example_wish: Maxi-Cosi Pebble 360 with FamilyFix 360 base, i-Size, less than 3 years old, never in an accident, under 200 euro

title: Buying a used crib (ledikant) safely
meta_title: Buying a used crib (ledikant): safety checks and prices
description: How to buy a used crib or ledikant on Marktplaats: bar spacing, mattress fit, screws, paint and the brands that last. Plus fair second-hand prices.
intro: A used crib is a good buy as long as it is sturdy, has every screw and bolt, and the bars and mattress fit leave no gap a baby can get stuck in. Always buy a new mattress. Solid wooden cribs from known brands are easy to check and resell later.

sections.heading: Sizes in the Netherlands
paragraphs: Dutch cribs come in two standard sizes: 60x120 cm and 70x140 cm. The larger one can often convert into a junior bed (meegroeibed) once the side is removed, which gives it a few extra years. Measure your bedroom before you go, and write down the mattress size from the listing, because a 60x120 mattress in a 70x140 frame is dangerous.
IKEA cribs (Sundvik, Gulliver, Smågöra) use the same standard sizes, so any matching mattress fits.

sections.heading: Brands you will see
paragraphs: Common on Marktplaats: Bopita, Quax, Childhome, Troll, Coming Kids, Europe Baby, IKEA, and at the top end Stokke Sleepi and Leander. Bopita and Quax are solid wood or MDF and usually come as part of a nursery set with a dresser (commode). Stokke Sleepi and Leander are oval, designer cribs with their own odd-sized mattresses, which you will have to buy from the brand.

sections.heading: Safety checks at the pickup
paragraphs: Ask the seller to leave it assembled so you can test it, then take it apart together so you see how it goes back.
bullets: Bars: a gap of roughly 4.5 to 6.5 cm between bars. If a soda can slides through, it is too wide.
Shake it. A crib should not rack or creak at the corners.
Check that every bolt, nut and the hex key are present. Ask for the manual or the model name.
Look for cracked or split bars and loose glue joints.
Bed base: slats or panel intact, and both height positions usable.
No sticking-out screws, decorative cut-outs or corner posts higher than the sides.
Teeth marks on the top rail are normal; splinters are not. Sand or skip.

sections.heading: Old cribs, paint and drop sides
paragraphs: Vintage or antique wooden cribs look lovely but often fail modern rules: wider bar spacing, drop-down sides and old paint. Paint from decades ago can contain lead, and babies chew on rails. If you love an old crib, use it as a doll bed or a plant stand, not for sleeping. Cribs with a side that slides down on a track should be avoided too, because the hardware wears and can leave a gap.

sections.heading: The mattress and extras
paragraphs: Buy a new mattress. A used one can carry mould and has lost its firmness, and a firm, well-fitting mattress is the main safety point in any crib. The rule of thumb: you should not fit more than two fingers between the mattress and the side. Skip bumpers and pillows for young babies.
A playpen (box) is a different item from a crib, but listings mix them up. A box usually has a raised floor and is not meant for nights. Check the listing's dimensions.

sections.heading: Second cribs and travel cots
paragraphs: Grandparents often want a second sleeping place. A folding travel cot (campingbedje) from Baby Dan, Joie or Hauck is cheaper and easy to store, but check that the frame locks rigidly and that the thin original mattress is present, since thick extra mattresses on top are a suffocation risk in travel cots.

sections.heading: Transport
paragraphs: Most cribs come apart into flat panels that fit in a hatchback. On vindje.com you can ask for a 70x140 wooden crib that converts into a junior bed, within cycling or driving distance, and skip the playpens that show up in a plain search.

price_guide.item: Nursery set: crib, dresser and wardrobe

faq.q: Is a second-hand crib safe?
faq.a: Yes, if it is stable, complete, has narrow enough bar spacing and you put in a new, well-fitting mattress.

faq.q: What size mattress fits a Dutch crib?
faq.a: Either 60x120 or 70x140 cm. The mattress should fit snugly with no more than about two fingers of gap at the sides.

faq.q: Can I use a used crib mattress?
faq.a: It is better not to. Mattresses lose their firmness and can hold moisture and mould, and a new one is cheap compared with the crib.

faq.q: Is an old wooden crib safe for my baby?
faq.a: Often not: bar spacing, drop sides and old paint can fail current standards. Use a modern crib for sleep.

example_wish: Wooden ledikant 70x140 that converts into a junior bed, white or natural wood, with all screws, under 120 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used high chair: Stokke Tripp Trapp and alternatives
meta_title: Used Tripp Trapp and high chairs: checks and prices
description: Buying a used Stokke Tripp Trapp or other high chair on Marktplaats: serial numbers, Baby Set fit, copies, what to check and fair second-hand prices.
intro: The Stokke Tripp Trapp is the classic used buy: solid beech, adjustable for years and easy to fix with spare parts. Check the serial number, the wood around the screw holes and whether the Baby Set is included. If the budget is tight, an IKEA Antilop or a Hauck Alpha does the job too.

sections.heading: Why the Tripp Trapp is a good second-hand buy
paragraphs: The chair has been made in largely the same shape since the 1970s, so parts like seat plates, footrests, screws and the Baby Set are still sold. A ten-year-old chair can look new after a sanding and an oil, and it resells easily. That makes the risk of buying used low.
Check the colour carefully if it matters: the natural and white versions are the most common, while painted colours chip at the edges after years of use.

sections.heading: Serial numbers and the Baby Set
paragraphs: Every Tripp Trapp has a serial number on the inside of one of the side pieces. It tells you roughly when it was made and which accessories fit. Older chairs may need an extension glider or different hardware for the current Baby Set, so before buying a chair and a Baby Set separately, look up the serial on Stokke's compatibility list.

The Baby Set (backrest plus front bar) is what makes the chair usable from about six months. The newborn set, harness and tray are extras. A listing with everything included is worth more, but you can add parts later.

sections.heading: What to check
bullets: Wobble the chair. Loose sides usually only need the long bolts tightened, but stripped threads in the wood are a bigger fix.
Look for cracks around the screw holes and at the bottom of the side pieces.
Check the plates slide into their grooves and do not bow in the middle.
The long bolts and the hex key should be included.
On the Baby Set, the plastic should be uncracked and click into place.
Painted chairs: look at chips on the feet and edges. Natural wood can be sanded, paint is harder to fix.

sections.heading: Copies and look-alikes
paragraphs: Many chairs use the same idea: Hauck Alpha+, Childhome Evosit, Kidsmill and lots of unbranded 'meegroeistoel' models. They are fine chairs at a lower price, but sellers sometimes list them under the Tripp Trapp name to get more clicks. A genuine one has the Stokke logo stamped or printed on the side and a serial number. No logo and no serial means you are looking at a copy and should pay copy prices.

sections.heading: Getting it home and setting it up
paragraphs: A Tripp Trapp fits in a bike crate or on the back of a cargo bike, so pickups are easy. At home, set the seat plate so your child's elbows are at table height and the footrest so their feet rest flat with knees at a right angle. Re-adjust every few months as they grow. If the chair wobbles after reassembly, loosen all bolts, square the chair on a flat floor and tighten them again.
Ask the seller whether the chair stood in direct sun. Natural beech yellows unevenly, and you can see the line where a tray or plate sat.

sections.heading: Alternatives
paragraphs: The IKEA Antilop is light, wipes clean in seconds and costs a few euros used, which makes it a favourite with parents who hate cleaning wood grooves. The Stokke Nomi is a newer, more modern adjustable chair. Bloom and Peg Perego make tall, padded chairs that take more space and are harder to clean.
If you want a Tripp Trapp in a specific colour with the Baby Set and tray, describing that on vindje.com saves you from scrolling through dozens of bare chairs and copies.

price_guide.item: Tripp Trapp with Baby Set and tray
Stokke Tripp Trapp Baby Set separately

faq.q: How do I know if a Tripp Trapp is genuine?
faq.a: Look for the Stokke logo on the side piece and the serial number on the inside. Copies have neither.

faq.q: Does a new Baby Set fit an old Tripp Trapp?
faq.a: Often yes, but very old chairs may need extra parts. Check the serial number against Stokke's compatibility information first.

faq.q: Can you refinish a used Tripp Trapp?
faq.a: Natural beech chairs can be lightly sanded and oiled. Painted chairs can be touched up but are harder to make look new.

faq.q: From what age can a baby use a Tripp Trapp?
faq.a: With the Baby Set, from when the baby sits up unaided, usually around six months. The newborn set is a separate accessory.

example_wish: Stokke Tripp Trapp in natural wood with Baby Set and tray, no cracks, under 170 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying a used baby carrier or sling
meta_title: Buying a used baby carrier or sling: what to check
description: How to buy a used baby carrier (draagzak) or wrap on Marktplaats: Ergobaby, BabyBjorn and woven wraps, buckle and stitching checks, fakes and fair prices.
intro: Baby carriers are a sensible used buy because they get a few months of use and wash well. Check every buckle, the stitching at the load points and that it is a genuine brand carrier, since copies of popular models exist. Try it on with a baby or a heavy bag before paying.

sections.heading: Types of carriers
paragraphs: A soft structured carrier (draagzak) has buckles and a waist belt: Ergobaby Omni 360 and Omni Breeze, BabyBjorn Harmony and One, Manduca, Tula and Najell are the common ones. They are quick to put on and suit most parents.

A wrap (draagdoek) is a long piece of cloth. Stretchy wraps are popular for newborns and cheap. Woven wraps from brands like Didymos and Little Frog last for years and hold their value, which is why you see them resold so often. A ring sling is a shorter woven piece with two rings, handy for quick carries.

sections.heading: Checks for buckle carriers
bullets: Click every buckle shut and pull hard on the strap. No cracks in the plastic and no slipping.
Inspect the stitching where the shoulder straps and waist belt join the body. Loose threads there are a reason to walk away.
Pull all webbing through the adjusters. Fraying or melted ends are wear signs.
Check the waist belt padding has not gone flat on one side.
Look at the label: model name, size range and the safety standard should still be readable.
Ask whether the infant insert is included if your baby is small; newer models often do not need one.

sections.heading: Checks for wraps and slings
paragraphs: Hold a woven wrap up to the light and look for pulled threads, thin spots and holes. A pulled thread is cosmetic; a hole or a thin patch is not. Measure or ask the size: woven wraps are sold in sizes like 4.6 m (size 6) or 3.7 m (size 4), and the size matters for which carries you can do. For ring slings, check the rings are made for carrying (welded, no seam) and not craft rings.

sections.heading: Fakes
paragraphs: Copies of Ergobaby carriers are sold cheaply online and then resold on Marktplaats as genuine. They can look close in photos. Signs: a price far below the usual range, poor or uneven stitching, wrong logo font, labels without a model name or batch number, and buckles without a brand mark. A carrier holds your baby at height, so if you are unsure, pass.

sections.heading: Which one holds up in daily use
paragraphs: For parents in a Dutch city, a carrier often replaces the stroller on trains, trams and stairs, so it gets heavy use. Look for models with padded, crossable shoulder straps and a wide waist belt if you plan to carry a toddler; small, unpadded budget carriers from the 2000s are hard on your back past about 8 kg. A hip seat carrier is another option for older toddlers who want to go up and down all day.

sections.heading: Fit and hygiene
paragraphs: Carriers fit people differently. Try it on at the pickup, ideally with your baby, or with a backpack loaded with a few kilos. The waist belt should sit on your hips and the baby should sit with knees higher than the bottom (the M position). Most carriers can go in the washing machine on a gentle cycle; check the label before you wash.
If you want a specific model in a particular colour with the newborn insert included, a search on vindje.com can filter out the listings that only sell an insert or a cover.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy a second-hand baby carrier?
faq.a: Yes, if buckles, webbing and stitching are intact and it is a genuine brand carrier. Wash it before first use.

faq.q: How do I spot a fake Ergobaby?
faq.a: Look for uneven stitching, missing model and batch details on the label, unbranded buckles and a price far below the going rate.

faq.q: Which carrier is best for a newborn?
faq.a: A stretchy wrap or a carrier rated from birth without an insert, like the Ergobaby Omni 360 or BabyBjorn Harmony. Check the minimum weight on the label.

faq.q: Can I wash a used baby carrier?
faq.a: Most soft carriers can be machine washed on a gentle cycle. Follow the care label and let it dry flat.

example_wish: Ergobaby Omni 360 or BabyBjorn Harmony carrier suitable from birth, all buckles intact, under 80 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying used LEGO: bulk lots, sets and fakes
meta_title: Buying used LEGO: bulk per kilo, sets and fakes
description: How to buy used LEGO on Marktplaats: fair prices per kilo, checking a set is complete, spotting Lepin and other fake bricks, and what to ask.
intro: Used LEGO is easy to find in the Netherlands, both as loose bricks by the kilo and as complete sets. Bulk lots are cheapest per brick but come mixed with dust, other brands and missing parts. For a specific set, check completeness against the online parts list before you pay, and learn to recognise the copy brands.

sections.heading: Bulk lots versus complete sets
paragraphs: A bulk lot (lego partij) is a box or bag of loose bricks sold by weight. It is ideal for free building and for kids who do not care about instructions. Sets are sold with or without box and instructions, and their value depends heavily on completeness, especially of the minifigures.

If you want a particular set, search with the set number. LEGO prints a four to six digit number on every box and instruction booklet, and sellers who know what they have usually put it in the title, like 'Lego 42115' or 'Lego City 60337'.

sections.heading: What bulk should cost
paragraphs: Unsorted mixed LEGO typically goes for around EUR 10-18 per kilo, depending on how clean it is and what is in it. Lots with lots of Technic, minifigures or recent themed pieces go higher. Duplo is cheaper per kilo because the bricks are big and heavy. Be wary of lots weighed in the storage box: ask for the weight without the container.
Ask for a photo of the bricks spread out on a table, not just a closed tub. Big baseplates and storage boxes add weight but little play value.

sections.heading: Spotting fakes and other brands
paragraphs: Copy brands such as Lepin (now mostly gone), Mould King, Cada, Lele and many unbranded 'bouwstenen' sets are sold alongside LEGO, and bulk lots often contain some mixed in. Some are clones of official sets, sold at a fraction of the price. Genuine LEGO has the word LEGO moulded on top of every stud (except some very small and transparent pieces) and on the inside of many parts.

Copy bricks often feel slightly different, clutch too tight or too loose, and have a duller colour. In a bulk lot a few stray copies are normal. A 'complete Star Wars set' at half the usual price with no box and no LEGO logos is a copy.

sections.heading: Checking a set before you pay
bullets: Ask for the set number and look up the parts inventory on Rebrickable or BrickLink.
Ask whether it was built and taken apart, or is still assembled. Built sets are easier to check.
Count the minifigures. They are often the most valuable part and the first to go missing.
Check for rare or printed pieces in the inventory and ask about those specifically.
Look for yellowed white or grey bricks, which happens with sunlight and lowers value.
Instructions can be downloaded free from LEGO, so missing booklets matter less than missing pieces.
Smell the box. Smoke and attic damp are hard to wash out of cardboard.

sections.heading: Cleaning used LEGO
paragraphs: Bulk lots arrive dusty and sometimes sticky. Wash the bricks in a mesh laundry bag or a bucket of lukewarm water (not hot, which can warp them) with a bit of dish soap, then dry them on towels. Keep stickered pieces, electrical parts and printed bricks out of the wash, and never put LEGO in a dishwasher at high heat.

sections.heading: Investment sets and retired themes
paragraphs: Some retired sets, especially large Star Wars, Creator Expert and Modular Buildings, sell for more than their original price, and you will see them listed sealed (nieuw in doos, sealed). Treat sealed boxes with care: check the tape seals on the sides and that the box is not crushed. If a seller asks well above typical BrickLink prices, ask why. For bulk with specific contents, such as mostly Technic with motors within driving distance, a plain-language search on vindje.com can sort the useful lots from the Duplo and copy brands.

price_guide.item: Technic bulk with beams and gears
Complete small to mid City or Friends set
Complete Technic flagship set from recent years

faq.q: How much is used LEGO worth per kilo?
faq.a: Mixed, unsorted LEGO usually sells for about EUR 10-18 per kilo in the Netherlands. Clean lots with Technic or minifigures go higher.

faq.q: How can I tell if LEGO is fake?
faq.a: Look for the LEGO logo on the studs and inside the bricks. Copies have no logo or a different brand name and often a duller colour.

faq.q: How do I check if a used LEGO set is complete?
faq.a: Look up the set number on Rebrickable or BrickLink to get the parts list, then compare it with what the seller has.

faq.q: Can you wash LEGO in the washing machine?
faq.a: Use a laundry bag on a cold, gentle cycle at most, or wash by hand in lukewarm water. Keep stickers and electronics out of the water.

example_wish: Bulk LEGO Technic, at least 3 kg, with gears and beams, no copy brands, under 70 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying a used trampoline
meta_title: Buying a used trampoline: checks, sizes and prices
description: How to buy a used trampoline on Marktplaats: Berg, Salta and inground models, checking rust, springs and the net, and how to take it apart.
intro: A used trampoline can save a lot of money, but you will almost always have to take it apart yourself, and the jumping mat, springs and net are the parts that wear out. Brands like Berg sell spare parts, which makes a worn one fixable. Rust on the frame legs is the main reason to walk away.

sections.heading: Sizes and types
paragraphs: Trampolines are sold by diameter in centimetres: 244, 305, 366, 380 and 430 are common. A 305 or 330 fits most Dutch back gardens. Measure your garden first and add at least a metre of clear space around it.

Inground trampolines sit in a pit at ground level. They look tidy and are safer for small kids, but buying one used means digging a new pit, and the frame may have spent years in damp soil. Ask how long it was in the ground and look closely at the legs and the retaining wall.

sections.heading: Brands worth looking for
paragraphs: Berg (a Dutch brand) is the most common higher-end trampoline on Marktplaats: Champion, Favorit, Elite, Grand and Ultim models. Salta, Etan, Exit and Avyna are also widespread. These brands sell replacement mats, springs, padding and nets per size, so an older one with a tired net is still worth having.
Cheap unbranded trampolines from garden centres often have thin frames and odd sizes. If a part breaks, finding a matching replacement can be hard.

sections.heading: What to check before taking it down
paragraphs: Go and see it standing up. Once it is in pieces, a worn mat is easy to hide.
bullets: Rust: scratch-test the bottom of the legs and the joints. Surface rust is fine, flaking or holes are not.
Frame: look for bent tubes and welds that have cracked, especially at the leg joints.
Mat: press it with your hand. Thin, faded or torn spots and broken stitching at the V-rings mean a new mat.
Springs: count them and look for stretched ones that hang longer than the rest.
Padding: UV damage makes the cover brittle. A new pad is not cheap, so factor it in.
Net: check for holes, rotten poles and the zip or entrance closure.
Ask for the brand, model and size so you can order parts.

sections.heading: Taking it apart
paragraphs: Most sellers expect you to dismantle it. Bring a spring puller (or strong gloves and a rope loop), a screwdriver, a socket set, a helper and an hour or two. Take photos as you go and put the bolts in labelled bags. Removing springs under tension can snap a finger, so pull them one at a time going around the circle, not one side first.
A 305 or larger needs a van or a trailer. The frame pieces are long but light; the mat and springs are surprisingly heavy.

sections.heading: Price and timing
paragraphs: Prices drop in autumn and winter when people clear the garden and nobody wants to stand in the cold dismantling one. Spring is when demand peaks. If you are flexible, buy in October or November and store it. On vindje.com you can ask for a Berg trampoline of 330 cm or more with a net and no rust in the photos, and skip the many listings for loose nets and covers.

sections.heading: Safety
paragraphs: A net and full padding are a must for kids. Place the trampoline on flat ground, away from fences and trees, and anchor it with a ground anchor kit: the Dutch coast and open polders get strong winds, and a trampoline can lift and fly. Many used ones are sold after exactly that kind of storm, which is another reason to look for bent tubes.

price_guide.item: Berg Champion or Favorit 330 cm with net
Salta or Etan 366 cm with net

faq.q: Is it worth buying a used trampoline?
faq.a: Yes, if the frame is not rusted through and spare parts exist for the brand. Factor in a new net or pad if those look worn.

faq.q: How do you take apart a trampoline?
faq.a: Remove the net and padding, then the springs one at a time going around the circle, then the mat and frame. A spring puller and a helper make it much easier.

faq.q: How long does a trampoline last outside?
faq.a: The frame can last many years if it is galvanised. Mats, nets and padding usually need replacing after a few seasons in the sun.

faq.q: What size trampoline fits a Dutch garden?
faq.a: A 244 to 330 cm model fits most terraced house gardens. Leave at least a metre of free space around it.

example_wish: Berg trampoline 330 cm or bigger with safety net, no rust on the legs, under 250 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying kids clothes in bundles (kinderkleding pakket)
meta_title: Buying kids clothes bundles: sizes, brands and prices
description: How to buy kids clothes bundles (kinderkleding pakket) on Marktplaats: Dutch sizes, a fair price per piece, brands that last and worn-out bundles.
intro: Bundles of kids clothes are one of the cheapest ways to dress a growing child: 20 to 40 pieces in one size, often for less than one new outfit. The trick is asking for the right photos, knowing the Dutch sizes and paying per piece, not per bag.

sections.heading: Dutch sizes in short
paragraphs: Dutch kids sizes are based on height in centimetres: 50, 56, 62, 68, 74, 80, 86, 92, 98, 104, 110, 116 and up in steps of six. Roughly, 56 fits a newborn, 74 fits around six to nine months, 86 a toddler of one and a half, 98 to 104 a three to four year old. Brands differ, so if your child is between sizes, buy the larger one.
Bundles are often split by gender and season: 'jongenskleding maat 104 winter' or 'meisjes zomerpakket maat 92'. Searching the exact size number gets far better results than 'kids clothes'.

sections.heading: What a fair price looks like
paragraphs: For everyday brands like HEMA, Zeeman, C&A, H&M, Lidl and Primark, think about EUR 0.50-1.50 per piece in good condition. Better brands such as Name it, Noppies, Tumble 'n Dry, Vingino, Z8, Petit Bateau and Mini Rodini sell for more, and individual items from Scandinavian brands can hold close to half their new price.
Count the pieces in the photos and divide. A bag of 30 items for EUR 25 is fair; 10 items for EUR 25 only makes sense if they are good brands or coats.

sections.heading: Photos to ask for
bullets: Every item laid out flat, not folded in a pile.
Close-ups of knees on trousers and fronts of tops, where stains and holes show first.
The size labels, so you know the bundle is not a mix of sizes.
Brand labels if the price is based on brand.
The inside of coats and snowsuits, including the zip.

sections.heading: Condition checks
paragraphs: The common problems are pilling (pluizen), faded colours from many washes, stains on the front of tops, and worn knees. Baby bodies and sleepsuits are usually fine because babies outgrow them before they wear out. Toddler trousers and school-age jeans are the opposite: they often come with knee holes.
Smell matters. Clothes from a smoking household or a damp attic need several washes and do not always recover. Ask, and if you pick up, open the bag before you pay.

sections.heading: Selling it on afterwards
paragraphs: Kids outgrow a size in three to six months, so think of a bundle as something you rent. Keep the better items clean and together, and you can sell the same bundle on in the next size down for close to what you paid. Many parents swap with one or two families nearby: you buy their size 92, they buy your size 86.

sections.heading: Pick up or ship
paragraphs: Bundles are light and are often sent by post, which widens your choice. Shipping a bag costs a few euros, so include that in the per-piece math. Use Marktplaats' own payment and shipping options rather than paying a stranger by bank transfer for an item that has not been sent.
Picking up lets you check the bag and skip the shipping cost. Sellers who live nearby often have the next size too, so ask.

sections.heading: Worth buying new instead
paragraphs: Shoes are the exception. Children's feet mould to the shoe, and a worn pair can push a new foot into the wrong shape. Lightly used party shoes or wellies are fine, but daily shoes are better new. Underwear and socks are also usually bought new.

For winter, a used snowsuit or coat is one of the best deals. If you want a specific set, such as winter clothes size 104 for a boy, mostly HEMA or Name it, at least 20 pieces and within cycling distance, vindje.com can read the listing descriptions and drop bundles in other sizes.

price_guide.item: Baby bundle size 56-68, 30-40 pieces, mixed brands
Better brand items (Tumble 'n Dry, Vingino, Name it)

faq.q: What size is a one year old in Dutch clothing?
faq.a: Usually size 80, sometimes 74 or 86 depending on the child and the brand.

faq.q: How much should I pay for a bundle of kids clothes?
faq.a: For everyday brands, about EUR 0.50-1.50 per piece in good condition. Better brands and coats are worth more.

faq.q: Is it safe to buy second-hand baby clothes?
faq.a: Yes. Wash everything before use, and check small buttons and decorations are firmly attached.

faq.q: Should I buy used kids shoes?
faq.a: For daily wear it is better to buy new, since shoes take the shape of the previous child's feet. Wellies and party shoes are fine used.

example_wish: Boys winter clothes bundle size 104, at least 20 pieces, HEMA or Name it, no stains, under 30 euro, within 10 km

title: Buying used fitness equipment: treadmills, rowers, bikes
meta_title: Buying used fitness equipment: treadmills, rowers, bikes
description: How to buy a used treadmill, rowing machine or exercise bike on Marktplaats: brands that last, what to test, transport weight and fair second-hand prices.
intro: Home gym machines are bought with good intentions and sold a year later, which makes the used market large and prices good. Buy a known brand you can get parts for, test it for at least five minutes, and plan the transport before you go: a treadmill can weigh over 100 kg.

sections.heading: Rowing machines
paragraphs: The Concept2 RowErg (formerly Model D and Model E) is the safest buy on the whole fitness market. It is simple, built for gyms, every part is available, and it barely loses value. Check the chain for rust, pull it out fully and let it return smoothly, and look at the seat rollers and the rail for grooves. The PM5 monitor is the newer one; older PM3 and PM4 work but have fewer features.
WaterRower machines are also durable. Look for algae in the tank (add a purification tablet) and leaks at the seals. Cheap magnetic rowers from webshops are usually not worth buying used.

sections.heading: Treadmills
paragraphs: Treadmills are where most bad buys happen. Home models from Flow Fitness, Focus Fitness, Kettler, Tunturi and Horizon vary a lot. Commercial models from Life Fitness, Technogym, Precor and Matrix are built to run all day, but weigh 150 kg or more and often need a 16 amp outlet or a separate group, so check the plug and the specs.

Run on it at a jogging pace for several minutes. Listen for a rhythmic thump (worn belt or deck), slipping when you push off, or the motor straining. Look at the belt edges for fraying and under the belt for a dry, worn deck.

sections.heading: Exercise bikes and spinning bikes
paragraphs: Hometrainers (upright bikes with a console) and spinning bikes are the easiest to buy used: few moving parts and light enough to move. Peloton bikes appear often; check whether the screen works and that the seller has removed the bike from their account, since a subscription is needed for the classes. Tunturi, Kettler and Schwinn bikes from the last decade are good basic buys.
On a spinning bike, check the flywheel spins freely, the resistance knob changes the load smoothly, and the emergency brake works when you press it.

sections.heading: Test checklist
bullets: Use it for five minutes at least, at moderate and high effort.
Listen for grinding, squeaks and clicks that repeat every revolution.
Check the console lights up and all buttons respond.
Ask for the power cable and any chest strap or tablet holder that came with it.
Look for rust, especially if it stood in a garage or shed.
Ask for the brand and model number so you can find the manual and parts.

sections.heading: Things to skip
paragraphs: Vibration plates, ab rollers with a TV-shop logo and folding multi-gyms with cables and pulleys tend to be sold for a reason: they are uncomfortable, rattle or are hard to adjust. Old treadmills without a brand name or model number are a gamble, because a single worn motor board can cost more than the machine is worth. If the seller says 'works, only needs a new belt', assume you are buying a project.

sections.heading: Transport and space
paragraphs: Ask the weight before you go. A folding home treadmill can be 70-100 kg, a Concept2 is around 26 kg and splits in two, a spinning bike is 40-60 kg. Most sellers will not help carry a treadmill down three flights of stairs. Measure your ceiling too: on a treadmill you rise about 20 cm, and a tall runner needs room above their head.
Crosstrainers (elliptical machines) are long and awkward, and the cheap ones wobble. Test one carefully before committing to the transport.

sections.heading: Timing and search
paragraphs: Prices are highest in January and lowest in late spring and summer. If you want, say, a Concept2 with PM5 under 800 euro within 30 km, vindje.com can read the descriptions and drop the monitor-only and parts listings that a keyword search mixes in.

price_guide.item: Concept2 RowErg / Model D with PM5

faq.q: Is it worth buying a used treadmill?
faq.a: It can be, if it is a decent brand, runs smoothly at speed and you can get it home. Cheap folding models often have worn belts and weak motors.

faq.q: Which rowing machine is best to buy second hand?
faq.a: The Concept2 RowErg. Parts are easy to find, it lasts for years and resells close to what you paid.

faq.q: How heavy is a treadmill?
faq.a: Home models weigh around 60-100 kg, commercial gym models 150 kg or more. Plan for two people and a van.

faq.q: Does a used Peloton work without a subscription?
faq.a: It works as a basic bike, but the classes need a membership. Make sure the seller has removed the bike from their account.

example_wish: Concept2 rowing machine with PM5 monitor, in good working order, under 800 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying a used kayak or SUP board
meta_title: Buying a used kayak or SUP board: checks and prices
description: How to buy a used kayak or SUP board on Marktplaats: inflatable or hard, leak and seam checks, brands worth paying for, and fair second-hand prices.
intro: The Netherlands has water everywhere, so kayaks and SUP boards are easy to find used. Inflatable boards are cheap and easy to store but need a pressure test, while hard kayaks last for decades if the hull is sound. Test for leaks before you pay, and know how you will get it home.

sections.heading: Inflatable SUPs
paragraphs: Most SUPs for sale are inflatable (iSUP). Budget sets from Decathlon (Itiwit), Aldi, Lidl and countless webshop brands are common; Red Paddle Co, Starboard, Fanatic and Aqua Marina are better built. Better boards use stiffer drop-stitch construction, hold higher pressure and feel less wobbly.
The weak points are the seams along the rails, the valve, and the fin box. A board that was stored wet or in a hot car boot can have delaminated rails or a sticky surface.

sections.heading: Testing an inflatable
bullets: Ask the seller to inflate it before you arrive, ideally the evening before, and check it is still firm.
Inflate to the recommended pressure (often 15 psi) and listen for hissing at the valve and seams.
Spray soapy water on the seams and valve. Bubbles mean a leak.
Look for bulges or lifting edge tape along the rails.
Check the fin clicks into the fin box and the D-rings are firmly glued.
Ask what is included: pump with gauge, paddle, leash, bag.

sections.heading: Hard kayaks
paragraphs: Polyethylene (plastic) kayaks from Prijon, Perception, Dagger, Wilderness Systems and Point 65 are tough and forgiving. Fibreglass and composite sea kayaks from Tahe, Valley, Nigel Dennis and others are lighter and faster, but cracks and gelcoat damage need attention.

Sit-on-top kayaks are popular for fun on canals and lakes and for fishing. Sit-in kayaks keep you drier and suit longer trips. Measure the cockpit if you are tall: legroom is the most common fit problem.

sections.heading: Checks for hard kayaks
paragraphs: Turn the kayak upside down and look along the hull. Deep scratches on plastic are normal; dents that stay pushed in (oil-canning) from storage on straps or in the sun are a problem, as are cracks near the bow and stern. On composite boats, press around any star-shaped cracks in the gelcoat.

Open the hatches and look inside for water, mould and broken bulkheads. Test the rudder or skeg cable, the footrests' sliders and the seat back. A missing rudder or broken skeg can be fixed, but price it in.

sections.heading: Transport and storage
paragraphs: An inflatable SUP fits in a backpack-sized bag, which is why many people in apartments choose one. A hard kayak of 3 to 5 metres needs roof bars and straps, or a trailer, and a place to store it out of the sun. Plastic kayaks warp if left in the sun for months or stored on a single point.

If you want a board that is easy to carry on a bike, describe that on vindje.com, for example an inflatable SUP of at least 10 foot with pump and paddle, so listings for paddles or fins alone drop out.

sections.heading: Paddles and safety gear
paragraphs: Budget sets come with a heavy aluminium paddle; a lighter carbon or fibreglass paddle makes a bigger difference to comfort than most upgrades to the board, and paddles sell well used. A buoyancy aid (zwemvest or drijfvest) should fit snugly and have intact buckles and foam. For a SUP, a leash is worth having on open water and rivers with current.

sections.heading: Timing
paragraphs: Prices peak in May to July. Late summer and autumn are better for buying, and a test on the water is easier in warm weather. Ask whether you can try the board or kayak in a nearby canal: many sellers will say yes.

price_guide.item: Budget inflatable SUP set (Itiwit, Aldi, Aqua Marina entry)
Red Paddle Co or Starboard inflatable SUP

faq.q: Is a second-hand SUP board worth buying?
faq.a: Yes, if it holds pressure overnight and the seams are intact. Budget boards lose stiffness over time, so a used premium board is often the better buy.

faq.q: How do I check an inflatable SUP for leaks?
faq.a: Inflate it to the recommended pressure, leave it for a few hours, and spray soapy water on the seams and valve to look for bubbles.

faq.q: Do I need a licence for a kayak or SUP in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Recreational paddling on most waters needs no licence, but some waters have their own rules, so check locally where you plan to paddle.

faq.q: Plastic or composite kayak?
faq.a: Plastic is heavier but takes bumps against quay walls and rocks. Composite is lighter and faster but needs more care.

example_wish: Inflatable SUP board of at least 10'6 with pump, paddle and bag, holds pressure, under 250 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying used camping gear and tents
meta_title: Buying used camping gear and tents: what to check
description: How to buy a used tent and camping gear on Marktplaats: pitching it first, mould and coating checks, sleeping bags, stoves and fair prices.
intro: Camping gear is a great used buy because most of it gets used a few weekends a year. The big risk with tents is mould and a peeling waterproof coating, which you only see when the tent is pitched or unrolled. Ask to see it up, smell it, and count the poles and pegs.

sections.heading: Tents: what you will find
paragraphs: The Dutch market is full of family tents: Outwell, Vango, Coleman, Easy Camp and Kampa tunnel tents, plus the classic Dutch bungalow tents from De Waard and Obelink-type cotton models. Inflatable tents with air beams (Vango AirBeam, Outwell Air, Kampa Air) are popular because they go up fast. For hiking, look for MSR, Big Agnes, Nordisk, Vaude and Hilleberg; the last holds its value very well.
Decathlon's Quechua pop-up tents (2 Seconds) are cheap new and used. Fine for a festival, but they do not fold down small and are a pain to carry far.

sections.heading: Pitch it before you pay
paragraphs: Most problems hide in the folds. Ask the seller to pitch it in the garden, or pitch it together at the pickup if there is space. For a big family tent this takes 20-40 minutes, so plan for it. If the seller refuses and the price is not very low, be careful.
bullets: Smell it. A sour, musty smell means mould from being packed away wet.
Look for black spots on the inner tent and in the seams.
Rub the inside of the flysheet. A sticky or flaking coating, sometimes smelling of vinegar, means the waterproofing is breaking down.
Check seam tape is not peeling.
Open and close every zip, including the doors and windows.
Count the poles and look for cracked sections and bent ferrules.
On air tents, check the beams hold pressure for the whole visit and the valves seal.
Ask for the original bag, pegs, guy lines and the pitching instructions.

sections.heading: Cotton and polycotton tents
paragraphs: Cotton bungalow tents and polycotton bell tents breathe well and stay cool, but they rot if stored damp. Look for small brown or black spots and weak fabric around them. A small spot can be treated; a large area means the canvas will tear. Cotton tents also need to get wet once to swell the weave, so a few drips the first night are normal.

sections.heading: Sleeping bags, mats and stoves
paragraphs: A used down sleeping bag is worth checking for loft: shake it out and see if it puffs back up evenly. Flat, clumped areas mean the down needs washing or is worn. Synthetic bags lose warmth over the years and are cheap new, so only buy them used if they look fresh. Self-inflating mats and air mats should be left inflated for a while to check for slow leaks.

Gas stoves (Campingaz, Primus, MSR) are good used buys. Check that the burner lights and burns evenly blue, that the valve closes fully, and that it uses a cartridge type you can find at a Dutch camping shop. Skip stoves with rusted connections.

sections.heading: Chairs, tables and cool boxes
paragraphs: Folding chairs and tables are cheap to buy used, but sit in every chair and lean back: aluminium frames bend at the joints and fabric seats split along the seams. Electric cool boxes (koelboxen) that run on 12 V and 230 V should be plugged in at the pickup and should feel cold inside within ten to fifteen minutes. Compressor cool boxes from Dometic or Mobicool are worth more than the thermo-electric type.

sections.heading: Bundles and timing
paragraphs: Families who stop camping often sell everything at once: tent, chairs, table, cool box, lamps. These bundles can be very cheap but come with things you do not need. Prices are lowest from September to February, highest just before the May holidays and the summer. With vindje.com you can ask for an air tent for 4 to 6 people that has been pitched for photos and has no mould, and listings for spare poles or awnings drop away.

price_guide.item: Outwell or Vango polyester family tunnel tent

faq.q: How can I tell if a used tent is mouldy?
faq.a: Smell it and look for black or brown spots on the inner tent and seams. Ask to see it pitched, since mould hides in the folds.

faq.q: Can you fix a sticky tent coating?
faq.a: Not well. Once a PU coating starts to peel or go sticky, the waterproofing is failing and it will get worse.

faq.q: When is the best time to buy a used tent?
faq.a: Autumn and winter, when people clear out storage. Prices rise in spring before the holidays.

faq.q: Are air tents reliable second hand?
faq.a: Usually yes, if the beams hold pressure. Spare air beams are sold for most brands, which helps if one fails.

example_wish: Inflatable family tent for 4 to 6 people, Vango or Outwell, no mould, pitched in the photos, under 400 euro, within 40 km

title: Buying used skis, boots and snowboards
meta_title: Buying used skis, ski boots and snowboards
description: How to buy used skis, ski boots and snowboards on Marktplaats: what fits, binding checks, base and edge damage, and fair second-hand prices.
intro: Used skis and snowboards are a good deal for the one or two trips a year most Dutch skiers make. Boots are the tricky part: they need to fit your feet, so try them on or consider buying them new. Have any used binding checked and adjusted by a shop before you hit the slopes.

sections.heading: Skis: length and type
paragraphs: For most recreational skiers, a ski roughly between chin and nose height works. Shorter is easier to turn, longer is more stable at speed. Look at the model year: skis from the last five to eight seasons are still modern in shape. Older straight skis from the 1990s are not worth having at any price.

Most skiers from the Netherlands want on-piste or all-mountain skis. Brands you will see: Atomic, Salomon, Rossignol, Head, Fischer, Volkl, Elan, Blizzard and K2. A ski sold with integrated bindings (system ski) is normal for this category.

sections.heading: Checking bases, edges and the top
bullets: Turn the ski over. Scratches are normal; deep gouges to the core (core shots) need a repair.
Run a fingernail along the steel edges. Rust is fixable; cracked or missing edge sections are not.
Hold the skis base to base. They should touch at tip and tail with a gap in the middle (camber), unless they are rocker models.
Look for delamination: layers separating at the tip, tail or along the sides.
On snowboards, check the same, plus the inserts where the bindings screw in.

sections.heading: Bindings need a shop
paragraphs: The binding is what releases your boot in a fall. Its release setting (DIN) depends on your weight, height, age, skiing level and boot sole length, so it must be set for you. Take used skis to a ski shop for a binding check and setting, and ask them to wax and sharpen them at the same time, which usually costs in the range of EUR 30-60. Some shops will not work on very old bindings that are no longer on the manufacturer's list, so check the binding model if the skis are more than ten years old.

sections.heading: Boots: try before you buy
paragraphs: Ski boots are sized in mondopoint, the length of your foot in centimetres (for example 26.5). Try them on with ski socks. Your toes should just touch the front when standing straight and pull back slightly when you bend your knees. A liner that has packed out from years of use feels roomy in the shop and loose on the slope.

Check the plastic shell for cracks around the buckles, that all buckles close and hold, and the soles are not worn down so far that the binding cannot grip. If you ski every year, new boots fitted by a shop combined with used skis is the best value.

sections.heading: Kids gear and helmets
paragraphs: Children outgrow skis and boots every season or two, which makes used kids sets the best deal in this category. Many Dutch families sell a complete set (skis, boots, poles) for less than a week's rental. Check the binding adjusts to the next boot size.
Helmets are different: a helmet that took a hard knock may be damaged inside. Only buy a used helmet from someone you trust, and check the production date inside.

sections.heading: Snowboards in a little more detail
paragraphs: Board length depends mostly on your weight and riding style; a board that reaches between your chin and nose is a common starting point. Check that the bindings match your boot size and that the straps and ratchets are not cracked. Burton, Nitro, Salomon, Jones and Rome boards are common. A twin shape suits park riding and riding switch; a directional board suits carving on piste.

sections.heading: Timing and search
paragraphs: Buy in spring, after the season, when people clear the attic. Prices go up from October. On vindje.com you can describe length, boot size and level at once, like all-mountain skis of 160-170 cm under 150 euro, and skip listings for loose poles and clothing.

price_guide.item: Adult skis with bindings, 3-6 seasons old

faq.q: Is it worth buying second-hand skis?
faq.a: Yes, if they are less than about eight seasons old and the bases and edges are intact. Have a shop check and set the bindings.

faq.q: Should I buy used ski boots?
faq.a: Only if they fit well when you try them on with ski socks. Boots that are too big or packed out make skiing harder and less safe.

faq.q: What length skis do I need?
faq.a: Roughly between chin and nose height for most recreational skiers. Beginners can go a bit shorter.

faq.q: Can I adjust ski bindings myself?
faq.a: It is safer to have a ski shop set them, since the release setting depends on your weight, height, level and boot.

example_wish: All-mountain skis of 160 to 170 cm with bindings, not older than 6 seasons, no core shots, under 180 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying used golf clubs
meta_title: Buying used golf clubs: sets, drivers and fakes
description: How to buy used golf clubs on Marktplaats: beginner sets, shaft flex, grips, cracked drivers, fake putters and fair second-hand prices in the Netherlands.
intro: Golf clubs lose value fast in the first two years, which makes slightly older models excellent used buys. Beginners can get a complete set with a bag for less than one new driver. Check the shaft flex and grips, look for cracks in metal woods, and be careful with designer putters at low prices.

sections.heading: Start with a half set
paragraphs: If you are new to golf or taking a GVB course (the Dutch golf proficiency certificate), you do not need 14 clubs. A half set with a driver or fairway wood, a hybrid, a few irons (7, 9, PW), a sand wedge and a putter is enough. Complete beginner sets from Wilson, Callaway Strata, Ben Sayers and US Kids (for children) come up often with a bag.

sections.heading: Shaft flex, length and hand
paragraphs: Shafts come in flexes: L (ladies), A or senior, R (regular), S (stiff) and X (extra stiff). Most recreational golfers use regular; faster swingers use stiff. The flex is printed on the shaft or a sticker near the grip. Steel shafts are common in irons; graphite is lighter and often found in senior and ladies sets.

Left-handed sets (linkshandig) are less common, which means fewer choices but also lower prices. Players taller than about 1.90 m may need longer shafts; ask the seller if the clubs are standard length.

sections.heading: What to check
bullets: Grips: shiny, hard or cracked grips need replacing, roughly EUR 8-15 per club including fitting.
Driver and fairway woods: check the face and crown for cracks or dents. A cracked face is unplayable.
Rattle: shake the woods. A rattle can be loose glue inside the head.
Shafts: look for dents and bends in steel and splinters or cracks in graphite.
Iron faces: worn grooves and rust spots are mostly cosmetic for a beginner.
Headcovers and the adjustment tool for adjustable drivers.
Check all clubs in an iron set are the same model and shaft.

sections.heading: Models that are good value
paragraphs: Game-improvement irons that are three to six years old are the sweet spot: Ping G410 and G425, TaylorMade SIM2 Max and Stealth, Callaway Mavrik and Rogue ST, Titleist T300 and Mizuno JPX 921 and 923 Hot Metal. They are forgiving and drop heavily in price after newer models arrive. Blades and forged player irons look nice but are harder to hit for beginners.

sections.heading: Fakes
paragraphs: Counterfeit golf clubs exist, especially Scotty Cameron putters, TaylorMade and Callaway drivers and complete 'Titleist' sets at low prices. Signs: poor paint fill, wrong fonts, cheap-looking grips, no serial number on the hosel of drivers, and a seller who has several identical items. Genuine Scotty Camerons have a serial number and are rarely cheap. If a full premium set costs under EUR 200, assume it is a copy.

sections.heading: Bags, trolleys and extras
paragraphs: A stand bag is handy on a short course; a cart bag fits on a trolley for longer rounds. Check the zips, the stand legs and the shoulder straps. Push trolleys from Clicgear, Big Max and Motocaddy are often sold cheap; fold and unfold them and spin the wheels. Electric trolleys need a test with the battery: lithium batteries that are several years old may only last nine holes.
Golf shoes and gloves are usually better bought new, but rangefinders (Bushnell, Nikon) are a good used buy if the display is clear.

sections.heading: Try a swing
paragraphs: Ask to take a few swings in the garden, or bring the clubs to a driving range before paying if the seller agrees. For irons in a specific flex and hand, such as regular steel shafts for a left-hander within 30 km, vindje.com can read the listing details so you do not have to open every ad.

price_guide.item: Iron set 5-PW, 3-6 years old (Ping, TaylorMade, Callaway)

faq.q: Are used golf clubs worth buying?
faq.a: Yes. Clubs lose a lot of value after a new model comes out, so a three to six year old set is cheap and plays nearly as well.

faq.q: Which shaft flex do I need?
faq.a: Most beginners and recreational players use regular flex. Ask a pro or try both at a driving range if unsure.

faq.q: How do I spot fake golf clubs?
faq.a: Look for poor paint, wrong logos, missing serial numbers and prices far below normal for the model.

faq.q: How much does it cost to regrip golf clubs?
faq.a: Roughly EUR 8-15 per club including fitting at a golf shop, depending on the grip.

example_wish: Ping G425 or TaylorMade Stealth iron set 5 to PW, regular steel shafts, right-handed, good grips, under 450 euro

title: Buying used dumbbells, plates and racks
meta_title: Buying used dumbbells, weight plates and racks
description: How to buy used dumbbells, weight plates, barbells and racks on Marktplaats: price per kilo, 30 mm or 50 mm plates, checking welds and fair prices.
intro: Weights barely wear out, so buying them used is one of the safest gym purchases. Think in price per kilo, make sure the plate hole fits your bar, and inspect racks for bent uprights and cracked welds. The biggest mistake is paying close to new prices for gear that is cheap to make.

sections.heading: Price per kilo
paragraphs: Weight plates and fixed dumbbells are best compared per kilo. Cast iron plates usually go for about EUR 1-2.50 per kilo used, bumper plates (rubber, made for dropping) a bit more. Fixed rubber hex dumbbells sell somewhat higher per kilo than loose plates. Prices go up sharply each January and when gyms are closed; they fall again in summer.
Ask the seller for the total weight and a photo of each plate's marking. Cheap vinyl plates filled with sand or cement often weigh less than stated and are bulky for their weight.

sections.heading: 30 mm or 50 mm
paragraphs: Plates and bars come in two main standards. Standard plates have a 30 mm hole (sometimes 25 or 28 mm) and fit cheaper home bars. Olympic plates have a 50 mm hole and fit the 2.2 m, 20 kg Olympic bar found in gyms. You can use adapters, but mixing systems is a nuisance. Choose one, and check every plate in a lot matches it.

sections.heading: Bars
paragraphs: An Olympic barbell should spin freely at the sleeves and be straight. Roll it on a flat floor and watch the middle: a bent bar wobbles. Look for rust on the knurling (light rust can be brushed off) and check the sleeves do not have play. Cheap 'Olympic' bars rated for 150 kg are fine for most home lifters; if you lift heavy, look for brands like Rogue, Eleiko, Gymstick Pro or Lifemaxx with a stated load rating.

sections.heading: Adjustable dumbbells
paragraphs: Bowflex SelectTech 552 and 1090, PowerBlock and Core Fitness adjustable dumbbells save a lot of space. Test the selector on every setting: dial or pin it, lift the dumbbell and make sure no plates stay behind or rattle loose. The plastic parts of selector systems can crack after drops, which is the main failure. Missing plates in a PowerBlock set are hard to replace.

sections.heading: Racks and benches
bullets: Uprights should be straight; sight down them from above.
Check every weld, especially at the base and the J-hooks. No cracks or rust holes.
Ask for the safety arms or spotter bars. A rack without them is far less useful.
Check the hole pattern fits accessories you want to add.
On benches, test the adjustments lock firmly and the padding is not torn.
Ask for all bolts and the manual, and photos of it assembled.

sections.heading: Transport
paragraphs: Weights are heavy in a small space. A car can carry 150-200 kg of plates if loaded over the rear axle, but check your car's payload. Bring a sturdy bag or crate and gloves. Racks come apart into long pieces, so you may need a van.
If you are building a home gym piece by piece, vindje.com can look for Olympic 50 mm plates within 20 km under 2 euro per kilo and drop the 30 mm sets and vinyl plates from the results.

sections.heading: Flooring, and what to skip
paragraphs: Set aside part of the budget for rubber floor tiles. Gyms and CrossFit boxes that close or renovate often sell 1x1 m rubber tiles of 15-20 mm thick for a few euros each, and they protect both your floor and your plates. Upstairs apartments with wooden floors need thick tiles and a bit of consideration for the neighbours.

Plastic sand-filled plates, rusty bars that wobble, racks without a brand or load rating and Smith machines with stiff guides are not worth carrying home. A cheap power rack from a well-known brand is a better buy than a rare multi-station machine.

faq.q: How much should I pay for used weights?
faq.a: Around EUR 1-2.50 per kilo for cast iron plates, a bit more for bumper plates and rubber hex dumbbells.

faq.q: What is the difference between 30 mm and 50 mm plates?
faq.a: It is the size of the hole. 50 mm plates fit Olympic bars; 30 mm plates fit standard home bars. They do not mix without adapters.

faq.q: Are used adjustable dumbbells reliable?
faq.a: Usually, if the selector works on every setting and no plates are missing. Test each weight before paying.

faq.q: How do I check if a barbell is bent?
faq.a: Roll it slowly on a flat floor and watch the centre. A wobble means it is bent.

example_wish: Olympic 50 mm iron weight plates, at least 80 kg in total, under 2 euro per kilo, within 20 km

title: Buying used padel and tennis rackets
meta_title: Buying used padel and tennis rackets: checks and fakes
description: How to buy a used padel or tennis racket on Marktplaats: spotting cracks and fakes, grip sizes, string checks, and fair second-hand prices.
intro: Padel has boomed in the Netherlands, and many players sell rackets after one season, so used ones are easy to find. Check for cracks in the frame, a worn surface and whether it is a fake, which is common with popular padel models. For tennis rackets, the grip size and a fresh string job matter most.

sections.heading: Padel rackets: shape and material
paragraphs: Padel rackets come in three shapes. Round shapes are easiest to control and suit beginners. Teardrop is a balance of control and power. Diamond shapes put weight in the head for power and suit experienced players. Beginners often buy a diamond racket because a pro uses it, then sell it after a few months, which is why so many lightly used top models show up.

Faces are made of fibreglass (softer, more forgiving) or carbon (stiffer, more power). The core is soft or hard EVA or foam. Common brands: Bullpadel, Adidas, Head, Babolat, Nox, Siux, Starvie, Wilson and Decathlon's Kuikma.

sections.heading: Checks for a padel racket
bullets: Look along the frame edge for cracks, especially at the top where it hits the wall and floor.
Press the face with your thumb in several spots. Soft or crunchy areas mean the core has broken down.
Run your hand over the face. Rough-surface rackets lose grip as the texture wears smooth.
Check the protector tape on the frame: under heavy scuffs there may be cracks.
Shake it and listen for loose bits inside.
Look at the grip and the strap. Both are cheap to replace.

sections.heading: Fake padel rackets
paragraphs: Copies of the Bullpadel Vertex, Adidas Metalbone and Nox AT10 models are widely sold online and turn up on Marktplaats. They often weigh differently, have sloppy graphics or no serial or hologram sticker, and feel dead on the ball. Look up the official product photos and compare details like the holes pattern, the bridge and the text on the frame. A current flagship at well below half the shop price, with no receipt and 'new in plastic', deserves suspicion.

sections.heading: Tennis rackets: grip and strings
paragraphs: European grip sizes go from L0 to L5; most adults use L2 or L3 (equal to 4 1/4 and 4 3/8 inches). Hold the racket in your normal grip: there should be room for a finger between your fingertips and palm. A grip that is too small can be built up with an overgrip; too large cannot be fixed easily.

Look for cracks at the throat and the top of the frame, broken grommets (the plastic strips the strings pass through), and the age of the strings. A restring costs about EUR 20-35 depending on string choice, so add that to the price if the strings are dead or broken.

sections.heading: Weight and balance
paragraphs: Padel rackets weigh between roughly 340 and 380 grams. Lighter rackets are easier on the arm and suit beginners and players with elbow problems; heavier ones give more power. Ask the seller to weigh it on a kitchen scale, which is also a quick check against fakes, since copies are often outside the official weight range. For tennis, the weight is usually printed on the frame as strung or unstrung.

sections.heading: Which models are good used buys
paragraphs: Tennis frames change little between generations. A Babolat Pure Drive, Wilson Blade or Clash, Head Speed or Yonex Ezone from two or three years ago plays almost the same as the current version at half the price. For padel, mid-range models from last season, like the Bullpadel Vertex or Hack in earlier versions or the Head Delta, are good value. On vindje.com you can ask for a round or teardrop padel racket for a beginner, genuine brand, under 70 euro, and it will skip the listings for covers and balls.

price_guide.item: Beginner padel racket (Kuikma, Head, Adidas entry)
Top padel model, 1 season old (Bullpadel Vertex, Metalbone)
Recent tennis racket (Pure Drive, Blade, Speed)

faq.q: How long does a padel racket last?
faq.a: For someone playing a couple of times a week, about one or two seasons before the core softens and the surface wears. Casual players can use one for years.

faq.q: How do I know if a padel racket is fake?
faq.a: Compare the graphics, weight and serial or hologram sticker with official photos. Fakes often have sloppy prints and are priced far below the going rate.

faq.q: What grip size tennis racket do I need?
faq.a: Most adults use L2 or L3. You should be able to fit one finger between your fingertips and palm when holding it.

faq.q: Should I restring a used tennis racket?
faq.a: If you do not know when it was last strung, yes. Old strings lose tension and feel dead.

example_wish: Bullpadel or Adidas padel racket, round or teardrop shape, no cracks, genuine, under 80 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used piano or digital piano
meta_title: Buying a used piano or digital piano: what to check
description: How to buy a used acoustic or digital piano on Marktplaats: free pianos and moving costs, tuning checks, Yamaha and Roland models, and fair prices.
intro: Acoustic pianos are often given away for free in the Netherlands, but moving and tuning one costs several hundred euros, and a bad piano is a burden. For most beginners and apartment dwellers, a used digital piano with 88 weighted keys is the better buy. If you want an acoustic, focus on the condition of the inside, not the cabinet.

sections.heading: Free pianos and the hidden costs
paragraphs: Search 'gratis piano' and you will find plenty. The catch: a professional piano mover typically charges a few hundred euros, more with stairs or a hoist through the window, and the piano will need tuning after the move. A piano that has not been tuned for years may need several tunings to settle, and some will not hold pitch at all.
Before you say yes, ask the brand, the serial number (inside, usually on the iron frame) and when it was last tuned. The serial number tells you the year of production.

sections.heading: Checking an acoustic piano
bullets: Play every key, soft and loud. Listen for keys that stick, do not repeat quickly or make no sound.
Play octaves across the range. Badly out of tune is common; wildly different pitch between notes can mean loose tuning pins.
Open the lid and look at the hammers. Deep grooves in the felt mean wear.
Look for cracks in the soundboard (the large wooden panel at the back) and the bridges.
Check for moth damage in the felts and signs of woodworm in the case.
Press all pedals and listen for squeaks or thumps.
Ask where it stood. Next to a radiator or in a damp room is bad for the wood.

sections.heading: Which acoustic pianos are worth it
paragraphs: Yamaha uprights (U1, U3, and the smaller b and P series) and Kawai models are reliable and keep their value. German brands like Schimmel, Seiler, Grotrian and Bechstein are well regarded. Many free pianos are old cabinet pianos from the 1960s and 70s from lesser-known makers: some are fine, many are tired. If you are paying more than a few hundred euros, a piano technician's inspection is money well spent.
Grand pianos (vleugels) need a lot of space and a careful move. Only consider one with a technician's opinion.

sections.heading: Digital pianos
paragraphs: Digital pianos have no tuning cost, a volume knob and a headphone socket, which matters with neighbours. Good used options: Yamaha P-45, P-125 and P-145, Roland FP-10 and FP-30X, Kawai ES110 and ES120 for portable models; Yamaha Clavinova CLP and Arius, Roland HP and Kawai CA for cabinet models. Look for 88 keys with weighted or hammer action; 61-key keyboards are fine for a start but not for learning piano properly.

Test every key at soft and hard velocity, all pedals, both headphone outputs and the speakers at high volume for rattles or crackling. Ask for the power adapter and the sustain pedal; the cheap square pedal that comes with portable models is worth upgrading.

sections.heading: Moving a digital piano
paragraphs: Portable models weigh 11-20 kg and fit on a back seat. Cabinet models like a Clavinova weigh 40-70 kg and usually need to be taken apart (stand, pedal unit, keyboard) to move, so ask the seller to help and photograph the cables before disconnecting. If you want a weighted 88-key digital piano with a stand and three pedals that you can collect by car, vindje.com can filter out the 61-key keyboards and accessories in a plain search.

sections.heading: Price expectations
paragraphs: Digital pianos lose value steadily, so a five-year-old model sells for well under half its new price. Good acoustic uprights hold their value much better, and a Yamaha U1 in good condition rarely goes cheap. Old upright pianos without a known brand are often worth nothing more than the cost of moving them.

price_guide.item: Portable digital piano (Yamaha P-125, Roland FP-30X)
Yamaha Clavinova CLP or Arius, 2-6 years old

faq.q: Is a free piano worth taking?
faq.a: Only if it plays evenly and holds a tuning. Moving and tuning cost a few hundred euros, so check it carefully first.

faq.q: How much does it cost to tune a piano in the Netherlands?
faq.a: Usually around EUR 100-150 per tuning, more if it needs extra work after years without tuning.

faq.q: Digital or acoustic piano for a beginner?
faq.a: A digital piano with 88 weighted keys suits most beginners: no tuning, quiet practice with headphones and easier to move.

faq.q: How old is my piano?
faq.a: Find the serial number on the iron frame or soundboard and look it up for the brand. Yamaha and Kawai publish lists by year.

example_wish: Digital piano with 88 weighted keys, Yamaha or Roland, with stand and three pedals, under 600 euro, within 25 km

title: Buying a used guitar: acoustic and electric
meta_title: Buying a used guitar: acoustic and electric checks
description: How to buy a used acoustic or electric guitar on Marktplaats: neck, frets and action checks, fake Gibsons, good beginner models and fair prices.
intro: Guitars are one of the best used buys: they do not wear out quickly, and most problems are cheap to fix with a setup. Check the neck, frets and electronics, play it for a few minutes, and be careful with big-brand guitars at low prices, since fake Gibsons and Fenders circulate.

sections.heading: Acoustic, classical or electric
paragraphs: Classical guitars (klassieke gitaar) have nylon strings and a wide neck, and are what Dutch music schools often use for children. Steel-string acoustic guitars (westerngitaar) are louder and suit singing along. Electric guitars need an amplifier but have thinner necks and lighter strings, which many beginners find easier.
Children need a smaller size: 1/2 for around 5-8 years old, 3/4 for around 8-11. Many used kids guitars come from music school pupils who moved up a size.

sections.heading: Checking the neck and frets
bullets: Look down the neck from the headstock like a rifle. A slight forward bow is normal; a twist or a big bow is not.
Play every fret on every string. Buzzing or dead notes can mean uneven frets or a setup issue.
Look at the frets under the first five positions. Deep grooves mean a fret job, which costs a lot.
Check the action: the string height at the 12th fret. High action makes playing hard.
Turn every tuner. They should move smoothly and hold pitch.
Ask if the truss rod adjusts. A seller who does not know is fine; one who says it is stuck is not.

sections.heading: Acoustic guitars: the body
paragraphs: Look at the bridge: if its back edge lifts from the top (you can slide a piece of paper under it), it needs regluing. Check the top behind the bridge for bulging, and look for cracks in the top and sides, especially near the soundhole and the edges. A small repaired crack is fine; an open one that grows in dry winter air is not. Dutch homes with central heating dry guitars out, so ask whether it was kept in a case.

sections.heading: Electric guitars: electronics
paragraphs: Bring a small amp or headphones amp, or ask the seller to have one ready. Play through every pickup position, turn all knobs and listen for crackle. Wiggle the cable in the jack; a cutting-out signal means a loose jack. Scratchy pots are cheap to clean or replace, but count it in your offer.

sections.heading: Fakes and parts guitars
paragraphs: Counterfeit Gibson Les Pauls and Fender Stratocasters from China are sold for a few hundred euros and resold as genuine. Warning signs: a Gibson with a bolt-on neck, a truss rod cover with the wrong shape, poor inlays, a serial number that does not match the model year, and a very low price. Also watch for 'partscasters': guitars built from mixed parts with a Fender logo decal. They can be good instruments, but should be priced as what they are.
If the price is far below the usual range, ask for the serial number and check it with the brand's own decoder before travelling.

sections.heading: Good used models
paragraphs: For beginners: Yamaha Pacifica and the Yamaha F310 or FG800 acoustic, Squier Classic Vibe and Affinity, Epiphone Les Paul and SG, Harley Benton (Thomann's brand, very common in the Netherlands) and Ibanez. Mid-range: Fender Player series (made in Mexico), PRS SE, Gretsch Electromatic. Yamaha classical guitars like the C40 and C70 are the standard student choice. On vindje.com you can ask for something like a Squier Classic Vibe Telecaster or Fender Player in sunburst with a gig bag within 30 km, and it will skip the many listings for straps, cases and amps.

price_guide.item: Yamaha C40 or similar classical student guitar
Squier Classic Vibe Strat or Tele

faq.q: What should I check when buying a used guitar?
faq.a: Neck straightness, fret wear, string height, tuners, cracks in the body and, on electrics, crackle in knobs and the jack.

faq.q: How do I know if a Gibson is fake?
faq.a: Check the serial number against the model year, look for a glued-in neck (not bolt-on), the correct headstock shape and the quality of inlays.

faq.q: What size guitar does my child need?
faq.a: Roughly 1/2 for ages 5-8, 3/4 for ages 8-11, and full size from about 11-12. Height matters more than age.

faq.q: What does a guitar setup cost?
faq.a: A basic setup at a Dutch guitar shop usually costs around EUR 40-80, plus strings. It fixes most high action and buzz issues.

example_wish: Squier Classic Vibe or Fender Player Telecaster, sunburst, no neck issues, with gig bag, under 450 euro, within 30 km

title: Buying a used sewing machine
meta_title: Buying a used sewing machine: brands and checks
description: How to buy a used sewing machine or overlock (lockmachine) on Marktplaats: Bernina, Pfaff, Janome and Singer, what to test and fair prices.
intro: A good older sewing machine from Bernina, Pfaff or Janome often sews better than a new budget machine, and they turn up on Marktplaats all the time. Always test it on fabric before you pay, make sure the foot pedal and bobbin case are included, and avoid modern plastic machines that are not worth repairing.

sections.heading: Older is often better
paragraphs: Mechanical machines from the 1970s to 1990s with metal internals are prized: Bernina Record 730 and the 1000 series (1008, 1010, 1020), Pfaff 1200-series with the built-in walking foot (IDT), Elna Supermatic and many Janome and Husqvarna Viking models. They handle thick fabric like denim well and can be serviced for decades.
Cheap new machines from discount stores are mostly plastic inside. A used one of those is only a bargain if it is almost free and works perfectly.

sections.heading: What to bring and test
paragraphs: Bring a few scraps of fabric (thin cotton and something thick like denim), a spare needle and thread in a contrasting colour.
bullets: Plug it in and run the motor slowly and fast with the pedal. It should start smoothly, not hum and stall.
Turn the handwheel by hand. It should turn freely without clunks.
Sew straight stitch and zigzag on both fabrics. The stitches should look the same top and bottom.
Check the stitch length and width controls change the stitch.
Try reverse sewing and the buttonhole function if it has one.
Check that the bobbin case, bobbins and presser feet are present.
Look under the needle plate for rust and packed lint.

sections.heading: Reading the stitches
paragraphs: Loops on the underside usually mean the top thread is not threaded correctly or the tension is off, which is easy to fix. Skipped stitches can be a bent needle or the wrong needle type. But if the machine keeps skipping with a new needle and correct threading, the timing may be off, which needs a repair shop. Ask whether the machine was recently serviced (onderhoudsbeurt); a service at a Dutch sewing machine shop often costs in the range of EUR 60-100.

sections.heading: Overlockers and embroidery machines
paragraphs: An overlocker (lockmachine) finishes edges like on bought clothes and is popular for sewing stretch fabrics. Brother, Janome, Juki and Bernina overlockers are common used. Threading one is fiddly, so ask the seller to leave it threaded and test it on knit fabric. Check the knife cuts cleanly.

Computerised and embroidery machines can be great but are expensive to repair if the board fails. Only buy one if every function works in front of you and the seller can show the embroidery unit and its cables.

sections.heading: Old Singers and cabinet machines
paragraphs: Antique Singer treadle machines in iron stands are everywhere. Many still sew, but they only do straight stitch and are mostly bought as decoration. If you want one to use, check the treadle belt, the bobbin shuttle (these are specific to the model) and that the machine head turns freely. Cabinet machines built into a table are heavy, so check the machine lifts out if you only want the machine itself.

sections.heading: Manuals, feet and accessories
paragraphs: A machine without its manual is still fine: most Bernina, Pfaff and Janome manuals can be found online as PDF by model number. Presser feet are another matter. Bernina feet from the old system do not fit the newer ones, and some Pfaff feet are model specific, so a box of extra feet adds value. Ask for the zipper foot and the buttonhole foot at least, and check the original hard cover or carry case is there if you plan to take the machine to a sewing class.

sections.heading: Searching
paragraphs: Sellers often write vague titles like 'oude naaimachine werkt nog'. On vindje.com you can ask for a mechanical Bernina or Pfaff with a foot pedal that sews thick fabric, under 250 euro, and the AI reads past the titles to the descriptions.

price_guide.item: Basic Singer, Brother or Toyota machine, working

faq.q: Which used sewing machine brand is best?
faq.a: Older mechanical Bernina, Pfaff and Janome machines have a strong reputation and are worth repairing. Cheap plastic machines usually are not.

faq.q: How do I test a used sewing machine?
faq.a: Sew straight and zigzag stitches on thin and thick fabric, check both sides of the seam and run the motor at different speeds.

faq.q: Is an old Singer sewing machine worth anything?
faq.a: Most antique Singers sell for EUR 20-120 and are bought for decoration. Working ones in good condition fetch more.

faq.q: What is a lockmachine?
faq.a: It is the Dutch word for an overlocker or serger, a machine that trims and finishes fabric edges with several threads.

example_wish: Mechanical Bernina or Pfaff sewing machine with foot pedal and bobbin case, sews denim, under 250 euro, within 20 km

title: Buying used power tools: brands, batteries, theft
meta_title: Buying used power tools: batteries, brands and theft
description: How to buy used power tools on Marktplaats: picking a battery platform, checking battery health, body-only listings, and spotting stolen tools.
