intro: Used power tools from the big brands are good value, but the battery is half the price and the part most likely to be worn. Pick one battery platform and stick to it, test every tool under load, and be alert for stolen tools: very low prices on professional gear are a warning sign.

sections.heading: Choose a battery platform first
paragraphs: Cordless tools only take batteries from their own system. The common 18 V platforms are Makita LXT, DeWalt XR, Milwaukee M18, Bosch Professional (blue) and Bosch Home and Garden (green, a different 18 V system that does not share batteries with blue), Metabo CAS, Festool, Hikoki and Ryobi ONE+. Once you own a few batteries, buying the tool without battery (losse body, zonder accu) is much cheaper.

For DIY, Ryobi, Bosch green and Einhell Power X-Change are affordable with a huge tool range. For heavier use, Makita, DeWalt and Milwaukee are everywhere on Marktplaats, which keeps used prices reasonable.

sections.heading: Batteries and chargers
bullets: Ask for the capacity (Ah) and roughly how old the batteries are.
Charge level indicators show charge, not health. Ask the seller to charge them fully before you arrive.
Use the tool hard for a minute: a tired battery drops off quickly or cuts out under load.
Look for swollen, cracked or very hot batteries. Do not buy those.
Check the charger works and fits the battery type.
Be wary of cheap copy batteries sold as originals. Compare the label and weight with the official one.

sections.heading: Testing the tool
paragraphs: Bring something to drill into or cut, like a bit of scrap wood. Run the tool at low and high speed. Listen for grinding or rattling gears, smell for burnt windings, and check the chuck holds a bit without wobble. On drills, test the clutch settings and the hammer mode. On saws, check the blade guard springs back and the base plate is not bent. On corded tools, look at the cable for cuts and taped repairs.

sections.heading: Stolen tools
paragraphs: Tool theft from vans and building sites is common in the Netherlands, and stolen tools get resold online. Warning signs: a lot of professional tools at well below market price, multiple identical items from one seller, engraved names or company codes that have been ground off, no batteries or cases, a seller who wants to meet at a street corner rather than at home, and a seller who cannot tell you anything about the tool.

Ask for the receipt or at least where it was bought. The Dutch police have a Stop Heling service where you can check a serial number against reported stolen goods. In the Netherlands, buying goods you should reasonably have suspected were stolen is itself an offence (schuldheling), and a stolen tool can be taken back without a refund.

sections.heading: Festool, track saws and higher-end tools
paragraphs: Festool holds its value well, and kits come in Systainer cases. Check that every accessory listed is in the Systainer and that the serial number plate is present. Track saws (Festool TS 55, Makita SP6000 and DSP600, Bosch GKT) need a straight rail without dents; sight along it. Domino joiners are among the most stolen items, so ask extra questions.

sections.heading: Corded tools and old classics
paragraphs: Corded tools are often the better used buy for jobs you do once a year. A corded Bosch or Makita hammer drill, angle grinder or jigsaw from ten years ago has no battery to wear out and usually costs less than EUR 50. For SDS-plus hammer drills, which you need for drilling into Dutch concrete walls, a corded model from Bosch, Makita or Hilti is a classic Marktplaats find. Check the brushes are not sparking heavily through the vents.

sections.heading: Searching smart
paragraphs: Listing titles mix bodies, kits and loose batteries. On vindje.com you can ask for a Makita 18 V impact driver body only, in good condition, within 15 km, and it will read the descriptions to drop listings with batteries you do not need or broken tools sold for parts.

price_guide.item: Makita or DeWalt 18 V drill or impact driver, body only
18 V drill kit with 2 batteries and charger
Festool TS 55 track saw with rail
Bosch green or Ryobi drill kit

faq.q: How can I tell if a power tool is stolen?
faq.a: Watch for very low prices, many identical tools, removed engravings and a seller who knows nothing about the tool. Ask for a receipt and check the serial number with the police's Stop Heling service.

faq.q: How do I check a used tool battery?
faq.a: Charge it fully, then use the tool under load. A worn battery loses power fast or cuts out. Skip any swollen battery.

faq.q: Are Bosch blue and green batteries compatible?
faq.a: No. Bosch Professional (blue) and Bosch Home and Garden (green) use different 18 V systems.

faq.q: What does losse body mean?
faq.a: It means the tool is sold without battery and charger, which is cheaper if you already own batteries for that brand.

example_wish: Makita 18V impact driver body only, no battery needed, works well, under 70 euro, within 15 km

title: Buying a used lawn mower or robot mower
meta_title: Buying a used lawn mower or robot mower: checks
description: How to buy a used lawn mower or robot mower on Marktplaats: petrol, battery and Husqvarna Automower checks, PIN locks, theft and fair prices.
intro: A used mower is a sensible buy for most Dutch gardens, but each type has its own trap: petrol mowers can hide engine problems, battery mowers can come with tired batteries, and robot mowers can be locked to the previous owner's account. Test it cutting grass and get the PIN and account release in writing.

sections.heading: Which type fits your garden
paragraphs: A small city garden of up to about 100 square metres can be done with a manual reel mower (kooimaaier) or a corded electric mower. For larger lawns, a battery mower from Bosch, Makita, Stihl or Greenworks is quiet and low maintenance. Petrol mowers from Honda, Stihl (Viking), Husqvarna and Sabo make sense for big gardens and long grass.
Robot mowers (robotmaaiers) are popular in the Netherlands. They take a few hours to install and work best on a lawn without many obstacles.

sections.heading: Checking a petrol mower
bullets: Ask the seller not to start it before you come. A cold start tells you more.
It should start within a few pulls and run steadily. Blue smoke means it burns oil.
Check the oil level and colour on the dipstick.
Look under the deck (with the spark plug lead removed) for rust holes and a bent or blunt blade.
On self-propelled models (zelfrijdend), test the drive on grass.
Engage the blade brake lever: the engine or blade should stop within a few seconds.
Ask about the last service and whether it was drained for winter.

sections.heading: Battery and electric mowers
paragraphs: For corded mowers, check the cable for cuts and the switch for a firm feel. For battery mowers, the battery is the expensive part. Ask how old it is, charge it fully and mow a strip of lawn for several minutes. If the runtime is short, a new battery may cost a large part of the price. Make sure the battery fits other tools you already own, which can make a body-only mower a good deal.

sections.heading: Robot mowers: the account and PIN
paragraphs: Husqvarna Automower, Gardena Sileno, Worx Landroid, Stihl iMow, Segway Navimow and Mammotion Luba are common. Most have an anti-theft PIN code and are linked to the owner's app account. A robot mower that is still linked or has an unknown PIN can be unusable, and stolen robot mowers are a known problem. Before paying, ask the seller to unlink it from their account and reset the PIN in front of you, and check that it starts with the new code.
Ask for the serial number and the original receipt. With Husqvarna and some others the serial can be checked with the dealer.

sections.heading: Robot mower checks
bullets: Ask for the charging station, the power supply and the remaining boundary wire and pegs.
Check the battery age and how long it mows on one charge.
Look at the blade disc and the wheels for wear; blades are cheap, motors are not.
Wire-free models like the Segway Navimow and Mammotion Luba need their RTK antenna included.
Ask how big the lawn was. A model rated for 500 square metres will struggle on 1500.

sections.heading: Scarifiers and trimmers
paragraphs: Garden owners often sell a mower together with a scarifier (verticuteermachine), hedge trimmer or grass trimmer. Scarifiers are used once or twice a year, so used ones are usually in good shape; check the blades or tines and the depth adjustment. Petrol trimmers and brushcutters are harder to judge: if it does not start within a few pulls when warm, walk away.

sections.heading: Timing and search
paragraphs: Prices drop in autumn, when people do not want to store a mower over winter, and rise in March and April. If you know what you want, such as a Husqvarna Automower for about 600 square metres with charging station and unlinked from the seller's app, describing it on vindje.com filters out listings for blades and boundary wire alone.

price_guide.item: Honda or Stihl self-propelled petrol mower

faq.q: Can I use a second-hand robot mower?
faq.a: Yes, if the seller has removed it from their app account and resets the PIN in front of you. Otherwise it may stay locked.

faq.q: How do I check a used petrol lawn mower?
faq.a: Start it cold, watch for smoke, check the oil, the blade and the deck for rust, and test the drive and blade brake.

faq.q: How long does a robot mower battery last?
faq.a: Often several years, depending on use. A worn battery shows as much shorter mowing time per charge.

faq.q: When is the best time to buy a used lawn mower?
faq.a: Autumn and winter, when demand is low. Prices go up in spring.

example_wish: Husqvarna Automower for about 600 m2 lawn with charging station and wire, unlinked from the app, under 600 euro, within 25 km
